In the tech industry, we might need something similar, especially if AI would take on handling of the simpler incidents.</span></p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>1. New trend of CPU shortages</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I was at dinner with a bunch of CTOs and Head of Infrastructure folks recently, and from the conversation it was clear that many companies are struggling to source CPUs in the current climate, and are coming to terms with the end of juicy discounts from cloud providers for machines in the new era of surging demand fueled by AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The ‘memory crisis’ afflicting sectors like video gaming is well established and has been extensively covered in terms of shortages of GPUs, but now it seems like things are just as hard for businesses in need of CPUs from cloud providers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a sign of how things are changing, the disappearance of CPU spot pricing was mentioned at the table. Customers used to be able to pay up to 90% less than the standard price for CPUs, as cloud providers slashed CPU prices for machines that were lying dormant and unused. But that’s no longer the case. It seems that spot pricing has vanished because there’s no longer any lack of demand for CPUs – quite the opposite.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I was surprised, but a lot of people chimed in; apparently, it’s now nearly impossible to get CPUs on spot instances without long-running connections with cloud providers. Also, reserving specific CPUs now needs to be done months in advance, and cloud providers will even turn down certain reservations because they don’t have enough CPUs or the right type of CPUs.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Even big players struggle to reserve CPUs</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I have asked turbopuffer CEO Simon Eskildsen about their experience of CPU availability in the cloud, since turbopuffer, as a product, runs on CPUs, not GPUs. They operate in AWS, GCP, and Azure, so I asked how easy it is to get CPUs these days. Simon’s response:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>Getting CPUs is not easy anymore. </span></strong><span>As Reinforcement Learning (RL) is becoming a large amount of the workloads: RL needs a lot of CPUs. So the labs are sucking up a lot of CPUs. During RL, they need to teach the models how to do things, like searching, and then they need the model to run software, which then takes CPUs to run.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Then, outside of RL, agents need to do all kinds of very general purpose things on a CPU. So as the demand curve is shifting to general purpose agents, CPU demand is also going up.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Even the big companies are fighting each other for the right to get the CPU allocations. </span></strong><span>I would assume that it gets a lot worse before it gets better on the CPU side.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I was able to confirm what Simon said about larger companies struggling; a VP of Engineering at a large inference provider told me they are at the limit on how much GPU and CPU capacity they can buy from their cloud providers. They have cash to spend and want to rent more capacity, and are willing to accept the longest leases. Despite that, cloud providers tell them no more is available!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>AI hogging CPUs</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn Lesse, Head of Platform Engineering for Claude Platform, has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce7ffe9e-e10d-46af-9b92-9ec123b7f8f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>written about</span></a><span> the reasons for the massive CPU demand increase:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“In the past few years, AI-fueled demand has skyrocketed, and these few companies suddenly needed multiple years and tens of billions of dollars to actually add enough capacity. We ended up with 3 separate bottlenecks in factory capacity that AI is exacerbating. At TSMC, GPUs are competing with CPUs (and with Apple, Qualcomm, and Broadcom) for production lines. And at SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron, HBM [High Bandwidth Memory] is competing with regular DRAM for wafers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What we’ve ended up with is CPUs getting squeezed from both sides. AMD doesn’t own fabs [semiconductor fabrication plants], so its CPUs need to come out of TSMC’s constrained allocation. Intel does own fabs, but it’s been working through yield problems and is now pulling some of its capacity from PC chips in order to make more server chips. And CPUs need DRAM which has gotten more expensive because memory production has shifted toward HBM. Analysts are expecting CPU supply to add more comfortable headroom before memory does, but their expectation is that it’s still going to be multiple quarters away.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI-fueled demand does increase CPU load, as shown in this graph from Uber, displaying the growth in agent requests over the past six months:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce86bafe-fb94-4a5b-b5e7-3a7cdd2b9071?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Ninefold increase in agentic requests over six months. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/399b9a25-afba-4758-935f-514b7cd5bcc6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Uber</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Increasingly, “agent requests” not only generate code which is inference-heavy – and therefore needs GPUs – but they also run tools that compile the code, run tests, run linters, and all of this is CPU-heavy. At companies like Uber, Ramp, and others, AI agents no longer run on the dev’s local machine, but on a dedicated instance in the cloud. So, the companies reserve more CPUs on their respective cloud providers for agentic workloads. </span><em><span>We recently covered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/da121b4c-8140-4e5e-984e-00a4312e2858?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>how Ramp built and runs its cloud agent, Inspect.</span></a></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Basically, the problem is:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>AI applications use more and more CPUs, </span></strong><span>thanks to agents running a lot more software. AI data centers used to have a ratio of 1 CPU to 8 GPUs. Now the ratio is more 1:4, and it could shrink to 1:1.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Companies that can manufacture more CPUs are busy on other hardware. </span></strong><span>TSMC is busy producing GPUs, which might be more profitable than CPUs. Meanwhile, CPUs also need DRAM, but DRAM manufacturers (SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron) are instead producing high-bandwidth memory (HBM) because it’s more profitable. This is why </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/10bb462f-a235-4156-88fd-bd1263e71876?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>memory prices are spiking</span></a><span>; even Big Tech is unable to buy RAM, as previously covered.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>To secure CPUs, it’s necessary to do capacity planning up to 12 months in advance. </span></strong><span>Katelyn says that server orders are being fulfilled in ~six months, instead of 1-2 weeks’ time as previously, and that prices are up by between 10-20%. So, it’s probably time for capacity planning. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce7ffe9e-e10d-46af-9b92-9ec123b7f8f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Katelyn</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Most of us have never capacity-planned CPUs. We planned databases, we maybe planned accelerators if we needed them, and we autoscaled on-demand into CPU capacity as much as our budgets allowed us to. But general purpose compute is now something many teams will need to commit to ahead of time, which means you should probably start to forecast and plan around it. If you’re operating at scale, there are some things to spend your energy on.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Using existing CPUs more efficiently is something to do, as of now. </span></strong><span>The CPU capacity shortage won’t go away, and any new CPU allocations requested could take months to turn up. So, what can we do if new capacity lags? One option is utilizing current resources more efficiently!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is a great time to review and to establish now which services are CPU-intensive, and whether or not they </span><em><span>need</span></em><span> to be. Also check on services which are utilizing little CPU: can they run on fewer nodes, so that some CPU capacity can be allocated to services that need it more?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The best time to secure more CPU capacity is most certainly </span></strong><em><strong><span>right now</span></strong></em><strong><span>. </span></strong><span>I’m hearing rumors that certain cloud regions no longer accept new tenants because all CPU capacity is leased, or negotiations elsewhere are difficult. I’m also hearing that customers are already paying </span><em><span>today</span></em><span> to reserve capacity that will only come online in data centers from December. This seems predatory by providers, but demand is so high that this is how they likely prioritize new capacity allocation – </span><em><span>while</span></em><span> </span><em><span>earning much higher profits than usual.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If your company has dynamic workloads, and you’ve used spot instances in the past, now could be a good time to allocate fixed capacity – even if it’s more expensive. If you expect meaningful growth, doing so now might mean having options at some cloud providers or in some regions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It seems like this issue has spread everywhere as a corollary of widespread AI adoption. There’s a GPU shortage, memory shortage, and now a growing CPU shortage as well. Back at the end of last year, there was even an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/12971a90-6bc5-4cd0-9a08-6c623c831414?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>hard drive shortage</span></a><span>. </span><em><span>The only compute primitive not in short supply seems to be networking!</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>2. Growth dream ends for more COVID-era unicorns</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Bending Spoons continues its shopping spree of buying up well-known VC-funded businesses which are desperate to sell, possibly because growth has dried up. Today, the company </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0685c470-33fc-465a-b67f-4cc7a34bc5b8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> its purchase of digital whiteboard startup </span><strong><span>Miro</span></strong><span> for $1.35B. Miro raised a total of $476M in funding, and was valued at a whopping $17.5B in 2022. The acquisition price being higher than what Miro raised, suggests that investors and equity holders should make money on the acquisition.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It comes after Bending Spoons </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/898dc03b-fd9b-4f02-baea-5f2a1fca2d06?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>bought</span></a><span> </span><strong><span>Airtable</span></strong><span> for $1.2B recently – a company that raised $1.4B in funding and was valued at $11B in 2021 during the pandemic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These days, Miro and Airtable likely have flat or sluggish revenue growth and no path to tap into “AI growth”. They depend on sales of their software to enterprises, but enterprise sales are expensive! Also, with AI agents spreading, it’s not clear how much moat that businesses like theirs will have against “AI-native” products, looking ahead.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the circumstances, the founders likely made a calculated decision that it is better to sell now for as much as possible than to run a stagnating business with apparently shrinking prospects in the longer term.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Miro was founded in 2011 and Airtable a year later. Miro became the global leader in the digital whiteboard market, while Airtable offered a fresh alternative to online spreadsheets. Both remain healthy businesses, generating well over $100M in revenue. But in around 2021-2022, each decided to raise money at massive valuations by riding the pandemic-era wave of demand for digital products, which exploded at the time. Back in 2022, I was skeptical these companies could live up to such high valuations when external conditions settled back to ‘normal’:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" Industry Pulse</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Overtime at Google to get Borg working on SpaceX’s data centers</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Google </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a371667-592d-43fb-ab6d-e6ae0b64ff11?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>is paying</span></a><span> SpaceX $920M per month to rent compute in SpaceX’s data centers, but utilizing all this expensive compute is causing problems inside the search giant – because of Borg!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/598aaaa1-bc1f-4ebe-9022-089cd6810412?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Borg</span></a><span> is the system that manages Google’s physical infrastructure. It’s a “Kubernetes, but before Kubernetes” type of software. Kubernetes was created based on learnings from Borg.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>From talking with current Google engineers, we’ve learnt that Borg makes assumptions on data center internals like networking and physical layout that are true for all Google data centers. The big issue is that these assumptions are wrong for SpaceX data centers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a result, engineers are struggling to get Borg to run on SpaceX’s infrastructure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>So, the Borg team is currently running on a ‘996’ working schedule</span></strong><span> (996 meaning 9am - 9pm, six days a week) because every day that Borg cannot run on SpaceX infra costs Google around $30M in infrastructure losses (given the monthly $920M cost). Google no longer has lots of long-tenured engineers who are deeply familiar with Borg internals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m hearing that it’s not all complaints from engineers about this, and that many enjoy taking on a “proper” infrastructure challenge, especially since Borg was supposed to have ‘solved’ infrastructure at Google. Well, it now needs to do it again, as running on non-Google infra is the new baseline at a time when compute capacity is constrained.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, the clock is ticking: Google will have to pay a massive amount to SpaceX, whether or not they can make Borg compatible with SpaceX data centers!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Spotify cuts Claude Code token usage by 90%</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Streaming platform Spotify has vastly </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a406cf6-9ffb-42f7-b117-663c1e483f79?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reduced</span></a><span> its Claude Code token usage by 90%. Here’s how they did it:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Do not use Claude for I/O work: </span></strong><span>much of what Claude Code does is reading and writing files, so why use an expensive model like Claude for this? Instead, Spotify has replaced it with a cheap model like Gemini 2.5 Flash for more basic tasks</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Use Claude only for reasoning: </span></strong><span>Claude is an expensive, capable model, which Spotify keeps in reserve for the most complex tasks that require reasoning</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Use a router to route to Claude or a cheaper alternative: </span></strong><span>Spotify created a Claude Code plugin called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ed3c9ec9-4e88-47d5-a403-df5bbfa1d6a6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shunt</span></a><span> which routes I/O work to cheaper models</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This work by Spotify fits into a wider trend of token cost-saving efforts by tech companies, which </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aebe2957-2dcf-42c9-b7f5-109b1b2c9ae4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>we covered last week</span></a><span>. The idea is pretty simple: don’t use expensive frontier models for work that is simple, and doesn’t require (or benefit from) the capabilities of frontier models.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple principle</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In March, Meta acquired Dreamer, an AI startup co-founded by David Singleton, Stripe’s former CTO. Dreamer’s vision was to let consumers create AI agents for things like managing email, scheduling, travel planning, and so on. A good portion of Muse seems to have been built by the Dreamer team – and the reception for Muse seems to be very positive.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With Muse Spark as a very capable coding model, and this Muse consumer app launch, Meta looks to be a serious player in the AI race.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>OpenAI’s agents go rogue again</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Reuters </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6858431e-28ca-4243-9033-774f8cea54f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reports</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, according to ​new research published Friday, and two people familiar with the matter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps as executives grappled with the fallout from ‌the July breach of the open source repository Hugging Face, the people said.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This incident happened before OpenAI’s model-in-training went rogue and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8d4f3510-8cc9-4c13-b817-28d677e35da8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>hacked Hugging Face</span></a><span>, back in July.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Whatever sandbox OpenAI is using for its AI training looks like it’s pretty leaky. Likewise, whatever monitoring they use to track agent actions is clearly not granular enough. Finally, the fact that OpenAI kept this incident under wraps because of fears about how it would look is concerning.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s no transparency on how AI labs train their AI agents or how they monitor them, and given that agents have a tendency to want to hack services and websites, it is not defensible for OpenAI to pretend that nothing happened. The company has pledged to do better at tracking and monitoring its models, Reuters reports.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>And it’s not just OpenAI: it’s also Anthropic. </span></strong><span>OpenAI’s chief competitor </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9765f846-8282-493b-99e8-ced61e40159f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>published reports</span></a><span> yesterday of their own model hacked external systems during a cyber evaluation. And Anthropic is supposedly the lab which was founded to focus on safety: and yet, they also cannot safely train or evaluate their own models!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If a person hacks into a website and is detected, they could well face criminal charges. When an autonomous AI agent does the same, it raises questions: who is the responsible party and who’s liable? Another point is how the law will decide in cases like this latest one in Germany – it’s surely just a matter of time.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>4. Do engineers lose touch when AI handles incidents?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/88b70b7b-38b4-449a-98e6-9d6fdf2dbc61?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>thoughtful post</span></a><span> has been published about what it means when AI starts “taking over” incident response duties. Software engineer Sylvain Kalache, who works at incident management startup, Rootly, wrote (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The better these tools become at resolving routine incidents, the less practice human responders will get. And when an ambiguous, high-severity incident comes in that automation cannot solve, responding engineers will be in trouble.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The problem is that routine incidents are also how responders “safely” develop an intuition for how their systems behave and fail. When AI runs into a hard, never-seen-before incident it cannot solve, engineers will have to take over with less practice than they would have had before.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Human-factors researcher Lisanne Bainbridge described this paradox in her famous 1983 paper, The Ironies of Automation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>She explained that automation reduces operators’ opportunities to practice routine work while leaving them responsible for new and abnormal situations.</span></strong><span> She argues that, therefore, operators need to be more skilled and receive even more training than before automation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the years to come, I predict that the average MTTR [Mean Time to Resolve] for most incidents will go down – thanks to AI-assisted incident response – but that the resolution time will shoot up for complex incidents because incident responders lost touch with their system and are struggling to investigate.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sylvain uses the aviation industry as an example, where pilots regularly rehearse responses to unlikely emergency situations – and must do so every six months!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>From my time at Uber, I recall the SRE team organized outage drills and these exercises were surprisingly useful. </span></strong><span>They simulated an outage to which we needed to respond by confirming whether it was an outage, then deciding on mitigation, communication, and how to resolve it. Afterward, we reviewed our actions and compared them to what should have been expected.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I did this exercise, and it was </span><em><span>very</span></em><span> useful, even though I knew it was staged. I felt a similar rush as during a real incident. It revealed that some things were not great in our response: we were missing runbooks on how to do routine things, we did not clarify who would communicate and where, and our debugging tooling was missing a few tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Sylvain himself argues that the software industry also needs incident simulators, and that they should become part of oncall readiness. Based on personal experience, I would have to agree. I recommend </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/88b70b7b-38b4-449a-98e6-9d6fdf2dbc61?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reading the full post</span></a><span>.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxNTA4MDA1MiwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODkwNjA3NjEsImV4cCI6MjEwNDYzNjc2MSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.keuVKKyyK_SoLnRkiUPVmmbrn7zPktsrm5aR_SpoTr4?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Imagine a simple scenario where an e-commerce web application calls an API endpoint that returns information about a customer order.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the application level, this looks like a pretty simple operation. But a lot is happening under the hood. First, the client queries the DNS for the IP address linked to the API endpoint. DNS might return the address of a load balancer rather than the address of a specific application server. The operating system then determines how packets should be sent to that IP address. It might choose to send them through the local network, an internet service provider (ISP), or several other routers. The ultimate goal is for the data packets to reach the destination network.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure protocol used for this is HTTP. However, before HTTP can send the request, the client usually needs to establish some form of connection with the destination server.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With traditional HTTPS, this means setting up a TCP connection. In this type of connection, the client and server perform a handshake by exchanging some initial packets so that both sides know a connection has been established. The client and server then perform a TLS handshake. Only after this can the HTTP request be sent securely. A load balancer receives it, selects a healthy application instance, and forwards the request. The application performs its work and sends the response back through the same path.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All of this falls under the realm of networking. Due to its ubiquitous nature, networking becomes an extremely important discipline for developers to master. In this article, we will look at the various aspects of networking in detail.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px Mirror from GitHub </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/71dfe7ce-88c6-4b74-b945-405b47ab6cb6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>with a single click</span></a><span> – I’ve already done so.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong>In this episode</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e8801a75-c763-4ae5-9dc6-d6db93c5bc0e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Tibo Sottiaux</span></a><span> is one of the engineers who created Codex, and today, he heads up the Core Products & Platform org at OpenAI which also includes Codex. He’s also one of the most public faces of Codex due to his frequent – and generous – usage reset announcements, like this one </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9860f328-13c3-46c3-9f9d-81629c9ed7c4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>yesterday</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this episode of the Pragmatic Engineer Podcast, Tibo and I discuss how Codex was built and continues to be iterated upon. We explore why the Codex CLI is written in Rust and was released as open source, how the harness and models have evolved, and why Codex supports models from multiple providers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tibo also shares details about how the OpenAI team uses Codex throughout the software development lifecycle, including code reviews, maintenance, and system rearchitecture. We look into how AI is lowering the cost of changing code – and some interesting side effects of this – the merger of ChatGPT and Codex, and also how Tibo uses the tools in his own work.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Tibo</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/43f76a50-4d28-432e-8e72-1f1dc6f632da?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/sLSTM9znQNs" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. A shock cancellation proved to be an important lesson. </span></strong><span>While at Google in London, Tibo spent two enjoyable years working on a project in the Ads organization – right up until a VP flew in from California and abruptly cancelled the whole thing. Tibo was shocked: there were hundreds of users and he was having a great time solving engineering challenges. Reflecting later, he realized he’d been blind to the fact that the product had no product-market fit and the feedback loop from users was poor. Tibo also learned that just because a product manager says a project is going well, doesn’t mean it is! That experience means he now always questions the impact of his work, and the importance of projects to which he contributes. </span><em><span>Looking at Tibo’s career since, it seems like a well-timed lesson!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Google had a “ChatGPT-like” project a year before OpenAI.</span></strong><span> At the start of the decade, DeepMind was largely focused on games and reinforcement learning, but some members, including Tibo, reckoned that scaling language models might lead to artificial general intelligence (AGI). Their “chat with an LLM” project spread like wildfire internally, but for some reason the product was never launched. Who knows what would have happened if Google had beaten OpenAI to the public launch of AI chatbots in 2022.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. Tibo was drawn to OpenAI because only 20 people worked on ChatGPT. </span></strong><span>Tibo had a great run at Google, but missed working somewhere where Research and Product collaborated more closely than at the search giant. When he learned in 2023 that ChatGPT was built and maintained by around 20 engineers – despite its massive popularity – he was very surprised and wanted to join.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. Codex is built using Rust, even though the AI models were much better at writing Python and TypeScript at the time. </span></strong><span>The Codex team had a vision of Codex instances running on millions of cloud machines, which meant performance, security, and engineering for efficiency and scale were the first design principles. This led to Rust, despite AI models then not being the strongest at writing Rust. The team’s decision to choose a performant language upfront and avoid a rewrite later reminds me of Casey Muratori’s point about the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/06b02327-bc99-4467-88b4-8eea101a622f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>need to architect for performance, upfront.</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. Codex is open source, which has upsides and downsides. </span></strong><span>Codex’s biggest competitor, Claude Code, is closed source, so I find it inspiring that the Codex team chose the open source path. Tibo says the upsides are trust and the community of contributors who are an energizing influence. A less discussed downside of open source is that the Codex team’s work sometimes gets copied and released in other tools before Codex. Tibo told me this stings, but it’s the price of working in the open.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. Open source is a big reason why Codex supports working with other AI models. </span></strong><span>Claude Code can only be used with Anthropic’s models, whereas Codex is usable with any model, not just OpenAI’s. Being open source means that even if Codex were locked down to a model, anyone could still fork the harness and change a few lines of code to support a different model. Tibo believes in winning by letting users use the best models; the Codex team themselves also try other models in the same harness. </span><em><span>Personally, I appreciate this approach of encouraging competition from a frontier lab!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>7. Cloud development environments (CDEs) never took off outside of Big Tech because of setup costs – but AI agents could change this. </span></strong><span>Tibo predicts a resurgence of fully cloud-orchestrated machines, where agents like Codex can configure and stay in sync with your local machine setup.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. The Codex harness is always slightly ahead of OpenAI’s latest model. </span></strong><span>The harness provides the model with crutches: guardrails, safety, efficiency, steerability, and the developer message injected into context at the start of each turn. As models improve, some “crutches” are discarded and the harness shrinks. This has been the development cycle between Codex and OpenAI’s new models to date.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. Codex “knows” a staggering amount because it’s plugged into pretty much every OpenAI system. </span></strong><span>I asked Tibo what pointers he’d give a new joiner on the Codex team. His answer: “have you asked Codex?” At OpenAI, it’s plugged into Slack, every document, and all code, by default. New starters are surprised about being able to ask it anything, including who’s working on something, or why a decision was made. The team purposely work in public channels and open documents with broad permissions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>10. Correctness checks and security reviews will be automated with AI. </span></strong><span>With code review changing under AI’s influence, Tibo believes that discussion about the intent of code doesn’t have to happen inside a code review, which is mostly about correctness, information exchange, and providing a forcing function for conversations that should’ve happened sooner. With AI code review, conversations about what the system should do still matter, and are probably best had before the code is written. This echoes the theme of this week’s Tuesday article about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/69446e1a-4c7c-4990-a975-95fd596e4840?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>what is happening with code reviews</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>11. Maintaining and re-architecting code is becoming very cheap with agents, especially time-wise. </span></strong><span>Maintenance tasks like dependency upgrades can be handled by a model blasting through the codebase within a couple of hours. Meanwhile, re-architecting for new tradeoffs that used to take years can now take days, at most. Tibo adds a caveat: quality code, good abstractions, and good test suites greatly affect how easy – or not – a codebase change is to make.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>12. Being “in the zone” is history; Tibo sees code as a tool for solving problems. </span></strong><span>During the podcast recording, we bonded over remembering the “good old days” of pulling late nighters and staying “in the zone” to solve difficult problems with code. These days, Tibo has adapted, like most people at OpenAI. He still opens an editor and writes a little code because it feels nice, but says that an upside of AI agents is being able to gather more data faster – meaning there’s less need for the lengthy coding sessions of yore. Instead of making gut calls, he can fire off an agent and get the data within a minute to make much better decisions with.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why LLM Applications Become Expensive</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The total cost of using an LLM API usually depends on the number of tokens processed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To be clear, a token is a small unit of text. A short word might be one token. But a longer word can be split into multiple tokens.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are usually two important token counts:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Input tokens include the user’s message, system instructions, conversation history, and any documents supplied to the model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Output tokens are the tokens generated within the response.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Depending on the LLM provider, input and output tokens can have different price points. Larger and more capable models generally cost more because they require more computing resources. They may also spend additional computation for reasoning. This extra capability is very important for solving complex problems. But this capability is wasted when the task is simple.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, imagine a customer-support application that has to process a million requests per month. Within those requests, some users may ask for refund policies. Others may want an address extracted from an email. Some might have complicated account problems that need careful analysis. If each request goes to the most powerful model, the company has to pay a premium price even for work that is quite simple for this capable model. You could think of this as hiring a senior software architect to rename files, sort support tickets, and format dates. Sure, the architect can technically do those things. But it would be a waste of the architect’s capability and a case of poor resource management.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Model routing is the process of checking an incoming request to decide which model is the best choice for handling it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With model routing, we don’t write application code that always calls one model blindly. We place a router in front of several models. The router can access a small model, a medium-sized model, and a highly capable one. Its job is to evaluate each request and send it to the most suitable model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, the router might receive a simple classification request and send it to the smallest model. Or the router might receive a request that contains a complicated legal comparison and send it to the most powerful model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: model routing as load balancing. But it has an important difference. A load balancer normally distributes traffic between largely equivalent servers. However, a model router has to choose between models with vastly different capabilities, costs, and characteristics.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Model routing is also quite different from a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model. In an MoE setup, routing happens internally between parts of a single model. In contrast, application-level model routing happens outside the models. It deals with deciding which model should receive the request and doesn’t deal with the internals of that model.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Model Routing Can Produce Big Cost Savings</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider a powerful model that costs 1 cent per average request. If an application handles a million requests, using that powerful model for everything would cost around $10,000.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now imagine a smaller model costs only 1/20th as much, while a medium model costs 1/5th as much as the powerful model. After studying the workload, we discover that 85% of requests can be handled by the small model, 10% need the medium model, and just 5% require the powerful model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this case, the average cost per request becomes:</span></p><div class="callout-block" data-callout="true" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;background-color: rgb(238,238,238);border-radius: 8px;margin: 32px 0;padding: 16px 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin: 8px 0;"><span>(0.85×0.05) + (0.10×0.20) + (0.05×1.00) = 0.1125</span></p></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This means that a system built with model routing can potentially cost just 11% as much as the system that uses the same powerful model for handling every request. This is almost a 10X reduction in costs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even more favourable traffic patterns or price differences could push the savings beyond tenfold. For example, if more than 90% of the workload consists of extraction, classification, formatting, and straightforward summary generation, the expensive model may be needed only occasionally.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ultimately, the best savings happen when three conditions are met: a large price difference between models, most requests being relatively simpler, and the router being able to identify the simple requests reliably.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How to Judge a Request Before Answering?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The greatest difficulty in model routing is around determining the difficulty level of a request without answering it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If a request is short, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the request is simple. For example, “Is the contract valid?” contains just 4 words. But to answer this query safely, the model might need legal expertise and extensive context. On the other hand, a long request is not always difficult. A user may have pasted a long document and asked the model to extract every email address. It is conceptually quite straightforward.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Therefore, a good router cannot rely only on message length to determine the difficulty level. It needs to check several signals while making a fair decision.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, the model router might consider what kind of task the user is requesting. This is because tasks like classification, extraction, translation, rewriting, and formatting often require less reasoning. However, tasks that involve planning, debugging, mathematical proofs, or comparing conflicting documents require much higher levels of reasoning.</span></p><div should also consider the risk factor. For example, a medical, legal, financial, or security-related question may be routed to a stronger model even if the query appears simple. This is because the cost of an inaccurate answer matters a lot.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another signal the model router could use is the amount of overall context. For example, if a model needs to inspect several documents, make sense of a long conversation, or connect different sources, it needs a larger context window or stronger instruction ability.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lastly, the model router may also need to check the output requirements before selecting the right model. For example, producing a valid JSON object with a few known fields may be an easy task. However, producing a detailed technical design that adheres to a bunch of critical constraints is much harder.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In other words, no single signal is sufficient. A smart model routing approach normally combines several signals to make the right choice.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Using a Small Model as a Router</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The most flexible approach to model routing is to use a smaller model to classify the request.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This so-called router model can work on instructions as follows:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>Classify this request as EASY, MEDIUM, or HARD.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>EASY:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Extraction, formatting, simple classification, or direct rewriting.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>MEDIUM:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Summarization, ordinary coding help, or moderate analysis.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>HARD:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Complex reasoning, conflicting evidence, high-risk advice,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>multi-document analysis, or strict multi-step constraints.</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The router can then return a small structured result:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>{</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “difficulty”: “hard”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “risk”: “high”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “recommended_model”: “powerful-model”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “reason”: “The request involves financial advice and several documents.”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>}</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since the routing prompt and the resulting response are quite short, the classification call won’t be too costly. Based on the response, the application then sends the full request to the selected model.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px deals better with natural language rather than coding fixed rules, it can have another cause of error. The smaller router model can misunderstand the request and send difficult work to a less-capable model. This is why production systems often combine model-based classification with fixed safety rules. A specific rule might clearly specify that certain medical or financial queries should always be sent to the strongest model, irrespective of what the router model suggests.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Cascading: Trying the Cheaper Model First</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us now look at another useful model routing strategy known as model cascading.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this strategy, we don’t try to predict the difficulty perfectly. Instead, the system first sends the request to a cheaper model. It then checks whether the answer appears good enough. If the answer fails the check, the system sends the request to a stronger model.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: href="https://substack.com/redirect/4b37e3dd-f8a8-429f-b3b1-577eae97821b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/da180cbf-b1a0-40ed-b573-49c09b807f39_2922x1382.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":689,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":172348,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/214202274?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fda180cbf-b1a0-40ed-b573-49c09b807f39_2922x1382.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This approach works quite well when answers can be checked automatically. For example, let’s say the application asks the model to extract a date, customer ID, and total amount from an invoice. The program can then verify that all required fields exist, the date is valid, and the amount is numeric. If the small model has produced malformed data, the second attempt goes to the powerful model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We get similar opportunities in the case of code generation. The application can run tests against the generated code. If the tests pass, it accepts the cheaper model’s answer. If they fail, it can escalate the task to the more capable model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, cascading gets difficult when quality judgement is subjective. There may be no simple automated test to find out if a business strategy is useful or whether an explanation is actually clear. In those cases, the application may use a separate evaluator model. However, such a model would have its own cost and can also make mistakes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lastly, the cascade process must be designed carefully because failed attempts also consume money and time. If most attempts made by the small model end up in failure, the application only ends up paying for both the small and the capable model. Routing ends up making the system slower and more expensive.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Semantic Routing</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In semantic routing, we choose the model based on the meaning of the request rather than specific keywords.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, consider an application that has specialized models or prompts for billing, technical support, product recommendations, and account security. However, users may describe the same billing problem in many different ways:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why did you charge me twice?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I see a duplicate payment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The same order appears twice on my card.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A typical keyword-based system might not be able to support many of these variations. But a semantic router converts the request into an embedding. For reference, an embedding is a numerical representation of a request’s meaning.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The router can then compare the embedding with examples of known request categories. If the request is close to billing examples, it goes to the billing model. If it resembles account-security examples, it goes to the security model.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure
