Review the plan/tests/database schema, but not the implementation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some devs and teams have stopped reviewing the code (the implementation), and instead review the “before” and “after” states:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Review the plan: </span></strong><span>spend a lot more time on the plan than before, to get a much more detailed spec. Using </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/056df39b-b6dd-4582-bb11-7f790bf6053c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The /grill-me skill</span></a><span> by Matt Pocock is a popular method, and I’m also a fan of it for thorough upfront planning, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/74c0bb31-b890-4b4f-9413-dc740853750f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>as is</span></a><span> Andrea Francesco Speziale, Principal Engineer at Musixmatch:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“After 3 hours of /grill-me, it better one-shot the implementation. I’m not spending a single minute on any review!”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Review the tests: </span></strong><span>via Test Driven Development (TDD) – which is much easier with agents when writing the tests upfront is a chore – or by focusing the review to ensure the software is tested.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One argument for this approach is that customers and users of software usually don’t care about the code. There’s a caveat that automated tests can verify a lot of different software – and are great at verifying business logic – but they don’t do a good job at verifying whether a UI </span><em><span>looks</span></em><span> and </span><em><span>feels </span></em><span>good.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Review the database schema. </span></strong><span>Jackie Luo, cofounder and CEO of AI startup Sigil, and formerly an engineer at Square, says:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“My current take is that all that really matters is the database schema. Speaking from a fast-moving startup perspective:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>1. Everything, besides data, is fluid and recoverable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>2. The schema is the “hard” representation of what’s been built and reveals the riskiest changes, so it’s a good attention/impact tradeoff.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>3. Business logic only matters because product behavior matters—so ideally align on that before interacting with a coding agent at all. Then, once the code is written, use abstractions to understand any other significant decisions made.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Understand the product over the code. Use abstractions to translate the latter to the former – except in the case of schemas!”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jackie’s point is that data (that is, the state) is the most “rigid” part of any system. Stateless business logic is now easy to change because it’s “just” code, and code is easy and fast to generate and regenerate. For startups, it’s worth getting the data schema – and thereby your state machine – right. Then, everything else will be easy and fast to iterate on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>My sense is this approach makes perfect sense for a startup iterating to get product-market fit. However, once you have a business, you’ll want to “guard” the business logic with tests: else your product could break, and existing users will be unhappy when this happens!</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>4. Produce less code</span></h2><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What about simply not accepting a future in which agents produce more and longer PRs, more verbose code, and more code to review? Some teams enforce sensible rules for pull requests that existed before AI:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Keep them small: maximum 500 lines per pull request. If bigger, then open standalone PRs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Have a PR do only one thing: don’t mix scaffolding, adding of business logic, implementing two features in one PRs, etc</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Use </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0c221a0c-e36c-441d-9dec-6fb3f78b9872?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>stacked diffs</span></a><span>: mainstream tools like GitHub have added support, so keeping pull requests small is easier</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is where it helps for engineers to be more hands-on with agents; when you pay attention to what the AI does, you can stop it from implementing functionality from scratch when it could use an existing module or an existing library, for instance.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>5. Review everything by hand</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s worth pointing out that reviewing code “by hand” is far from entirely dead across the tech industry; indeed, some engineers and teams still swear by it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Building a better release process could still be more impactful than automating code review. </span></strong><span>This is what </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c5fc1ad5-567d-4686-8c5b-d737c66781cc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>George Salakirov</span></a><span>, VP of Product Engineering at WeTravel, told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We still do human code review, and use our ‘vanilla’ coding agents to generate code. While I see a potential for a good product with AI code review tools, the gains compared to us reviewing our own code still feel marginal with the current generation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In our case, building a good release process and moving over to a monorepo are both projects we expect to improve engineering productivity a lot more: so we’ve prioritized these, before we’d look into potential code review automations. We’re already seeing a lift from these investments in our developer productivity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, the gap seems to be closing when AI code review tools could be useful enough for us: and we re-evaluate available tools on the market every quarter.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Software engineer Dima Belyaev </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7376cc73-96a8-4ab7-88fe-a672453aaf82?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>also prefers</span></a><span> to review code by hand, even if it is “skimming”:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I’m still in the camp of code reviewing everything, even though we have agents doing that too. So far I’m only skimming through well-scoped internal changes as long as there is a working reproduction of the code (CI, internal docs etc).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I stopped reading tests in the PRs, though: I’m quite confident in their quality and fine if they’re more verbose than they could be, those tests are easy to fix later.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most of the AI code review tools test the product first, leaving architectural / API questions next, with clear understanding of which are easy fixes for an agent to apply vs which are questions for the author to make a decision / push back.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Most of my code review comments / questions these days</span></strong><span>: so in case an agent does another pass, they could explain the reason why it’s implemented this way and either have me agree or push back with more context and specific direction.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>It may turn out that regulation and compliance concerns preserve human code review from extinction, longer term. </span></strong><span>For example, some companies interpret security assessments like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2dd49600-84c4-4f3f-a5ae-f9c5b77d0643?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>FedRAMP</span></a><span> as requiring humans to review every single line of code that goes into production. However, FedRAMP itself doesn’t necessarily demand line-by-line human review: it’s down to the company and the auditor to agree on how to interpret the regulation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/885beae6-ea7f-4afa-b0e5-8fe89fb02773?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>PCI DSS</span></a><span>, human code review is mandatory when code review is the chosen review method, but it also allows other review techniques.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>6. No more human code review?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I expected to hear from engineers who have completely removed the human from the code review process, and that was the case.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The teams that I could confirm have ditched human code reviews for production software are early-stage, “AI-native” startups. </span></strong><span>For example, here is the cofounder of Glide, an AI spreadsheets startup, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/49afd425-ae5e-414b-942d-7c84cf8eea07?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explaining</span></a><span> their approach. Simon Fletcher says:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We went fully agentic around four months ago. The throughput gain has been significant, roughly 4.5x more PRs merged per month. The system’s state continues to hold up. Surprisingly, security and reliability are actually higher than when we had our human process in place. The agentic review allows us to have agents work on these toil tasks more autonomously.  I will admit, it does require guardrails and other forms of backpressure in the system to fully trust it.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Glide built an “agentic rollout pipeline” before throwing away human code review. This internal platform is called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2e6d274-3051-49ed-a379-7639322a76b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Slipstream</span></a><span>:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Tests and evals</span></strong><span>: these run after the AI code review, and have to pass for the next step to begin</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Human sign-off:</span></strong><span> Glide doesn’t deploy automatically to prod: a dev looks through the AI code review and CI results before greenlighting to deploy</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Agent “babysits” the deploy</span></strong><span>: using a feature flag, an agent gradually rolls out the change and checks for degradation in metrics, which are flagged in Slack</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s how Slipstream looks in action:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On one hand, I like agentic gradual rollout as an automation a lot! On the other, it involves a bunch more infrastructure work to make core reviews no longer mandatory. Also, when code reviews are no longer part of development, is there a risk of more tech debt making it into the codebase faster?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It will be interesting to see how the codebases and products of startups that go all-in on agentic code reviews, are holding up in 6-12 months’ time. </span><em><span>Regardless, I’m all for experimentation, and we see some neat experimentation by Glide!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Other incidences of complete automation I heard about were side projects, single-person businesses, or very early-stage startups with no product-market fit. Basically, places where shipping a broken prototype is not a big deal.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>7. Why do we review code, anyway?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’ve covered how teams are responding to ever more code being generated by AI which is correspondingly harder to review. At this point, it’s worth returning to fundamentals and considering </span><em><span>why</span></em><span> we do code review in the first place. It’s been a tech industry norm for decades, and long a mandatory part of the development process, but is it becoming pointless and redundant?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, with AI agents being able to do more than ever, the question arises of why people should be involved in the process; what are the benefits of not letting the AI tool do it all? From my perspective, the reasons for human code review are manifold:</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Technical reasons</span></h3><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Conversations about architecture. </span></strong><span>For better or worse, many architecture discussions take place within code reviews; such as about scaffolding or building new components, whether a method should belong to a class, or if a functionality be in a separate module, etc. This kind of debate is better to have during implementation than afterward; (although the optimal time would be even earlier!) </span><em><span>Of course, the reality of building software involves figuring out design details as the software is built.</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Missing tests / ignored conventions. </span></strong><span>In teams without lint rules on conventions or test coverage, code review comments can reveal when things are missing. Yes, automating this feedback is pretty trivial, but automated code review still remains far from great at deciding whether a test is good or was “written to pass.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Less tech debt.</span></strong><span> Code review is a great place for experienced engineers to call out shortcuts that add tech debt and need to be addressed before committing, or in an immediate follow-up review. Cases may include when a method gets overly complicated, or a dev adds more code to an already messy component in need of a cleanup.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Extra bug-catching layer. </span></strong><span>There’s often an expectation that code reviews will catch bugs; however, in my experience, code reviews have always been a poor line of defense against bugs by themselves. It is a benefit of human code reviews that an experienced engineer can sometimes spot obvious issues that would lead to problems. Still, catching bugs is better done by other means, like via a thorough test suite.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Nitpicking</span></strong><span>. Nitpicking can go too far when engineers add comments on minor, unimportant details which then trigger lengthy back-and-forth debates about variables not being in alphabetical order, or whether a variable name is the right length, etc. But within reason, nitpicking still forms part of healthy, robust debate on a team, unless it’s a symptom of other issues – see below.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Team reasons</span></h3><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Knowledge sharing and reducing the “bus factor.”</span></strong><span> By doing code reviews, team members learn how new code works, which is useful because they can take over the work, add to it, and fix issues when needed. This reduces the risk of a project failing or ceasing to work as people leave and move on from it; aka the ‘bus factor’.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Professional growth.</span></strong><span> For junior engineers, code review feedback from experienced devs is a professional growth opportunity. In my early career, I worked hard to not repeat the mistakes of past code reviews, and felt pride when a senior dev with a high code review bar said “good job” about a longer code change.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cross-team collaboration. </span></strong><span>At companies with an “internal open source” model where anyone can raise pull requests against any part of the code, it’s a lot easier to raise a PR than to call a meeting with the other team, or raise a JIRA ticket. Comments on the pull request often turn into discussions about what the other team intends to do, and how they could do it better. It could lead to engineers starting to talk more to each other; for example, if a code review shows there was a misunderstanding.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Code review can reveal team dynamics. </span></strong><span>As a manager, I found that a good way to spot conflict and frustrations among team members was in code reviews, such as excessive nitpicking, passive-aggressive language, or when normally-quiet devs started commenting a lot on others’ coding efforts. Reviews enabled me to detect conflicts early and then talk with devs to figure out if there was a problem (there usually was!) With AI code reviews, does intra-team conflict disappear, or is it just less obvious? I don’t know, but it will surely create </span><em><span>new</span></em><span> dynamics to deal with.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Organizational reasons</span></h3><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Create accountability and traceability. </span></strong><span>Signing off a code change creates accountability, as it’s not just the engineer who wrote the code who is accountable, but also the person who signed it off. It’s not uncommon during code freezes to only allow code that’s been signed off by a Staff+ or Director+ level to be deployed, when stability matters more than speed. Also, code reviews make it easy to know who saw and approved the code going out.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Compliance and governance. </span></strong><span>Some code reviews are mandated at regulated companies; for example, a security team might need to do a mandatory security review of critical parts of the codebase in order to follow an internal process.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In many cases above, code review could be replaced or augmented with another layer, and the process of catching bugs could be more effective with a thorough test suite, or via dogfooding, running the system inside a hostile simulation before deploying, or monitoring in production. Of course, today an argument can be made for AI tools as a replacement, but that necessarily comes at the cost of some of what makes human-centered code review useful in teams and orgs.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As engineers, we’ve pretty swiftly moved to allow AI agents to generate the code, but reviewing that code doesn’t yet seem a responsibility that can be easily delegated to AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Right now, there are a few reasons for this; AI code review tools tend to be too noisy, and many professionals simply don’t trust them sufficiently for the task, as things stand. As software engineers, we’re paid to solve problems of the business and its customers. There’s a well-established process for this: understand the problem → make a plan → write the code → validate that it works → ship to production → ensure it keeps working.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By delegating the writing of code to an AI agent, we make ourselves one step removed from the code itself. In this case, it only makes sense to spend more time on either specifying it upfront (places which spend more time planning or on database schemas) or validating it (with test suites or code reviews).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I admit that reviewing code has never been my favorite activity as it’s not creative like building software is, and I wonder how close we’ll be able to stay to the code after many of us stop writing it. If it is only a matter of time until agents have more feedback loops to confirm that code works as expected, then devs will spend most of our time specifying what to build, but then not actually building it. In that scenario, our role will be to just review that things “feel” right after the fact.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>These changes are unfolding in real time, and I’m interested to hear from you about it. Comment below on how code review is changing in your team or company? What is the good and bad of relying ever more on AI code review, and how far can this approach be pushed today?</span></em></p><p class="button-wrapper" How To Be Direct And Strategic

Yue Zhao

"I saw an issue with a process on my team recently and brought it up directly in a team meeting a few days later. I was very direct about the problem, gave all the details, and explained how it impacted everyone. To my surprise, my manager shut it down completely, and now I cannot get any buy-in from anyone. What happened? Where did I do wrong?"

#Leadership Communication

#Management Productivity AI

But there is one major difference. Apart from normal processing, the application also sends data to a large language model (LLM). It then uses the model’s response to carry out a task. For example, a customer support chatbot might depend on an LLM to answer user queries. A document-processing system can use an LLM to extract names, dates, and invoice amounts from the uploaded documents. A coding assistant might ask an LLM to write a piece of code and integrate it into the logical flow.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On face value, we might feel that building such an application is quite simple:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The user sends a request.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The application sends a prompt to an LLM.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The LLM returns an answer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The application displays that answer or uses the same for some other processing.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, there are chances that any of these steps can fail. The network might be unavailable. The LLM provider might reject the user request for various reasons. The request might go through, but the model might return invalid JSON. The LLM can misunderstand the instructions and invent false information due to hallucinations. They might also take a long time to respond.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The techniques for resiliency and error handling help prepare the application to handle these situations in the best possible manner. 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Meaning of Error Handling and Resiliency</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before we get into the details, let us understand what error handling and resiliency exactly mean.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You can think of error handling as a part of the program responsible for deciding the appropriate action when something goes wrong. For example, consider an application that calls an LLM API. If the request is successful, the program processes the response in a normal way. But if it fails, the program might have to choose from various options, such as retrying the request, showing an explanatory message, using a backup model, or recording the failure for further investigation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Any of these approaches is much better than allowing the entire application to crash. But we also cannot treat every problem in the same manner. A real production application should be able to distinguish between different types of failures so that we can take the right action. Therefore, good error handling needs an understanding of what failed and why.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, resiliency is an application’s ability to continue doing its job even when some parts of the system are failing. We don’t need an application to operate perfectly to be resilient. Failures are fine. But they should happen in a controlled manner. This is also known as graceful degradation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, consider a travel assistant that uses an LLM to build personalized itineraries for travellers. If the primary LLM it depends on is unavailable, the application can use a smaller backup model for creating the itineraries. If that model also becomes unavailable, the application can display previously created destination guides for the same locations. Of course, these answers won’t be personalized, but the user won’t just see a useless error message.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While error handling deals with an individual failure, resiliency is more concerned about the behavior of the entire system even when things are failing.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why do LLM Applications Need Special Treatment for Error Handling?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Traditional software apps work according to well-defined rules. If we write a function that adds 5 and 7, it will always return 12. If the function returns successfully, the result is deemed valid.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With LLMs, we don’t have this luxury. This is because the output from LLMs is probabilistic. In other words, the same prompt can produce different answers every single time. Also, a successful API request to an LLM doesn’t guarantee that the response we receive is correct or even usable. For all we know, the response might be utterly gibberish. This means that an LLM API call might appear successful based on status code, but it might be a failure in logical terms. There are several things that could be wrong with the response:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The model might have ignored some part of the instructions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It might have returned a pure text response when the application expected JSON.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The LLM might hallucinate and invent a product, policy, or piece of information that has no basis in real data.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The model might return an incomplete response because it reached its token limit.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The LLM can refuse a harmless request because it misunderstood the context.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The LLM might select the wrong tool or call a tool with invalid arguments.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Lastly, the LLM might return an answer that violates some important business rule.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We can broadly notice two categories of failures over here:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Technical Failures: </span></strong><span>They happen when the system can’t even complete the operation. This involves stuff like network errors, timeouts, unavailable service, invalid credentials, and so on.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Semantic Failures: </span></strong><span>These types of failures show up even when the operation is technically successful. But the result might be incorrect, unsafe, irrelevant, or even unusable.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Conventional error handling focuses on dealing with technical failures. However, LLM-powered applications need to handle both technical and semantic failures.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Does a Request Flow in an LLM-powered App?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LLM-powered apps contain much more than an LLM. We have many different components that come together to make an application complete. See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/a2f65095-e983-4bae-849e-27ad771a7ea3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f734b2ff-1f7f-4c07-a7da-0955c6fd1ab6_2048x1214.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":863,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="325.9958791208791" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!u90q!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff734b2ff-1f7f-4c07-a7da-0955c6fd1ab6_2048x1214.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As an example, consider a shopping chatbot that checks products based on the user’s preference. It first runs a search on a product database and gives the results back to an LLM. It then asks the model to select the right products for a particular user and then calls an inventory API to find out the availability of those products.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We can have failures at every boundary within this application. The user might provide some invalid information. The product search may return no results. The request to the LLM might time out due to external reasons. The model may return an unknown product identifier. The inventory service might go down. Lastly, even if the response is somehow generated, it might be interrupted while streaming to the user.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To make an application truly resilient, we can’t treat the LLM as an isolated component. We need to consider the path of the request from the beginning to the end and identify potential problems.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Main Types of Errors and Failures</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us now look at the main types of errors and failures that can occur in such an application.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Invalid User Input</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some failures can show up even before the LLM is called. For example, a user may submit an empty message, upload an unacceptable file format, provide an extremely large document, or enter an invalid date.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In such cases, the application should be able to validate obvious requirements. There is no need to call an LLM to find out if a mandatory email address is missing or if an uploaded file exceeds the size limit. If we reject invalid requests early, we can save time and processing costs. We can also provide much clearer error messages to the users since the rules are fixed.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Network and Connection Failures</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An application talks to an LLM provider over the internet. However, the connections can be interrupted. We can have DNS lookup failures. Responses might be lost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Such type of failures are temporary. We can retry the request. But the application cannot retry indefinitely. We also need to consider whether it is safe to repeat the operation and whether there are any unforeseen side effects.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Timeouts</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this case, the LLM may take longer to respond than the application can wait. If there’s no timeout, the request can remain stuck while consuming resources.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The timeout value defines how long the application can wait. For example, an interactive chat application might have a timeout of 20 seconds. But an offline document-analysis job might allow several minutes. Also, the timeout should depend on the user experience. For example, a user waiting on a screen should have a shorter deadline than a background task that runs overnight.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Rate Limits</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LLM providers have a limit to how many requests or tokens a specific account can use within a time period. If the application goes above this limit, the LLM provider may return a rate-limit error. This is represented by the HTTP status code 429.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Getting a rate limit response doesn’t mean that the service is broken. It means that our application is making more requests than what the provider can handle at a given point in time. To handle this, the application may need to delay the requests, reduce concurrency, put the work in a queue, or switch to another model that might have available capacity.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Provider and Server Failures</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In certain situations, the LLM provider might be down due to a temporary internal problem. These failures are commonly represented by HTTP 5xx status codes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this case, a limited retry attempt could be a good idea because the failure might vanish quickly. However, if the failures continue, repeated retry calls only increase the load upon an already struggling service. is reasonable because the failure may disappear quickly. The application should stop retrying and switch to an alternative execution path if possible.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Authentication and Permission Failures</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If the application provides an expired or invalid API key, it might also result in a 401 or 403 response from the LLM provider.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this case, there is very little point to retrying. The application should record the failure, alert the relevant parties, and return an appropriate message to the user. It must take care not to expose API keys or other internal security details to the user.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Context-length Failures</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every language model has a limit on how much text it can process in one request. The prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool definitions, and expected answer are all part of this context window and consume space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If the application sends a lot of information to the LLM, the LLM may reject the request, or it may have too little space for the answer. An application designed with resiliency in mind usually counts tokens before sending the request. It can also remove old conversation messages, summarize earlier content, retrieve fewer documents, or divide a large job into smaller pieces to stay within the limit.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Malformed or Unexpected Output</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say our application expects a result in the following format.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>{</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “customer_name”: “Adam Smith”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “priority”: “high”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>}</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, the model might reply something like: “The customer’s name appears to be Adam Smith, and this looks urgent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Such an answer might make sense to a human being, but the application that expects a JSON response can’t process it. To get around this, the application should use a structured-output feature if the model provider supports it. It should also validate the response against a schema before using it.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Incorrect or Invented Information</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The most dangerous LLM failures happen in the form of plausible answers that are completely wrong. This occurs due to model hallucination.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, a customer-support assistant might invent a refund policy that doesn’t exist. A research tool might generate a source that doesn’t exist. An inventory assistant might recommend a product that is not even there in the catalog.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Such problems can’t be detected by catching exceptions because no technical exception occurred. To handle these types of issues, the application needs additional checks, trusted data sources, or some form of human intervention to proceed further.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Tool Failures and Partial Completion</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LLMs are also now used as agents that can make API calls, search databases, send messages, or perform transactions. This gives rise to a major problem. The specific action taken by the LLM might succeed even when the surrounding workflow fails.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, suppose the LLM assistant calls a payment service. The payment succeeds, but the network connection breaks before the application gets the confirmation. If the application retries the payment blindly, we might end up charging the customer twice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the reason tool-based systems need idempotency, state tracking, and recovery mechanisms.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How to Classify Failures to Take Appropriate Action</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So how do we deal with all these different types of errors in an LLM-powered application?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first step is to classify them. There are main categories:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A transient error is temporary and usually disappears if we attempt the operation again. For example, network problems, rate limits, and server failures.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A permanent error continues until there is a change in the request or the system. Such errors include invalid credentials, unsupported file types, permission issues, and malformed requests.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A semantic error occurs when the response is technically correct, but doesn’t solve the application’s requirements. Examples are invalid JSON, unsupported tool arguments, hallucinations, and so on.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once we are able to classify an error, we can deal with it appropriately. For a transient error, we should retry after a short delay or use a fallback. For permanent errors, we need to report to the concerned parties who can correct the problem. For semantic errors, we need to validate, repair, or request human review.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, not every error also fits neatly into a single category. For example, a context-length error is permanent for the current prompt. However, it can be solved by making the prompt shorter.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How To Retry a Request Correctly?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us look at some techniques to deal with failures. The first one to check out is retrying a request.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Retries are one of the simplest ways to improve an application’s resiliency. If an operation fails because of a brief network problem, chances are that it will work fine once the application waits for a while and tries again.</span></p><div used for timeouts, temporary network failures, 429 responses, and some specific 5xx responses. We shouldn’t use them for failures such as invalid credentials, prohibited requests, bad input, or other problems that will produce the same result every single time.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How to Manage Fallbacks and Graceful Degradation?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In an application, the fallback path is an alternative path. It is used when the normal preferred path fails due to some failure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An application can use the fallback approach in the following manner:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Attempt to use the primary model, which is usually of high quality.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>If that model is unavailable, switch to a smaller backup model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>If no model is available, return a pre-defined fallback response or cached information.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Lastly, if the request can’t be handled safely through any option, transfer it to a human for further action.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 approach depends on the task. For example, we might be okay to use a smaller model for summarizing an internal meeting. However, it might not be a good choice for interpreting a complicated legal document. Similarly, a cached response may be good enough for a general FAQ type scenario. But it won’t be suitable for something like the current account balance.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In other words, the fallback strategy should not violate the original requirements of the operation. We can’t just plug any available model into the flow. It’s also important to avoid dependency on a single point of failure. For example, if both the primary and backup models are accessed through the same provider, an outage can disable both. For real redundancy, we should have separation between the two pathways.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Do Circuit Breakers Work in this Setup?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider a scenario where the LLM provider is unavailable. Every request is timing out. In such cases, it is not wise to keep sending more requests. They only waste resources and make users wait for failures.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A circuit breaker can temporarily stop calls to a failing service. It commonly has three states:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the closed state, we can send the requests at normal cadence.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the open state, requests get rejected or redirected immediately. This is because the service is considered unhealthy.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the half-open state, a small number of test requests are allowed to go through. They help determine whether the service has recovered to some extent.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: requests in the half-open state succeed, the circuit can close. But if they fail, the circuit goes back to the open state. In this way, circuit breakers help get rid of repeated failures from infecting the rest of the application. They also let us configure the appropriate fallback behaviour.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Rate Limiting, Queues, and Concurrency Control</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An LLM-powered application can’t accept unlimited LLM work just because users can submit it from the UI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, if 10K requests arrive at once, forwarding all of them to the LLM provider immediately might exhaust provider limits, database connections, memory, or the application’s budget.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Using rate limiting, we can control how frequently a user or client can submit requests. With concurrency control, we can limit how frequently a user or client might submit requests. Also, concurrency control puts a cap on how many requests the application can process simultaneously. A queue stores extra work until capacity becomes available.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Interactive requests where a user is waiting for the response should usually receive higher priority over background work. For example, a user waiting for a chat response should not be blocked because thousands of documents are being summarized in the background.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The application should also place limits on token usage, document size, number of retrieved passages, number of tool calls, and total workflow duration.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we have taken a detailed look at resiliency and error handling aspects when it comes to LLM-powered applications.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The key takeaway is that LLM-powered applications can have failures that are different from traditional applications. This is because of the inherent probabilistic approach of the LLMs. The important thing is to classify the type of failure so that proper action can be taken by the application.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Despite the differences in the types of errors, we can still borrow many of the techniques for error handling from traditional applications.
