item.title: The startup's Postgres survival guide
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The startup's Postgres survival guide

Alexander Belanger

14 minutes by Alexander Belanger Alexander shares practical lessons from running Postgres in a growing startup. He explains how to design schemas, write efficient queries, manage connections, handle migrations, and tune autovacuum. He also covers query planning, batching, partitioning, locking, and large data migrations. The goal is to help engineers keep Postgres fast, reliable, and stable as their applications scale.
item.description: The startup's Postgres survival guide

item.title: simple terms
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
simple terms

Nadeem Shaikh

4 minutes by Nadeem Shaikh Oracle's Orasort algorithm compares 8 bytes at a time by converting string chunks into 64-bit integers, instead of the traditional one byte at a time approach. This reduces CPU cycles and makes sorting up to 5 times faster. After its patent expired in 2024, open-source databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL began adopting it, and cloud companies now benefit from lower computing costs.
item.description: simple terms

item.title: Fornax's guide to ridiculously fast ethernet
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Fornax's guide to ridiculously fast ethernet

Wim

28 minutes by Wim Getting a 100 Gbps server to actually run at full speed takes serious tuning across the entire system. Key Linux network settings need adjusting, including TCP buffer sizes, congestion control, and memory limits. The network card also needs careful configuration through ethtool, covering ring buffers and interrupt timing. Critically, disabling the IOMMU in the BIOS often makes the biggest difference, yet almost no guides mention it. Cores in space: The core memory module from a 1980 Spacelab
item.description: Fornax's guide to ridiculously fast ethernet

item.title: computer
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
computer

Ken Shirriff

25 minutes by Ken Shirriff Spacelab, a reusable lab carried in the Space Shuttle's cargo bay, used a French-built computer with 128 kilobytes of magnetic core memory instead of modern semiconductor chips. Core memory stores each bit in a tiny magnetic ring, which can hold data without power and resists radiation, making it ideal for space use. Built in 1980, this was an advanced late-era core memory system using high-density components and a design that boosted performance by removing the need for inhibit wires. Semiconductor memory eventually replaced it in the 1990s.
item.description: computer

item.title: Parity before cutover
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Parity before cutover

Alex O'Callaghan

3 minutes by Alex O'Callaghan Big rewrites held back from production let risk build up silently. Bugs pile up, fixes get missed, and two versions drift apart until a painful cutover reveals everything at once. Downgrading to an older Python version first made it possible to run one codebase in both old and new infrastructure, so each migration step changed only one thing. By the time the cloud switch happened, it was uneventful. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Parity before cutover

item.title: How to make AI write high-quality code in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to make AI write high-quality code in .NET

Anton Martyniuk

AI can write .NET code quickly, but it does not always follow your coding standards. Anton explains how to make AI-generated code more reliable using build rules, static analyzers and centralized package management. He shows how to use separate AI code reviews and Claude skills to catch clean-code issues before human review. The goal is to make your standards enforceable instead of relying on prompts. See one of the few solutions purpose-built for generating real
item.description: How to make AI write high-quality code in .NET

item.title: System.Text.Json
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
System.Text.Json

Andrew Lock

.NET 11 and C# 15 are adding support for both union types and closed class hierarchies. In this post, Andrew looks at how System.Text.Json handles these new type hierarchies, the differences between them, as well as some of the sharp edges to watch out for.
item.description: System.Text.Json

item.title: Nullable GUID route constraints in ASP.NET Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Nullable GUID route constraints in ASP.NET Core

Sebastian Nilsson

ASP.NET Core has a built-in GUID route constraint, so no custom code is needed. Add guid to a route parameter to block non-GUID URLs from reaching your endpoint, and add `?` to make the parameter optional. These constraints only control which endpoint gets selected, not whether the value is valid for your business logic, so always validate that separately inside your endpoint. Signal shingle: A novel architecture for high-performance ASP.NET
item.description: Nullable GUID route constraints in ASP.NET Core

item.title: multi-widget sites
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
multi-widget sites

Scott Galloway

Dashboards look like one page but trigger many expensive database calls per visitor, and the problem multiplies fast under load. Signal Shingle solves this by pre-rendering each widget as a cached fragment derived from a single generation-stamped data model, so responses read from cache rather than starting fresh database work. A separate scheduled process handles refresh within a measurable cost budget, meaning heavy traffic makes the system do less work, not more. The page stays fast and coherent even when data is slightly older, and the age is always shown honestly.
item.description: multi-widget sites

item.title: Generate and review the public API of a .NET library
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Generate and review the public API of a .NET library

Gérald Barré

Meziantou.Framework.PublicApiGenerator creates a readable C# file showing the library’s public surface, making API changes easier to spot and review. The tool supports multiple target frameworks, modern .NET 11 features, and CI validation, helping developers detect accidental breaking changes before they reach users. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Generate and review the public API of a .NET library

0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In consistent hashing, you distribute data across different machines or servers using a virtual circular ring.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>PubSub is an asynchronous messaging pattern that decouples service creators from service consumers.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In circuit breaker distributed pattern, it stops an application from repeatedly executing an operation that is likely to fail.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In Retry with a backoff pattern, you handle temporary network glitches or brief service timeouts. It is a resiliency pattern. </span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the leader election pattern, you designate a single master node to manage actions and maintain cluster state. It’s what stops two nodes from thinking they’re in charge.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In quorum read/write pattern, you ensure enough replicas agree on each read and write so that the set overlaps. It is a data consistency pattern that is used in distributed databases to guarantee up-to-date information.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Saga is a design pattern that manages distributed transactions through a sequence of local transactions across multiple microservices. machine runs a complete operating system, Windows, Fedora, or Ubuntu, with its own kernel, drivers, and libraries. The hypervisor (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM) sits directly on hardware and emulates physical machines for each guest OS.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">This makes VMs heavy but isolated. No separate OS per container. Just isolated processes with their own filesystem and dependencies.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">The container engine (Docker, containerd, CRI-O, Podman) manages lifecycle, networking, and isolation, but it all runs on top of a single shared kernel. Lightweight and fast. Containers start in milliseconds because you’re not booting an OS, just launching a process.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">But here’s the catch: all containers on a host must be compatible with that host’s kernel. auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When you open a website, the difference between HTTP and HTTPS decides whether your data travels safely or in plain sight. Here’s what actually happens under the hood:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">HTTP:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Sends data in plain text, anyone on the network can intercept it.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The client and server perform a simple TCP handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Fast but completely insecure. Passwords, tokens, and forms can all be read in transit.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">HTTPS (SSL/TLS):</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Step 1: TCP Handshake: Standard connection setup.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">Step 2: Certificate Check: Client says hello. Server responds with hello and its SSL/TLS certificate. That certificate contains the server’s public key and is signed by a trusted Certificate Authority.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">Your browser verifies this certificate is legitimate, not expired, and actually belongs to the domain you’re trying to reach. This proves you’re talking to the real server, not some attacker pretending to be it.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">Step 3: Key Exchange: Here’s where asymmetric encryption happens. The server has a public key and a private key. Client generates a session key, encrypts it with the server’s public key, and sends it over. Only the server can decrypt this with its private key.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;">Both sides now have the same session key that nobody else could have intercepted. This becomes the symmetric encryption key for the rest of the session.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Step 4: Data Transmission: Now every request and response gets encrypted with that session key using symmetric encryption.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;">Over to you: What’s your go-to tool for debugging TLS issues, openssl, curl -v, or something else?</p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table item.title: The Rise Of The End-To-End Operator
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Rise Of The End-To-End Operator

Wes Kao

“At all types of organizations, I’m seeing more high-performers get rewarded when they can handle projects end-to-end. If a normal operator is an infantry soldier, these operators are Navy SEALs. They can parachute into unknown territory to quickly assess a situation. Then determine the best course of action.”

#CareerGrowth
item.description: The Rise Of The End-To-End Operator

item.title: Load-Bearing People
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Load-Bearing People

Mike Fisher

“Pick your most critical system, process or relationship and name the one person holding it up. Then ask what happens if that person is unreachable for a month starting tomorrow. If the answer scares you, write it down before the feeling passes, because these risks survive on the decision to think about it later.”

#Management TeamHealth
item.description: Load-Bearing People

item.title: The Art Of Simplifying Decisions
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Art Of Simplifying Decisions

David Pereira

“For too long, we’ve endured complex decision-making approaches. Now that decisions are clearly our bottleneck, I’m bullish on those who can simplify them. I want to share my approach with you, and how you can bring it to your scenario. I hope this helps you simplify what others complicate.”

#Leadership DecisionMaking
item.description: The Art Of Simplifying Decisions

item.title: The Mistakes You're Allowed To Make
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Mistakes You're Allowed To Make

Steve Huynh

My friend said something to me once that I’ve been repeating ever since: “Bad news delivered early is just called news.” I think about that line every time I make a mistake.

#Communication CareerGrowth
item.description: The Mistakes You're Allowed To Make

item.title: The Safest Job From AI May Be Writing
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Safest Job From AI May Be Writing

Murat Demirbas

While the programmer's job description is getting completely refactored, writing remains surprisingly unaffected. LLMs have gotten very good at generating code, but I am appalled at the absolute shit they spew as prose... I am increasingly convinced LLMs will not threaten decent writers anytime soon. My prediction rests on the three observations below. Tell me where my logic does not hold up.

#AI CareerGrowth
item.description: The Safest Job From AI May Be Writing

item.title: Let's Build A Compressor From Scratch
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Let's Build A Compressor From Scratch

Adolfo Ochagavía

“Compression is one of those wonderful things we have grown accustomed to in the computer world. You wave a magic wand and — poof! — a file suddenly shrinks to a fraction of its size! You wave the wand again and — pop!— the original file is restored down to the last bit. How can this possibly work? Let’s find out!”

#DeepDive Algo
item.description: Let's Build A Compressor From Scratch

item.title: Building Autonomous Goal Loops That Deliver
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Building Autonomous Goal Loops That Deliver

Jarred Kenny

“The agent keeps moving, but movement is not the problem. The tests only protect what we already know, and the important failures sit outside them. A screen can look complete while it stores nothing. An agent can give the right answer for the wrong reason. A scorer can reward behavior no user wants. More turns make each of those failures cheaper and faster.”

#Testing AI Agents
item.description: Building Autonomous Goal Loops That Deliver

Here’s what CEO William Ready said (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Our approach to model deployment includes our own compact fit-for-purpose models built for Pinterest-specific use cases and suitable open source models post-trained in our own environment within our secure cloud infrastructure. When we leverage open source models, such as with Pinterest Assistant, we are seeing superior performance for our use cases when compared to closed third-party models because we are able to post-train open models on our highly unique data.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>With open models, we are achieving cost per transaction at less than 8% of the cost of comparable closed proprietary models. </span></strong><span>This gives us substantial headroom to deepen and extend these capabilities over time in a way that is differentiated, highly effective, and cost efficient.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Basically, what used to cost Pinterest $100 to run on a closed, frontier model, they now spend $8 on by using open models on owned or rented inference!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AT&T: 56% savings by swapping Claude for open models</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With 100,000 employees, AT&T is a big spender on AI. The telco giant cut its AI bill by 56% while measuring a 2% decrease in the quality of AI’s output, after they moved workloads over to open models. From </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/10153f47-8aff-4d49-b647-cbd17236b0e8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The Information</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Austin said he’s found that open source models are “just as good or better” than older models sold by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI. For instance, AT&T’s software developers still rely on cutting-edge models for complex tasks like generating code, but can use cheaper open source models for less intense tasks like generating summaries of previously submitted code, he said.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After the company began using router provider LiteLLM, the costs of some advanced AI tasks such as coding fell by as much as 56% while the quality of the AI’s performance fell just 2%, Austin said.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Anthropic overpriced compared to the rest of the market?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Only a few months ago, Anthropic was the preferred model (Claude) and harness (Claude Code) among engineers. But Anthropic’s models are becoming steeply more expensive at a time when open weight models – and also OpenAI – are getting much cheaper. Meanwhile, Opus 5 is 100x more expensive (!!) than models like GPT-5.6 Luna xhigh and DeepSeek. That may be simply too much to ignore for some tech companies:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 1);"><span>2. Automatic software maintenance experiments by Linear and Anthropic</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two interesting experiments took place involving getting agents to automate some parts of maintenance:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Karri Saarinen, cofounder at Linear </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a31aeccb-a872-47cd-9c38-b984e9890a25?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shared</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Our bug autofix loop in Linear has fixed 300+ bugs in the last 30 days.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The team set it up as part of triage: it connects to Datadog and Sentry to investigate issues, then assigns them to Linear’s coding agent to fix.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Elsewhere, Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code, is also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/59bc3134-9655-486c-9c50-494866a8af0b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>experimenting</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A weird experiment I’ve been trying the last few weeks is having Claude take over day-to-day maintenance of our apps. Seeing early signs of life that this might be possible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The setup is straightforward: we have a Slack channel called proj-claude-maintains-apps. In it, Claude Tag runs a bunch of daily routines across iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI, and Agent SDK:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Crash fuzzer: open the app in a simulator and tap around to find ways to crash it, then root cause and fix the crashes</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Dup unifier: scans the codebase for similar-yet-slightly-divergent abstractions, and puts up PRs to unify them</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Dead-code remover: removes statically unreachable code, and adds logging to suspected dead code to check if it’s really dead and if so, remove it the next day</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Abstraction police: fixes leaky abstractions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A bunch more..</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Results have been surprisingly positive. Over the last few weeks, these routines have opened 388 PRs across our repos, 180 of which we merged after Claude Code Review + human review. We’re now thinking about how to streamline this to make merging these kinds of mechanical changes easier.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In each case, the opening of PRs is automated and engineers decide whether or not to merge it. For Anthropic, 45% of PRs raised were worthy of merging. This doesn’t mean we’re close to “maintenance on autopilot”, but agents automatically raising PRs for bugs or maintenance tasks, is something that would have looked like science fiction even two years ago!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/59b8fb6b-f36b-4dbc-a9f4-44bd5700d5fe?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Amp</span></a><span>: supports GPT-5.6 or Fable 5.1 models, does not support Gemini</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>… and, until recently, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8ae7727c-c667-42c1-b07a-94c8a5e393e8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Cursor</span></a><span>, which supported GPT-5.6, Opus/Sonnet/Fable 5, and Gemini models</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This week, however, OpenAI announced the removal of GPT-5.6 from Cursor, effective November. Tibo Sottiaux, heading up Codex, explained (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We unfortunately have decided that we cannot continue providing access to our models through Cursor and are ending our partnership. </span><strong><span>It boils down to trust </span></strong><span>and we’ve asked that this takes effect on November 12 to give you some time to plan.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a rule, frontier AI labs don’t like it when their cutting-edge models end up inside a rival’s product, supporting its success. For example,</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>OpenAI’s GPT models cannot be used from Anthropic’s Claude Code, or from Google’s Antigravity</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Anthropic’s Claude cannot be used with OpenAI’s Codex, out-of-the-box (even though Codex supports using other models when you bring your own API key), and Google’s Antigravity only offers seven month-old Claude models (Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, which are considered so outdated that even Anthropic does not offer these anymore)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Google’s Gemini cannot be used from Claude Code or Codex (unless using it via API, in Codex)</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI announced this change right after SpaceX acquired Cursor and cited trust as the problem. In a longer, official statement, OpenAI </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c54140a5-b201-4823-8f48-8a53eba9fc48?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>spells it out</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk’s companies violating contracts.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI has a point, as Elon Musk is known for acting as if legally binding contracts don’t apply to him: he just breaks them and forces the other party to sue for damages, which might take years. For example, when the world’s first trillionaire bought Twitter in 2022 and laid off 75% of employees, he refused to pay people’s contracted severance. Thousands of folks owed severance had to launch a class-action lawsuit in 2023, which lasted three years. X </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8452470b-7406-46c3-9ffe-997bfdf3d9f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>finally settled</span></a><span> for only </span><em><span>almost</span></em><span> the previously legally due amount! People fought three years in court to win </span><em><span>less</span></em><span> severance than they were due. Perhaps Musk’s disdain for the law was rational after all!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was a fairly typical case of his way of doing business, so it’s unsurprising that OpenAI assumes SpaceX may not heed terms and conditions in the future about not using GPT-5.6 outputs to train its own next-generation model. That’s not allowed, but when did that stop the SpaceX owner from doing anything?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Interestingly, Anthropic has not pulled Claude from Cursor, but Anthropic is dependent on SpaceX for infra. </span></strong><span>To me, OpenAI pulling GPT from Cursor is a clear story. I was confused as to why Anthropic did not follow: because a year ago, the AI company cut off Claude usage for Windsurf, after rumors of OpenAI buying Windsurf were floating around. As TechCrunch reported at the time:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Anthropic co-founder and Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan said his company cut Windsurf’s direct access to Anthropic’s Claude AI models largely because of rumors and reports that OpenAI, its largest competitor, is acquiring the AI coding assistant.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I think it would be odd for us to be selling Claude to OpenAI,” Kaplan said.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a kicker: Windsurf was not bought by OpenAI – Google acquired the company instead. So Anthropic was decisive in cutting access based on a rumor. And yet, with SpaceX acquiring Cursor, Anthropic is content with a major frontier lab (SpaceX) offering Claude. This is surely because Anthropic is paying $15B per year to SpaceX to use their Colossus 1 data center, which provides critical compute to Anthropic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s rare to see a frontier lab like SpaceX have so much leverage over the leading AI lab, Anthropic: and given that Elon Musk is someone who is hard to trust in business, I assume Anthropic is looking for a way out of this awkward situation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the meantime, I’m sure Anthropic won’t be offended, should SpaceX not follow Claude’s own terms and conditions, especially on the anti-distillation clauses!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. HR tech startup operates with a “one dev per project” approach</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9a0c2354-43b0-485c-8121-8851ccadc83e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reported</span></a><span> recently how projects at Anthropic are now done with a maximum of two software engineers, and one startup is taking this a step further with its one-dev-per-project model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ashby, a Series D HR tech company with around 70 engineers, also has zero deadlines and no standups, according to cofounder and VP of Engineering, Abhik Pramanik, who </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/abcdccdc-67d2-49e5-892d-46b29d1d8aab?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explained</span></a><span> how things work there:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Project teams of one engineer</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Engineers make both product and design decisions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Engineers own features from product spec through launch</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>No standups, no JIRA tickets, no deadlines, no estimates</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Project teams which consist of one person at Ashby are clearly a result of AI tooling: a backend engineer, a frontend engineer and a designer are no longer needed to ship a new feature that touches the service layer, the frontend, and that looks decent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, early-stage, VC-funded startups worked in similar ways pre-AI before product-market fit was found. Once it was, deadlines let customers know when to expect key launches. Ashby has definitely found product-market fit: it has more than 2,700 businesses paying for its recruitment platform, an Applicant Tracking System (ATS), and keeps iterating on it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I also wonder if “no deadlines” is a good fit for most SaaS businesses. </span></strong><span>A software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform needs to keep up with how the industry operates and evolves, and keep solving the pain points customers have. When completing a project takes days instead of months, then why bother with deadlines?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Deadlines work best when used sparingly for major projects. I reckon Ashby does use – or will use – deadlines for either projects like a new product line, or when there’s an external deadline like a major event with a partner, an important sales demo for a large potential customer, etc.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7e1768cd-0883-4eb2-97d8-94561c598a28?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>interview</span></a><span> with NextPlay reports that the startup looks for the following skills:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Autonomy</span></strong><span>: own your work, end-to-end, and don’t be someone who depends on a PM to write tickets on what to do</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Great written communication skills</span></strong><span>: and knowing when and how to communicate with colleagues, usually in writing (since they’re all heads down, building projects with a bunch of agents)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Comfortable working full remote with few interactions</span></strong><span>: People who value social interaction highly are likely not a good fit, as the setup is remote and disincentivizes meetings.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s good to see full-remote companies like Ashby thrive. Full-remote work culture comes at the cost of less collaboration and conversation, but some people thrive in this environment!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. Industry Pulse</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Meta moved over to Slack for better agent interoperability</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are some eye-catching details in reports that Meta dropped Google Chat in favor of Slack because Google Chat has essentially no agentic capabilities, whereas Slack is excellent at integrating with AI agents. There’s a lot to unpack:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Meta used Google Chat?? </span></strong><span>Meta built its own internal chat tool called Workplace Chat, which has been used for close to a decade. But as I previously confirmed with current Meta engineers, the social media giant discontinued development. It was unclear why Google Chat was chosen; probably because Meta was already using Google Workspace for emails and docs, and Google Chat is free!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>How is Google Chat nearly a year behind Slack in AI capabilities? </span></strong><span>Slack announced adding MCP support in October 2025, and made the feature generally available this February. Meanwhile, Google Chat announced adding MCP support four months later. Today, in September 2026 it’s only in developer preview, not generally available. Meanwhile, Slack has already shipped </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6afc4595-ad9a-4e60-a40c-fca70609aa2e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Slack Code</span></a><span>, a neat interface for AI coding agents to plug into Slack, including making it easy to review code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>SaaS is definitely not dead when Meta spends $15-20M/year to buy a chat app. </span></strong><span>Meta has around 75,000 employees, and I estimate it spends in the range of $15-20M annually on Slack. But for much less, it could surely assemble a team of three engineers with a bunch of AI tools and a token budget to build something similar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Well, Meta did similar with Workplace Chat and after 10 years the result was a product that was worse than Slack; indeed, current Meta engineers told me it had worse performance than Google Chat. AI or not, building a product that works seamlessly for tens of thousands of people and continually adding support for the latest new integrations and AI agents, would take more than a few engineers and some AI tools!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If Meta prefers to pay tens of millions for a chat tool, it’s probably unrealistic for smaller companies to build their own chat SaaS solutions. It could be a reminder of how profitable it can be when you’re the best at doing one thing, like Slack is for chat + AI agent integrations.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Layoffs at Uber and PagerDuty</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Unfortunately, layoffs are back:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Uber: 10%</span></strong><span> (3,000 people) let go this week. Managers have been cut to reduce the number of layers, “micro-teams” (where managers have 1-2 reports) were halved, and plenty of software engineers have been dismissed. It may or not be pertinent that there wasn’t a single mention of AI in the layoff announcement; instead, Uber said it had too many layers, and had probably overhired in recent years.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>PagerDuty: 15%</span></strong><span> (170 people). The paging company has been struggling to grow its business for years, while new startups like Rootly, FireHydrant, incident.io </span><em><span>(note: I’m </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ee66fb9b-c240-47d1-a7a6-2785c362d59f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>an investor</span></a><span>)</span></em><span>, and others are eating their lunch. Uber </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0cc3175a-4a1c-46eb-8c34-185748ecaa66?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>dumped</span></a><span> PagerDuty after 12 years over reliability concerns, and moved to a more reliable startup.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both Uber and PagerDuty are profitable: Uber is generating $9B of profit (net income) on $55B of annual revenue, while PagerDuty generates $185M profit on $495M of revenue. It’s just that business is not growing as much as before; the stock price demands growth of revenue and/or profits. Both companies likely hope to boost profits by reducing costs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s been a while since the wave of layoffs in 2023, but they keep happening at mature tech companies.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Anthropic upsets devs with usage limit “raise” that’s actually the opposite</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anthropic predictably angered devs by decreasing usage limits, only days after saying the precise opposite. Is this what happens when corporate comms people take over the writing of announcements?</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px Uber experiencing a 9x increase in agent requests this year is a case in point</span></p></li></ol><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Demand for Apple Mac mini & Mac Studio surges on AI</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI companies are buying Mac mini and Mac Studio models like candy because of their powerful M-series processors (M6 or M5 Ultra in the latest ones), and the memory it supports (up to 512GB for Mac Studio and 32/64GB for Mac mini). From </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c64f902-3d37-4f1b-b368-c1b2d788fc08?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The Information:</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Some AI labs like OpenAI have bought tens of thousands of Mac minis and Mac Studios for the task of reinforcement learning, a technique where the AI learns through trial and error, said people familiar with OpenAI. OpenAI is using these Macs for training computer-use agents and is desperate to acquire more of them, the people said. Anthropic also rents Mac minis from Amazon’s cloud service, Amazon Web Services, people familiar with Anthropic’s efforts said.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some startups are even building out Mac-only cloud services, in anticipation of a future where demand for Apple hardware grows so much that some AI developers will want to run on Macs in data centers rather than locally.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Demand is so big that NVIDIA is starting to see Apple as its biggest competitor for running local AI workloads. Equally amusingly, Apple has no enterprise strategy, nor any engineering teams focused on its biggest customers, despite enterprises being the biggest buyers of Mac minis and Mac Studios.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Typical Apple: build amazing hardware and hope everything else will follow!</span></p><h3 break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Imagine a bank account with $100. Let’s assume that two separate withdrawal requests of $10 each arrive at the same moment. However, after the two withdrawals are made, the account still ends up $90.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On a purely technical level, both withdrawal requests completed successfully. There was no error. But the account balance is wrong. The remaining balance should have been $80.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On its own, both transactions were correct. Each read the correct balance and performed the correct calculations. And yet, there is a bug. The reason for this bug was the overlap between the two transactions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You might think this type of overlap is a rare condition. However, this is not true. Overlapping transactions are more or less the normal condition in which databases operate. At any given point in time, multiple processes are trying to write something to a database, often on the same set of records. It just takes two of them to collide with each other inside a window of a few milliseconds for these types of bugs to show up.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So how do we handle such bugs?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is what we are going to try to answer in this article. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Different ways to handle data conflicts</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So he rebuilt that layer first — one platform carrying data across fabs on three continents, with identity, permissions, and audit trails handled once instead of per project. However, the success of any such RAG system depends on the quality of the embedding model (the model that helps translate words into numbers) that is used by the RAG system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider the example where a particular product’s documentation specifies that annual subscriptions can be refunded only within 30 days. A chatbot built using RAG is supposed to answer customer queries based on this support documentation. However, when a customer asks whether a subscription bought 45 days ago can be refunded, the chatbot confidently answers “yes”.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why did the chatbot make a mess of this seemingly simple question?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The answer lies in the behaviour of the embedding model, which is kind of a translator for AI. This model controls the answer-searching process and is different from the language model that generates the actual answer. No matter how good the language model might be, it cannot give correct answers if the embedding model doesn’t do its job properly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we’re going to look at how this embedding model works in an RAG setup and what makes it such a critical part of the system. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why a RAG System Searches Before Answering</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A generic language model’s knowledge depends on what it was taught during training. You can’t expect such a model to know about a company’s private documents, policies, or internal source code. It won’t even know about the company’s latest information that might have been published after the model was trained. Technically, it’s quite costly to retrain a language model every time there’s a change in the information.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is where RAG helps. It separates the ability to generate language from finding relevant details from a pool of stored knowledge. While the language model handles the understanding and writing parts, the external knowledge collection contains the actual information that should be used for writing the answers.</span></p><div documents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: text.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It divides the text into smaller passages known as chunks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It sends each chunk into an embedding model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It filters and reranks those chunks, placing them inside the language model’s prompt.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Finally, the language model writes an answer using the prompt that was provided.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure from all this is that RAG doesn’t place the entire document collection into the model’s prompt. This is because doing so would exceed the model’s context limit and fill it with irrelevant information. It also increases costs and latency. The retrieval phase, led by the RAG’s embedding model, serves as the selection step, reducing thousands of passages to a small set for the language model to check.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>How Embeddings Make it Possible to Search by Meaning</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding is basically just a list of numbers that represents a piece of text. A real embedding might contain numbers such as 384, 768, 1024, or several thousand numbers.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/d0041822-acb6-4e6d-9ece-202bb7b9b55e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/80859fee-bbe4-4fd9-abf5-8088ebff967b_2408x1366.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":826,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":87156,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/212751164?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F80859fee-bbe4-4fd9-abf5-8088ebff967b_2408x1366.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="312.0192307692308" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!iWE7!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F80859fee-bbe4-4fd9-abf5-8088ebff967b_2408x1366.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These individual numbers don’t have simple labels describing their meanings. You cannot look at a particular value and say that this means “subscription” while another means “refund”. The overall meaning is distributed across the complete vector. Think of the vector as the coordinates of a point in a mathematical space. An embedding model is trained to place text with related meaning near each other within this mathematical vector space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is how the system can connect a term like “yearly plan” with “annual subscription”. It can also connect complex phrases like “get my money back” with “receive a refund”. In contrast, a keyword search struggles when a question and the document use different words to explain the same concept. But an embedding model tries to compare the ideas present within the text rather than just the vocabulary. Common techniques behind this are cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance. In a nutshell, the goal of an embedding model is to produce a mathematical score that indicates how close two vectors are to each other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The embedding model often returns the first k results. This is known as top-k retrieval. For example, if k is 5, the retrieval returns the top 5 highest-ranked chunks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Embedding models also support asymmetric retrieval where the query and document have different forms. The query may be a short question. But the matching document is a longer explanatory passage. For example, the query could be something like: “Can an annual subscription be refunded after 6 weeks?” The answer passage is a statement like: “Annual subscriptions can be refunded within 30 days.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding model trained to compare similar sentences may not perform as well as a model that is trained to connect questions with the relevant passages. To summarize, the embedding model defines what the RAG system considers similar.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why Related Information is not Always the Right Information</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding model is trained to identify semantic similarity. But a RAG system requires something a bit more strict. It needs to find passages that might contain the information needed to answer a specific question. The problem is that a passage can be related to the question without clearly answering it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, a customer asking how long a refund takes might receive a passage explaining who qualifies for the refund. Both these pieces of information concern refunds, but only one talks about the actual processing time. See the diagram below that shows the concept of semantic search space.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/e67f3312-3680-4b15-827f-48deaa6eaa97?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/fc0152b6-129d-4fe4-8e52-551b5119c32a_3194x1778.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":811,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":220264,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/212751164?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffc0152b6-129d-4fe4-8e52-551b5119c32a_3194x1778.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}"
