style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Multiple failure modes can pop up in this situation:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Similar Subject, Different Question: </span></strong><span>The query asks “How long will an approved refund take to arrive?” The retrieved passage says: “Purchases can be refunded within 30 days.” The passage is relevant to refunds but does not answer the timing question.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Same Words, Different Entity: </span></strong><span>The query asks “how can the billing address be changed.” The retrieved passage explains how to change the account’s email address. Both talk about changing account details. But they refer to completely different fields.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Negation: </span></strong><span>Consider the two passages: “Administrators can delete archived projects”, and “Administrators cannot delete archived projects”. Most of the words are identical. This means their embeddings may be close. But as you can see, they have opposite meanings.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Versions and Dates: </span></strong><span>A knowledge base may contain an old policy and its replacement. The text may be almost identical except for a date, limit, or price. Embeddings cannot automatically know which document is authoritative. Metadata filters or version management rules may need to exclude outdated content explicitly.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Numerical Identifiers: </span></strong><span>The two sentences “Annual subscriptions can be refunded within 30 days” and “Annual subscriptions can be refunded within 60 days” are semantically very similar. But there is a difference in one number, which determines the final answer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Domain-specific Meanings:</span></strong><span> General models can misunderstand special vocabulary. For example, “capture” has one meaning in an ordinary language and a specific meaning in payment processing. Similarly, the word “port” can refer to networking, hardware, or moving software between platforms. The best model for general web text may not be the best model for legal contracts, medical reports, financial documents, or source code.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Multi-part questions: </span></strong><span>A customer may ask multi-part questions. For example, there could be a question like “Can I cancel the subscription, and how long will the refund take?” The answer for this requires at least two passages. One might explain eligibility for cancellation. Another might explain processing time. The model that retrieves only one subject may produce an incomplete answer.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why a Better Language Model Cannot Repair Bad Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In an RAG system, the language model just sees the user’s question and the selected passages. It doesn’t see every document that might have been stored in the vector database.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, if the annual refund policy document is not retrieved, the language model won’t have any idea about the missing information. A more capable language model may recognize that the retrieved information doesn’t contain the answer. This is useful because it can at least choose not to respond with invalid information. However, this failed retrieval scenario also creates several possible outcomes:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The model answers from its general training knowledge.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It incorrectly applies a related passage.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It might invent a plausible rule.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It says that the available information is insufficient.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It combines conflicting passages incorrectly.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A prompt such as “answer only from the supplied documents” can reduce unsupported answers. But it cannot make the correct document magically appear.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is why testing and debugging are so critical during the development of an RAG system. Developers need to inspect retrieved chunks before changing prompts or swapping language models. It takes a lot more time to solve a retrieval problem in the generation phase.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>What Makes an Embedding Model Suitable For a RAG System</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The most important concern when choosing an embedding model should be retrieval performance. The model should be really good at connecting short questions with longer sentences that might contain the answers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The following characteristics matter:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Domain and Vocabulary:</span></strong><span> The model should understand the language used by the documents and users. Testing should include the use of abbreviations, internal product names, technical terms, and so on. If a company calls annual subscriptions “yearly plans” in the UI, but “annual contracts” in their legal documents, the model should be able to connect those expressions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Language Support: </span></strong><span>A multilingual model is critical when documents, queries, or both may use different languages. The model should be able to connect a query in one language with an answer found in another language.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Embedding Dimensions: </span></strong><span>Embedding dimension is the number of values in each stored vector. Larger vectors preserve more information. But size does not guarantee better retrieval. Also, dimensions have a direct impact on raw storage costs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Maximum Input Length: </span></strong><span>A model with a limit of 8192 tokens can embed much longer text than one limited to 512 tokens. But it doesn’t mean each document should become one big chunk. A long chunk might discuss multiple things like refunds, cancellations, billing addresses, and so on. A focused question may match it less precisely than it would match a smaller passage specific to the relevant policy.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Model and Query Speed: </span></strong><span>Indexing speed determines how much time it takes to embed the document collection. Query speed affects every user request. Some important metrics to consider are the number of chunks embedded per second, query-embedding latency, CPU or GPU requirements, memory use, and the cost of running the model. A model that gains a bit of retrieval quality at the cost of a substantial increase in latency may not be the right choice.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Deployment Requirements: </span></strong><span>Embedding dimensions determine the size of each output vector. Model size determines how much memory and computation are needed to run the embedding model. These are key details required to plan for the model’s deployment.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why Changing the Embedding Model Later Is Expensive</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each embedding model creates its own vector space, which is unique to the particular model. This means that the embeddings produced by Model A have no dependable relationship with the embeddings produced by Model B.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider an example where all document chunks are embedded using Model A. If we suddenly start to embed the incoming questions using Model B, the system will end up comparing vectors from incompatible spaces. It will be like an apples-to-oranges comparison. Even if both models output the same number of dimensions, the numbers can mean very different things.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This means that the entire corpus of documents needs to be re-embedded using Model B. In other words, migrating an embedding model needs a lot more than just running the new model. It involves the following steps:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Generate new vectors for every chunk.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Build a new vector index.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Apply the correct metadata and access permissions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Keep new or modified documents synchronized during the migration.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Test retrieval quality.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Move production searches to the new index.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Retain a rollback path if the new system performs poorly.</span></p></li></ul><div migration process include embedding API charges or GPU time, index-building time, paying for temporary duplicate storage, data transfer costs, evaluation work, and operational risk.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The migration also changes rankings. For example, a model with a higher benchmark score may perform worse on the application’s specific domain terminology. Therefore, application-specific testing is extremely important to make sure that the answer quality has not gone down.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few design choices can make it safer to implement future changes:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The original chunks should remain the source of truth. A vector database should not be the only place where processed text exists.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Each chunk should have a stable identifier and a content hash. The hash helps determine whether the text changed and needs a new embedding</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Embedding records should include:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Model name</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Model version or revision</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Embedding dimension</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Query and passage format</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Normalization method</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Chunking version</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Creation time</span></p></li></ul></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A new model should receive a new index or vector field. Its embeddings should not be mixed with old embeddings.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To summarize, a safe migration resembles the classic blue-green deployment approach where the old index continues to serve production traffic even as a new index is built in parallel.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To be clear about things, changing the embedding model is just one of the operations that requires a rebuild. Changing the chunking strategy, parser, cleaning rules, prefixes, or stored dimensions may also require the documents to be rebuilt.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>How Matryoshka Embeddings Offer More Control Over Vector Size</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A basic embedding model produces a fixed-size vector. Its dimensions are meant to work together. We cannot delete most of these dimensions without severely reducing the quality of retrieval.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, a Matryoshka model is trained differently. During training, such a model is configured to produce useful representations at different prefix lengths, such as the first 256, 512, 1024, and full dimensions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While the initial dimensions contain a useful coarse representation, the later dimensions pack more detailed information. For example, in a 1024-dimensional embedding, the first 256 dimensions can contain a useful small representation. Similarly, the first 512 dimensions contain a more detailed representation. At the end, all 1024 dimensions provide a complete representation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are three practical storage designs to support Matryoshka models:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Storing the smaller vector: </span></strong><span>The system creates an embedding. It then keeps the first 256 dimensions and normalizes the shortened vector if needed. Only these dimensions are stored. This reduces the index size and overall search cost. However, the discarded dimensions are gone forever. If we want to migrate the system to a larger dimension, we need to generate the embeddings again.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Storing the full vector with a smaller search representation: </span></strong><span>The system stores the complete vector in secondary storage. But it places a smaller prefix in the fast vector index. This supports future flexibility. We can build a larger index from the stored vectors without the need to rerun the model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Storing smaller and full vectors for two-stage retrieval: </span></strong><span>The system makes a search on the entire corpus using just 256-dimensional vectors (the reduced dimension). It then retrieves the full vectors for the best candidates and compares them precisely. This brings down the cost of the large initial search. But it retains full precision for the shortlisted candidates.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure Matryoshka embeddings don’t solve incompatibility between different models. They mainly help support different usable sizes within a model’s vector space. Switching to another embedding model still requires the entire re-embedding process we talked about earlier.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As we discussed, an RAG system can’t generate a reliably grounded answer unless it first retrieves the details required for that answer. This makes an embedding model the most important part of an RAG setup.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This doesn’t mean that other things are not important. Retrieval quality of the RAG system also depends on various factors such as:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The existence of the correct documents</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How well the parsing process keeps their content intact</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How the documents are divided into chunks</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How versioning is managed</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Metadata filters and their working</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How a reranker improves the candidate list</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Nevertheless, the embedding model remains central because it helps decide which information enters the language model’s context. It acts as the first major relevance decision in a typical RAG pipeline. The key lesson is to choose an embedding model that retrieves the correct evidence for the questions at an acceptable cost and speed.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b4674b0a-149a-404c-bbca-6b0afa3d612d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Twitter</span></a><span>. The topic was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2c10b0a-42b6-4752-ad33-8651646d49c7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>the seniority rollercoaster</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My personal expectations weren’t high back then; the subscription model for newsletters on platforms like Substack was starting to take off, but the focus was strongly on politics, business, and finance. It wasn’t clear if there was any demand for a publication about software engineering, written by a software engineer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I soon found out there was demand that surpassed </span><em><span>all</span></em><span> my expectations – and then some! Fast forward to today; the newsletter has more than 1.1M readers, tens of thousands of paid subscribers, a podcast, and more than 500,000 YouTube subscribers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>But the numbers aren’t the most validating thing for me; that would be the feedback sent in by readers. </span></strong><span>Via email, in DMs, or in-person at events, it’s great to hear how an article or a podcast we published helped someone try a new approach, or to gain confidence that theirs was the right one, or that an article helped convince a team to change things. It also means a lot to learn that The Pragmatic Engineer helps people feel more confident about keeping up in this fast-changing industry.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Thanks again for your support! </span></em><span>It’s the reason why The Pragmatic Engineer is a viable business and a growing publication, and means we can “scale up” our coverage to deliver ever-more detail about how software gets built, today.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today’s issue covers:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Diving deeper, year after year. </span></strong><span>The evolution of the Pragmatic Engineer’s coverage over five years, getting in through the “front door” instead of the “back door” for deepdives, launching the podcast, The Pragmatic Summit, and growing our team.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>What’s next? </span></strong><span>What we’re excited about, the second Pragmatic Summit, and how you can expect us to stay focused on how building software is changing, and the ways that successful engineers, teams, and companies adapt.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cash-prize writing contest: </span></strong><span>Software is changing faster than ever. Send us your essay about how things are changing for you, for the chance to win cash prizes worth up to $10,000. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/35a2a2e1-5efa-47ed-a0af-2015bf1ecd66?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Read more on how to take part</span></a><span>.</span></p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. Diving deeper, year after year</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Pragmatic Engineer was 15 years in the making and not an overnight success; I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f663af13-6f5e-4b39-ae42-a90f355b2366?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>started</span></a><span> to write a blog in 2007 about software development, which was “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/65c76e2b-7847-4b7b-a23f-03b7579b125d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>rebooted</span></a><span>” as “The Pragmatic Engineer Blog” in 2015. At the time, it was read by almost nobody! </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b7867433-c79d-478b-a629-fc4d351b0c47?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>In 2019</span></a><span>, I launched an email digest (“v0” of the newsletter), and a year later, I decided to focus on the newsletter fulltime after quitting Uber as a manager following job cuts in 2020, when a quarter of my team was laid off and the rest were disbanded due to the pandemic. I took an employment break, planning to finish </span><em><span>‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce26b6d4-2b75-4cbc-ab40-612f58cee120?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The Software Engineer’s Guidebook</span></a><span>’</span></em><span> in six months and then start a VC-funded startup. In the end, finishing the book took another two years, and I didn’t kick off that VC-funded startup! Instead, I decided to go all-in on writing a newsletter targeted exclusively at software engineers and engineering leaders.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: underline;"><span>first-ever Pragmatic Summit</span></a><span>, which took place in February this year in San Francisco, with great help from the excellent Statsig team (many of whom now work at OpenAI). With 500 attendees, 15 standout speakers – and with it being the first-ever conference I’d organized – it was a smashing success. A one-minute video recap of the event:</span></p><div class="video-player-with-background is-static video-player-wrapper" role="region" aria-label="Video player" style="flex-grow: 1;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin-top: 0.5em;"><a class="video-player video-player-with-background" href="https://substack.com/redirect/0c4a7523-a0d0-4b0c-b379-bbf318649142?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;display: block;width: 100%;cursor: pointer;background-color: rgb(0,0,0);height: auto;border-radius: 8px;padding-bottom: 0"><img class="video-player-preview" width="550" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Zxm2!,w_1100,h_618,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/l_play_button_usfui2,w_144,e_colorize:0/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-video.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fvideo_upload%2Fpost%2F213733051%2F52a9f314-6944-4251-ae8f-28d27af4320c%2Ftranscoded-00001.png" data-component-name="VideoPlayer-PreviewImg" data-testid="video-player-static-preview-image" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;top: 0;left: 0;width: 100%;max-height: 100%;background: black;cursor: pointer;object-fit: contain;position: relative;border-radius: 8px;"></a></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Based on the feedback from attendees, there will be another Pragmatic Summit in San Francisco next year. I’ll share details in the coming weeks; we’re in the middle of putting this event together now!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>2026: Growing the team in order to dive deeper</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Predictably, the most time-consuming task in The Pragmatic Engineer is working on deepdives. We often spend up to two months on a single deepdive, educating ourselves on the topic being covered, talking with expert engineers, and generally getting deep into a topic in order to deliver a deepdive worth reading.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I say “us” because this year, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c375114-17fe-4bd6-aedd-24843d9fdfba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Jessica Salmon</span></a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/97f2d4d7-7fb1-466f-98d4-12706ad3d672?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Ivan Klaric</span></a><span> joined the team. Both are software engineers with startup and Big Tech experience, who enjoy spending time getting to understand topics and contributing to longform articles.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. What’s next?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With a larger team than before, we’ve continued to produce deepdives for readers. A few recent ones:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb024a87-ec94-4662-b55b-a0473ec32fca?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Why Ramp built its own in-house coding agent, Inspect</span></a></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a526402-8d8b-4e7c-8200-7580c7d903bb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b6574b4a-1c32-49ba-aa9e-566372648f53?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: href="https://substack.com/redirect/9be45588-7d9f-4f51-a92b-b7dd1acb2fce?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>State of the software engineering job market in 2026</span></a></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I’ve found there are no shortcuts for producing an in-depth article on a relevant topic for readers. You simply have to put the time and effort into it. </span></strong><span>This involves spending a lot of time on thinking and understanding things, going directly to engineers who build what we want to learn about, and then spending even more time on organizing research material into a lengthy article that’s informative and hopefully not dull to read.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Needless to say, we’ve experimented with the analytical powers of AI tools in parts of the research process. The technology is good at gathering publicly-available sources and does a decent job of summarizing them, but that’s been more or less the limits of AI’s usefulness for our purposes to date – except as a spelling and grammar checking tool after a full draft is written by a person.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If anything, AI can easily lead you down the wrong track by theorizing about non-existent connections and confidently espousing theories which some basic critical thinking could easily debunk!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Aside from research and correcting (most) typos, we don’t use AI in this publication. That’s because we are writing for a readership of humans and believe in the value of human voices. What you read, hear, and see in The Pragmatic Engineer comes from me and other engineers, and plenty of thought goes into each sentence.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>What comes next?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a company that doesn’t have any venture funding, we can be ambitious without chasing any “growth goals.” In the near future, our goal is to keep doing what we do, and do it better. This means:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>More ambitious deepdives. </span></strong><span>We’ll keep bringing you deepdives from inside companies and teams building cutting-edge, fascinating software; how do they do it, what is working for them, and why? The more you understand about why engineering approaches work in certain places and situations, the more likely you’ll be able to effectively apply them in your own setting.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>In-person events. </span></strong><span>The Pragmatic Summit returns to San Francisco in February 2027. It’s my long-term goal to have a second summit in Europe, as well. Meanwhile, I’ll keep attending in-person events, like the upcoming shows in New York City with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2a9ec1cd-9ca3-4e7e-bd96-d1f256d977db?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>turbopuffer</span></a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3275cd00-ac77-440e-a9ba-44cb45bac642?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>WorkOS</span></a><span>, and let you know in the newsletter when these happen.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Interesting podcast conversations. </span></strong><span>Recording conversations with software professionals and leaders is something that keeps filling my bucket. Expect more great conversations coming your way.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Keeping up with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0d211d4-86dd-4ad3-b652-9f0843ca9314?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The Pulse.</span></a><span> </span></strong><span>I spend most of the week talking with engineers on various channels and at companies as part of my efforts to check ‘the pulse’ of the tech business: what’s happening and what’s changing. Writing The Pulse on Thursdays remains a personal highlight of my week.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building more of our own software stack – on the side. </span></strong><span>One thing that AI has made easier is context switching between writing and building software. In the past six months, I’ve found myself building more parts of The Pragmatic Engineer backend stack, such as landing pages, through to API endpoints used for group subscriptions, refunds, and more. This year, I’ve probably built more software scratching my own itch at the publication than in previous years combined! </span><em><span>Of course, our software stack is not our top focus, but it’s a welcome distraction to work on.</span></em></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>A big theme for the rest of 2026 is how software engineering is changing: </span></strong><span>tools used for decades like IDEs are falling out of style, and processes long considered as best practices, like code reviews, are becoming optional. Of course, the biggest change is that we’re spending little to no time on typing out the code, which has never been the case since computing existed. Even before computer keyboards, programmers were writing programs on punch cards!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The good news is that we see that fundamentals still matter: many software engineers who were considered standout devs before seem to be even more in demand than ever, while picking up AI engineering appears to be easier than learning a new programming language.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nonetheless, this change is destabilizing, fast-paced, and no one has figured out the “right” way to build software with AI. We’ll keep reporting on cases of teams and individuals that adapt well, while also paying attention to those things that don’t change, such as how teams, as a “core” unit of a business, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fbda43e6-b5fc-469e-8817-04a0058251d5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>seem to be just as important</span></a><span> at leading AI labs as they were pre-AI.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. How software engineering is changing: essay challenge</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To finish, we’re delighted to announce an essay challenge on the prescient topic of how software engineering is changing for professionals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As mentioned, the pace of change in software engineering is only accelerating, with rapid industry-wide adoption of LLMs, AI tooling, and AI infrastructure. At The Pragmatic Engineer, we aim to cover much of what’s going on, and as part of that, we’d love to pull in more perspectives than what our team can cover alone.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Send us an article no more than 10,000 words long on how you see things changing at your startup or tech company. We’ll award $10,000 for the best essay we read, </span></strong><span>and other leading entries can win smaller prizes. Articles sent to us will be eligible for publication in future editions of the Pragmatic Engineer. </span><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/35a2a2e1-5efa-47ed-a0af-2015bf1ecd66?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>See more details here.</span></a></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, tell us what’s new, different, better, or worse in your part of the tech industry since AI has been in your workflow.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Submissions close 4 October at midnight (PST). </span></strong><span>Read all </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/35a2a2e1-5efa-47ed-a0af-2015bf1ecd66?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>details of the challenge here,</span></a><span> and we look forward to reading your article about interesting and consequential changes in your part of the industry.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thank you for being a reader of The Pragmatic Engineer; we value your attention and support, and never take it for granted. With that, onwards to the next five, exciting years!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>– Gergely and The Pragmatic Engineer Team</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>Thanks for subscribing to </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxMzczMzA1MSwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODgyODMyMTIsImV4cCI6MjEwMzg1OTIxMiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.aY0YAGvVQSji07wxjiF5VmJSeprkeGVqaYV5BsxTIOE?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">What Makes a Language Model Intelligent?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Large language models like ChatGPT are quite different from normal software programs. They don’t depend on typical if-else statements to decide what should happen next.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A large language model is essentially a very big pile of numbers called parameters or weights. These weights are the foundation of a language model’s intelligence. For reference, a model with 70 billion parameters means 70 billion numbers or weights. Each weight is normally stored in 16 bits, which is two bytes. Two bytes multiplied by 70 billion comes to 140 GB, which is basically considered the size of the model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The weights are arranged into matrices. A single weight matrix is a grid, often something like 4096 by 4096. This comes to roughly 16.7 million numbers in a matrix. A 70 billion parameter model has hundreds of these matrices stacked across 80 or so layers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, weights in themselves aren’t the whole story behind a model’s capability. Multiple components work together to make a model intelligent. For example, the model needs an architecture like the Transformer to route data and perform attention. It also needs a context window that holds the prompt and everything generated during the conversation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, the architecture is made up of a few hundred lines of code. The prompt may be a few kilobytes. In contrast, the weights form the bulk of the language model. Without the proper weights, a language model cannot work as intended. The weights perform a bunch of tasks:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">They store patterns such as grammar, facts, and reasoning shortcuts.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Once the training is finished, the weights freeze into an immutable network of numerical values.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The weights decide how strongly one simulated neuron influences the next.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Running the model means pushing the input through these weight matrices until the next word comes out of the other end.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One thing to keep in mind over here is that no single weight means anything on its own. If you opened a model file and looked at weight number N, you might see something like 0.0293. On either side of this number may be other numbers such as -0.0117, 0.004, -0.0862. On their own, each of these numbers hardly makes sense. The ability of the model is hidden in the relationships between the various weights. Think of it like a photograph where every pixel comes together to show something recognizable. Even if we modify every pixel’s brightness slightly, we can still make out the things in the picture. This is because the information isn’t sitting in one single place.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Following on from all this information, it is quite easy to figure out that to shrink a model, we’ve to somehow deal with these weights. And this is exactly where the techniques come into the picture. However, a couple of points can help us make better sense of the techniques to shrink a model:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Firstly, not all weights matter equally. Most of the weight values are close to zero and barely impact the final output. However, a small handful are large and produce a bigger impact.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Second, we can only judge a model based on its behaviour, not its internals.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Let us now look at the techniques.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Three Techniques to Shrink the Model</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The techniques to shrink a model revolve around using fewer bits to store a weight or using fewer weights. There are three main techniques:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Storing Each Weight in Less Detail (Quantization): </strong><span>In this approach, we keep all the weights, but describe each one in a less precise manner. For example, two bytes become half a byte.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Removing Irrelevant Weights (Pruning): </strong><span>This approach involves finding the weights that contribute nothing and deleting them.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Building a Smaller Model to Mimic the Larger One (Knowledge Distillation): </strong><span>In this approach, we don’t touch the original model, but train a new, smaller model to behave in a similar way.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Going back to our photograph example, we can think of quantization as taking a picture with a cheaper camera that has a slightly lower resolution. Pruning is more like cutting away the blank edges of the photograph that might not be adding any value to the picture. Distillation can be thought of as paying a skilled painter to reproduce the picture at a quarter of the size.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The great part about all these techniques is that they can be stacked. For example, a model can be distilled by the lab that made it. It can be pruned by a research team. Lastly, it can be quantized by the user before it is loaded on a specific machine. In other words, stacking can make it possible to run a high-end large language model on normal consumer hardware.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Let us now look at each of these techniques in more detail.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Shrinking a Model by Packing Fewer Details</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The first technique to shrink a model is to pack fewer details for every weight. This technique is known as quantization.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Let’s say a particular weight might be stored as 0.02934517. This takes a lot of space, but in a 70 billion parameter model, it just happens to be one single weight. Whether it is stored as 0.02934517 or 0.029 makes almost no difference to the model’s output. In other words, a lot of storage is spent on precision that might not even be important.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Quantization is a technique that takes away this precision.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The first bit of quantization happens even before the model is shipped. During training, model weights are normally stored as 32-bit (4 bytes) floating-point numbers. This is also known as the FP32 format. Since training involves making millions of tiny adjustments to each weight, high precision is needed. But when the model is distributed, the precision is usually brought down to 16-bit float format, which is also known as FP16 or BF16.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, we can bring the precision down even further. To understand how, we need to first be clear about how a float value is actually built.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A floating-point number splits the bits into three parts: a sign, an exponent, and a mantissa. FP32 gives 1 bit to the sign, 8 bits to the exponent, and 23 bits to the mantissa. BF16, on the other hand, keeps all exponent bits and cuts the mantissa down to seven. This is basically the same range as FP32, but with less detail. For clarity, BF16 is slightly different from FP16, which gives the exponent only 5 bits and keeps more bits for the mantissa. BF16 has largely replaced FP16 in practice.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">An integer has an even greater difference. An 8-bit integer is a whole number from -128 to 127. A 4-bit integer is a whole number from -8 to 7. There is no exponent and no scale. In other words, converting a float into an integer not only causes a loss of precision, but also removes each weight’s scale.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" complete process of quantization:</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">1 - Mapping Ranges</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the first step, we find out the minimum and maximum values of a data set and divide the total span into a fixed number of steps.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">To be clear, “the data set” is not the entire model. It’s just a small group of neighbouring weights. We can call it a block, and it should ideally be pretty small.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For example, consider these eight weights: 0.021, -0.017, 0.004, -0.048, 0.011, 0.033, -0.006, 0.070. They span from -0.048 to 0.070. The largest value in either direction is 0.070. With 4 bits as our target precision, we can write whole numbers from -7 to 7. In other words, seven steps in each direction. Therefore, one step can be calculated as 0.070/7, which comes to 0.010.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">2 - Rounding Values</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Instead of keeping a long decimal, each original number is rounded to the closest available step. To do so, we divide each weight by the step size and round it to the nearest whole number.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The table below shows the new weights:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/7bbadccb-42e5-45b0-bc0f-3e988e5a8c1a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">As you can see in the table, the right-hand column values are the ones that go into the model weights file eventually. Every entry here is a whole number between -7 and 7.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The original weights were floating-point numbers. Since a float carries its own scale, rounding off to engineers removes the precision as well as the scale of every weight. This scale has to be stored somewhere.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">3 - Using a Scale Factor</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We need to keep track of the scale factor so that the compressed numbers can roughly reconstruct the original values when the model needs to read them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In our example, the scale factor is the step size (0.010). It is stored once for the entire block. To recover a weight, we can multiply the stored integer by the scale factor.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So, for example, the stored weight of 2 is multiplied by 0.010 to arrive at the value 0.020. Of course, it is still different from the original value of 0.021, but the error is much less now. In other words, the model is still quite unchanged. We still have the same weights (with some error), the same matrices, and the same layers. However, it takes a lot less storage.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Shrinking the Model by Removing Unused Weights</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The second technique takes the opposite approach. Instead of trying to store each weight in less space, we delete some of them. This approach is known as pruning.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Pruning works because not all weights matter equally. Most of them have a value close to zero, such as 0.00004, -0.0011, and so on. These values are so small that they don’t impact the output in a meaningful manner. However, billions of such weights are produced during training. They are useful during the training phase, when the model is taking its original shape. You could think of them as driveways and service roads that are never used but still shown on a city map. Even if you remove them, they won’t have any impact on the people who are using this map to commute through the city.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The key decision with pruning is which weights to remove. The easiest approach uses the size. We sort the weights by how far they are from zero in either direction and delete the smallest ones. For example, if this approach helps prune 20% of the weights, it comes to around removing 14 billion weights from a 70 billion model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, there is a flaw in this approach. The influence of a weight also depends on the pathway on which it sits. A better method runs a few hundred sample texts through the model first. It then monitors how large the typical inputs are to each weight. Based on this, each weight is assigned a final score.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There is another factor that should be considered when it comes to pruning. It is related to the mechanism of removing weights. There are two main approaches:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Setting to Zero: </strong><span>The first approach is to set the chosen weights to zero. This does minimal damage. But we end up with a matrix that is full of zeros in no particular pattern. The GPU still has to run the calculations with those entries.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Removing Structural Pieces: </strong><span>The second way is to remove the structural pieces such as an entire neuron, an attention head, or even a complete layer. This helps shrink the matrix. But this is also a coarser approach. Removing one neuron might mean removing every weight attached to it. Some of these weights may be important, but they are also deleted. In other words, the overall damage to the model is greater in this approach.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">See the diagram below that shows the two approaches:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Ultimately, pruning is rarely a complete solution. It is much better to use pruning in combination with some other techniques.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Shrinking the Model by Mimicking Behaviour</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The third technique to shrink the model creates a new smaller model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In this technique, we take the big model. It is called the teacher model. Next, we build a new model from scratch using the same architecture. However, it has fewer layers and smaller matrices. For example, a model with 7 billion weights instead of 70 billion. We call this new model the student model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The student model starts its life with random weights that are meaningless. This model goes through the training process, but we don’t use the raw text from other sources on the internet. Instead, the student model is trained on the teacher’s behaviour. This involves feeding both the student and the teacher the same input and pushing the student model towards producing output closer to what the teacher model produced.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This technique is known as knowledge distillation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This type of approach might appear counterintuitive. But it works because of how the model works internally.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When a model predicts the next word, it doesn’t just produce a single word. It produces a probability score for every word in its vocabulary. For example, given the sentence “the cat sat on the…”, the teacher model might say “mat 41%”, “floor 12%”, “couch 9%”, and so on. In an ordinary training approach, the student model only receives the correct answer. But during distillation, the student model receives the whole distribution of probable answers. In other words, the student model learns that “couch” was also a pretty sensible guess, but maybe the word “purple” was quite absurd.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">See the diagram below:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0
