layoffs and even larger forced reassignments</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Knowingly or not, Meta creates an internal “mercenary” culture, where more of the people who stay are in it for the money and little else. Everyone knows they could well be laid off at any time the AI becomes good enough to replace them. People cannot control whether they end up on a list of positions to be cut, so it’s sensible to just make as much money as possible while awaiting the seemingly inevitable. </span><em><span>That sounds like a pretty miserable place to work.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It could also lead to a situation where the workforce becomes more populated by those with no better options, who are not in demand from other companies.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Do social impacts matter to Meta?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A final element of the planned drastic job cuts, as revealed in the Reuters report, that I want to touch on is the potential wider, external impacts. Honestly, I’m surprised that none of Meta’s leadership seems to have considered this angle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>By executing massive layoffs for the sake of AI, Meta could have invited more regulation of the emerging AI sector. </span></strong><span>Meta is one of the largest tech employers in the US, and the CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI are on record for predicting mass unemployment, and calling on governmental intervention should it happen. In fairness, other tech companies have also held major AI-related layoffs; Block let go 40% of its workforce, about 4,000 people in February.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Meta is not just another tech company: it’s the world’s leading social media company, and just </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c64024e-625d-44ca-8535-727f29c54e6a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>lost a major US lawsuit</span></a><span> alleging that its platforms harm children and faces an $18B fine. As a result, it has committed to make its platforms less addictive. If the planned cuts had happened at Meta and all those staff became unemployed, how would it have dealt with complying with the court’s ruling to make its products safer for children? Could AI be relied on to deliver this with much less human input?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In light of the recent legal defeat, it wouldn’t be a good look for Zuckerberg’s company to blatantly put profits ahead of people by dismissing a load more workers. The combined effect of the two events would create terrible optics. In response, the government could decide that Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s CEOs were right about the threat to society of mass job losses and roll out things like:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Stricter employee protection, specifically around AI-related layoffs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Higher taxation on profits of companies that “replace” staff with AI, and channel the revenue to deal with widespread whitecollar unemployment</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Start taxing AI at source whenever tokens are sold, and use the surplus to counter the social ills of unemployment</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Or the government could do nothing and leave it to the market to deal with unemployed whitecollar workers by creating enough new companies to employ highly-skilled software engineers, PMs, designers and other folks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Overall, the canceled plan to cut thousands more jobs in this climate just adds to the feeling that there are no adults running Meta. </span></strong><span>Since Sheryl Sandberg quit in 2022 as Chief Operating Officer and Zuckerberg’s “right hand”, Meta has acted irrationally, irresponsibly, and unpredictably:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>2022-2023: laying off 25% of staff</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>2024-2025: immediately rehired even more people so that 2025’s headcount returned to 2022 levels, raising the question of what the point of layoffs even was</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>2026: on track to overtake Google as #1 in advertising revenue this year</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>May 2026: conducted sudden layoffs and forced reassignments of engineers, while aiming to replace as many devs with AI as possible for no obvious reasons like external pressure or competitive threats.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’ve long had a generally positive view of Meta’s engineering culture, but with the company’s leadership seemingly worshiping AI and holding their colleagues in disdain, you have to wonder which software engineer would choose to work at Meta if other options are available. There are many tech companies that value their human software engineers, understand that great teams make for great companies, and that AI is a tool and not a replacement for human energy, motivation, and thoughtfulness. But Meta is clearly not among them.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. More thoughts on Ramp’s in-house AI infra</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thanks for all the feedback on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ddee51b1-838e-424d-8378-b79f4a4a9839?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>this week’s issue</span></a><span> on how and why Ramp built its in-house coding agent. A few additional notes:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building AI tools in-house is like an “internal bootcamp” for AI Engineering. </span></strong><span>I asked Inspect co-creator Zach Bruggeman, if they had access to a similar system from a vendor, would they have built Inspect? He told me they would because they learned so much and developed a lot of AI infrastructure “muscle.” Plus, it was a lot less effort than a similar project would have been in the past.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building in-house AI infra allowed Ramp to quickly launch </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3ff4a790-0b90-42c5-bb55-d28aad7efb4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Router.com</span></a></strong><span>. Stripe made a strategic move by acquiring LLM gateway OpenRouter. Having built something similar internally, Ramp made their Ramp Router infra publicly available within a few days of the Stripe announcement. It’s rare to see a fintech company launch AI infrastructure, but Ramp evidently has enough “AI infra muscle” in-house to do so.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building internal, dev-facing AI infra feels like a low-risk, high-reward investment. </span></strong><span>What’s the worst that can happen when a few engineers inside a company build out AI infra? They get hands-on with AI engineering, spend some money on AI infra providers, and create a product that could work better than what AI vendors offer out of the box. And there’s less to worry about in terms of vendors accessing sensitive data. In the best case, you’ve built infra that competitors don’t have, and can potentially attract AI engineers more easily than rivals. Meanwhile, current engineers there who want to get into AI Engineering don’t leave for AI startups as they can do this kind of work in-house.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>It’s not just Ramp that is building AI infra; many 100+ person companies are also doing it. </span></strong><span>Reader Nick Pleatsikas shared that at his 200-person company, they built AI coding infra to pipe company-specific context to the models without worrying about vendors logging sensitive information. Other similarly-sized businesses are doing the same.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The effort to build this kind of coding agent is relatively minor compared to the potential upside. Plus, it’s interesting and challenging to do. </span><em><span>The question isn’t necessarily “why” to do it, but rather, “why not?”</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Industry Pulse</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>GitHub’s load increase speeds up</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In April, after a large GitHub outage, we</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/21ae857e-53ea-464c-8cc0-89fb3c8671e8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span> looked into</span></a><span> how much its load had increased over the past three years. It was an average load increase of 3.5x; high, but not impossible to plan ahead for. Last week, new details about the increased load became available after GitHub suffered another lengthy eight-hour outage. The company’s post showed that load had nearly doubled since April, to stand 5-6x higher than three years ago:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: If so, that will create some interesting challenges for us software engineers to solve!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Stripe acquires OpenRouter</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In June, we covered the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fa3b8ca7-4130-4acf-ae66-8a7a8ae15b4c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>trend of “smart model routing:”</span></a><span> automatically selecting the right AI model for the right task as a way to reduce AI token spend. OpenRouter is the leading LLM gateway, with routing built in. A week ago, Stripe </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dc6244c2-6106-4acc-8ee8-421ff0a521ce?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> it will acquire OpenRouter for $7.5B, an incredible exit for a startup founded in 2023!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why would Stripe spend so much on an AI infra company? A few possible reasons:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Business model: </span></strong><span>OpenRouter charges a 5.5% fee when users buy credits through its interface. This is a very similar business model to Stripe’s of charging 2.9% on top of a transaction.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Growth of AI token usage. </span></strong><span>AI token usage is increasing exponentially across the tech industry, and surely so is OpenRouter’s business. It generates $140M in revenue from its fees (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6b6f5d12-4192-4be3-be1a-c76ce784c85f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>per The Information</span></a><span>). If dramatic growth continues, OpenRouter would be on course to generate billions in revenue per year.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Becoming an AI payments infra company? </span></strong><span>The cost of AI lies with the price of tokens, and if Stripe becomes a provider of tokens, it would basically become a payments infra company; all without having to develop state-of-the-art AI models!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Stripe’s upcoming IPO. </span></strong><span>Stripe is likely to go public at some point, and being seen as an AI infra company could attract a higher valuation in the current climate than “just” being a payments company.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This acquisition looks like a smart move by Stripe.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Ramp launches Ramp Router in public</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A week after Stripe announced acquiring OpenRouter, fintech competitor Ramp launched a very similar offering. The company bought the domain </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3ff4a790-0b90-42c5-bb55-d28aad7efb4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Router.com</span></a><span> and launched a service that’s near-identical to OpenRouter. Under the hood, it’s powered by Ramp Router and promises to cut AI costs by 40% on average.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One reservation I have about Router.com is its data retention policy: unlike OpenRouter that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0e25cc53-0335-4ff7-b945-6036d5b12801?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>offers</span></a><span> Zero Data Retention (ZDR), Router.com only offers ZDR to select US-hosted models. Additionally, Ramp’s Router “stores model inputs, outputs, and metadata and uses this data to improve the service.” Basically, Ramp Router by default stores potentially sensitive data sent to the service: a red flag in any serious usage!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Such data retention is hardly a good use case for a company, and suggests that Ramp may be targeting the hobbyist crowd with this offering – at least until they get more serious about data privacy.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That Ramp felt the need to launch </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3ff4a790-0b90-42c5-bb55-d28aad7efb4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Router.com</span></a><span> suggests to me that Stripe’s move to buy OpenRouter probably caught them by surprise, and they are not ready to let Stripe become the leading LLM gateway without a fight.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4ace60f3-1a9d-49a9-9f1d-e00244804ee0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Financial Times</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What could be the cause of this eye-catching drop? RevenueCat is the leading in-app purchase SDK, and CEO Jacob Eiting </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4ad7a3d7-28f1-40fd-997d-ce491d66cd3b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explained</span></a><span> how they see it:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Gaming revenue down 4.5% year-on-year (YoY); the majority of the decrease</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Non-gaming revenue (apps) up 14.6% YoY</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Web payments share rose from 20% last year to 26% this year.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, it’s a mix of people spending less on games IAPs, and more companies bypassing Apple’s in-app-purchase flows (where Apple levies the 30% “Apple Tax”) in favor of web checkout. A 2025 court ruling </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bdf6a291-0a5d-477d-83fe-05b3a606842c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>forcing</span></a><span> the iPhone maker to allow web payment links on iOS is also likely to be a factor.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>What’s a bug, anyway?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m a big fan of Claude Code creator Boris Cherny, but must part ways with his definition of ‘bug’, as per a recent post from him. It came after a Claude Code user </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7f4297e5-707a-4617-a735-b02813e5bff9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>complained</span></a><span> on X that the agent could not be hot reloaded. Boris looked into it and declared it was a “UX issue” and not a bug. As the Community note helpfully pointed out, that is also known as a bug:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Consider what can happen when someone uploads a profile photo to a web application.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Depending on the use case, the application may resize the image into different sizes. It might run the image through a content check process. It can also push the resized images to a content delivery network for faster access. Lastly, it will also update the user record with the latest metadata. Now, imagine if all of these operations take place during the same picture upload request path. As all of these functionalities are carried out, the user sees a spinning button for several seconds, wondering whether the photo has been uploaded successfully. Needless to say, it would be a pretty poor user experience.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If we move all of that extra work outside the request path, the upload can more or less respond immediately as soon as the image file is stored in an object storage. The image still gets resized, scanned, and distributed, just not in the same flow. This is known as background work, and here are some examples of why it is needed:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A user action may have triggered it. For example, someone signs up, and a welcome email goes out.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The clock may have triggered it. For example, nightly reports, monthly invoices, hourly cache refreshes.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Another system could have triggered it. For example, a webhook arrives, or a file is stored in object storage.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Perhaps the sheer volume of work made it worthwhile. For example, some work is naturally cheaper or safer done a thousand items at a time.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most of the time, teams start with a single scheduled script on a single machine. It can handle a great amount of background work. However, as the system gets bigger and more complex, the amount of background work requires different strategies. In this article, we will look at various such strategies to perform background work in detail.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: He’s a programmer and videogame developer, founder of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f10f1948-73fd-4402-83d7-25432155c500?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Molly Rocket</span></a><span>, and creator of  </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3caf1391-4863-4c48-82d4-dfc1ef6a02f1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Handmade Hero</span></a><span> – a long-running series about building a game from scratch. He also evangelizes about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b149cfff-4b22-489a-8545-1e12c35ce3b4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>performance</span></a><span> on his Substack, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6ab2af8a-9a78-4942-9917-af638f41d8d8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Computer, Enhance</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We got to know each other about three years ago, first via messages, including this one from Casey:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Why does the industry zeitgeist place so little emphasis on software performance when there seems to be overwhelming evidence that performance is critical to their bottom line?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like you, I run a Substack for professional programmers, but I focus exclusively on software performance. Although we are quite large by Substack standards, so a certain subset of programmers must believe performance is important, I nonetheless hear lots of dismissive excuses when I post on social media. This happens so frequently, I devoted an entire article to cataloging the extensive pro-performance evidence we already have from the world’s leading software companies: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aac47fa8-eb28-4f66-bd7f-b901f83b9cc3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Performance Excuses Debunked</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Strangely, nobody has a rebuttal to why performance is important</span></strong><span>. When I point people to this, they actually tend to agree. But the prevailing attitude nonetheless stays the same.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m delighted we finally have Casey on the podcast because it’s overdue! In this episode, we discuss why software performance matters, why it’s overlooked, and how developers can get better at writing performant code. We explore why performance should be considered during design, the value of learning to read assembly & understanding how CPUs work, Casey’s critique of ‘clean code’, and why he believes testing shouldn’t drive software design.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We touch on how videogame development has changed, and influential game engines. Casey also tells us why he prefers to write code by hand, not with AI, and more.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Casey</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/b30480e1-8e6f-4460-b596-31009cee3298?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/8xBJPa_480Q" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. DirectX might not exist without an “unauthorized” internal Microsoft project. </span></strong><span>DirectX is a very popular Microsoft library that standardized rendering on top of GPUs, used mostly for games. Casey tells how Chris Hecker built a library for fast on-screen rendering at Microsoft called WinG, which was never authorized; it was a total “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/55f0d75c-195d-4006-831a-a8c936d63c8c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Skunk Works</span></a><span>” project. DirectX’s roots go back to WinG, which its three founders were testers on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Is performance starting to matter to businesses? </span></strong><span>Enterprise software buyers care mainly about cost, compliance, and capabilities – but not performance. Even so, there are some products gaining major popularity and market share due to their performance, such as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8a5cd597-d8bb-4846-b706-0765bb95a892?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>File Pilot</span></a><span> (next-gen file explorer) and the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/058d988d-ce52-4c15-8040-981d66c011c9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Blick video editor</span></a><span>. Is the tide turning?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. Profiler-driven performance optimization is the wrong way to optimize. </span></strong><span>The standard way of optimizing is to profile the application, tweak hotspots, then check if the stats have improved. But this only finds a local minimum; Casey says every engineer he’s worked with who was a great “optimizer” began by establishing what the hardware could theoretically do, and then did not stop until they’d closed the gap to that performance level.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. If you care about performance, learn to read assembly (no need to write it). </span></strong><span>There are about 20-30 instructions you need to learn to be able to read basic assembly. For example, here’s a program that calculates the value of 5 + 3 - 1 (which is 7), then prints it out:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: _start), then prints the result to stdout</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. Take a grain of salt with conventional wisdom that premature optimization is the “root of all evil”. </span></strong><span>Many devs use it as an excuse to delay performance optimization, but Casey says that not optimizing in time could mean that only performance hotspots can be fixed later, and not the architectural issues that create poor performance. Architect your system to be performant, or you’ll have trouble solving problems without a rewrite!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. Only three things are needed to understand how CPUs work. </span></strong><span>Casey believes that knowing them means you’ll be able to tell from any CPU announcement roughly how well it performs. Those three pillars of understanding:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How data moves in and out: load/store units and L1–L3 caches</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How instructions flow through the pipes: branch prediction, i-cache</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Execution unit scheduling: raw throughput per operation type</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>7. Why are game studios so secretive?</span></strong><span> Before licensable videogame engines existed, the game engine was a studio’s “core” intellectual property (IP), and every studio built rendering, pathfinding, and other tools from scratch. This is how Blizzard rolled Warcraft 1’s engine into Warcraft 2. Any competitor making a rival game had to start from scratch, which was a reason for game studios to closely guard the secrets of how their own game engines worked.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. The games industry already had its “AI moment” – and it wasn’t pretty. </span></strong><span>When game engines became licensable, pretty much any developer could build and publish a game with the likes of Unity and Unreal, on a platform like Steam.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Initially, this change empowered new devs to build interesting games. But soon enough, the market was flooded with tens of thousands of releases per year, which destroyed organic discovery. Without a marketing strategy, the chances of a game gaining traction today are basically zero, says Casey.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. Old games don’t look dated anymore, and that’s a problem. </span></strong><span>For decades, graphics were a vital barometer for showing how videogames improved over time; a new release in 1995 was guaranteed to be visually superior to one from 1990. But a new game in 2026 likely doesn’t look much different from one that’s nine years old, and new releases face ongoing competition from older games.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>10. Casey’s problem with test-driven development is the “test” bit. </span></strong><span>Casey believes tests should be a cost/benefit decision, and not put in place by default. For some projects, doing tests upfront – or doing any tests at all, in some cases – is simply a bad choice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>11. One trait of almost every great engineer: refusing to accept programming wisdom untested in the real world. </span></strong><span>As Casey puts it:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I find there’s a lot of received programming wisdom that’s just nonsense. Clearly, no one’s ever tested it. In order for something to be received wisdom, you should have to at least demonstrate concrete upsides, but often this cannot be done. I would say focusing on what actually works in practice is a huge plus.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>12. No AI in Casey’s upcoming game. </span></strong><span>He acknowledges that many developers will disagree, but insists there’s nothing wrong with being outside of mainstream tastes, just like some people chose handmade furniture over the flatpack kind. His reasoning for omitting AI is straightforward:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I want to program things in a game because I want to program them. If I only wanted output, I’d just get the Unreal Engine.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro a loop. Loop engineering adds a loop around the agent itself, enabling it to evaluate its output, try again when the work falls short, and refine its instructions when the same mistakes recur. Today, you perform that role: reviewing the work, diagnosing what went wrong, and prompting the agent again. This article shows how to automate that process with a working example, while exploring where human judgment still belongs.</p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/Orkes_082626","text":"Read the post","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/6c9d01bc-fd81-4877-9101-6b017f97690b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Read the post</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A 70-billion-parameter model requires reading roughly 140 GBs of weights out of the GPU memory. On a modern data center GPU, this transfer can take tens of milliseconds. The actual calculation applied to these weights takes a fraction of that time. This means that the processor’s math units are unused for most of the time taken by the token generation step.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Speculative decoding is a technique that converts this unused capacity into output. A second, much smaller model produces several candidate tokens in advance. The large model evaluates all of them in a single forward pass instead of one pass per token, resulting in 2-3 times faster generation. To make things better, the text produced remains statistically identical to the output of the large model running alone.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will look at how speculative decoding works. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Autoregressive Decoding</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Text generation works one token at a time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model reads everything produced so far, computes a probability distribution over its vocabulary, selects the next token, appends that token to the input, and repeats the cycle. Each cycle is called a forward pass, and every forward pass runs the input through all layers of the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, token 50 depends on token 49 being present in the input, and token 49 depends on token 48, and so on. Computing them simultaneously would break the dependency chain that makes the output coherent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The implication is that a 500-token response requires 500 sequential forward passes, each one completing before the next begins. Since the duration of a single pass depends on the size of the model, the total generation time equals the number of output tokens multiplied by the time per forward pass.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This explains why the response speed stays roughly steady whether the answer is a short factual reply or a long block of code, because the per-token cost stays the same either way. It also explains why a larger model produces text more slowly on identical hardware.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Modern inference systems use a KV cache, which stores the attention state for tokens already processed so that each new pass only computes attention for the newest position. This cuts the work done inside each pass to a large extent, though the requirement for one pass per token still remains.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Memory Bandwidth</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since the number of passes is fixed by how much text we want, it leaves the second half of the equation. What does a single forward pass actually spend its time doing?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To put it simply, a forward pass spends most of its duration moving data rather than performing arithmetic calculations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Model weights live in the GPU memory, usually called VRAM. To compute anything with those weights, the GPU has to transfer them into the compute units where the multiplication happens. For a 70-billion-parameter model stored at 16-bit precision, this transfer amounts to roughly 140 GBs for every single token.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The arithmetic performed on those 140 GBs is quite small by comparison. One token means one narrow vector flowing through each weight matrix. The GPU loads an enormous matrix out of memory, multiplies it against that vector, discards it, and loads the next one.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The consequence is that during prompt processing, compute utilization is around 90 to 95 percent. However, during token generation, it falls to somewhere between 20 and 40 percent. The math units are unused for most of every step while the memory bus runs near capacity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The difference is driven by how much work each weight read supports:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Prompt processing reads the weights once and applies them to thousands of input tokens simultaneously.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Token generation reads the same weights and applies them to exactly one token.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is capacity that has already been paid for, but underutilized.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But why does this matter practically?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A GPU with higher memory bandwidth improves generation speed more than one with more raw compute.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure capacity only helps if there is useful work to put into it. The question is whether a single forward pass can produce more than one token’s worth of output.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Parallel Verification</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A single forward pass can evaluate many positions at once.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Transformers process an entire sequence in parallel. When we feed in a sequence of tokens, the model computes a next-token prediction at every position in that sequence during the same pass. For example, a five-token input produces five predictions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These predictions stay valid because of causal masking. Inside the attention mechanism, position 5 can access positions 1 through 5 while positions 6 and beyond are masked out, and position 3 can access only positions 1 through 3. Each position is therefore conditioned on exactly the tokens preceding it, identical to the conditioning it would have received had we generated the sequence one step at a time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the property that makes prompt processing fast. A 2,000-token prompt runs through the model in one pass rather than 2,000, because all 2,000 positions are computed together.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When applied to verification, the consequence is direct. For example, if we append four candidate tokens to the context and run one forward pass, we receive the model’s own prediction at each of those four positions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One thing to understand here is that verification and generation are basically the same operation. The target model performs identical work at each position. The cost savings comes from performing that work across several positions in a single pass instead of across one position in each of several passes.</span></p><div Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Draft and Verify</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The complete loop combines a fast source of candidate tokens with the batched evaluation described above.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This setup uses two models:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The large model we want output from is called the target model</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Running alongside it is a much smaller draft model with 10 to 20 times fewer parameters. It is usually drawn from the same family and uses the same tokenizer.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each round has three steps:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The draft model produces K candidate tokens through its own serial loop. Those passes are sequential as well, though each one costs a small fraction of a target model pass.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The candidates are appended to the context. The target model evaluates the extended sequence in one forward pass.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Working left to right, each candidate is compared against the target model’s prediction at that position. The matching candidates are kept, and as soon as the first mismatch appears, the remaining candidates are discarded.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The mismatch point plays an important role in this. The verification pass already computed the target model’s prediction at that position, so that token gets used directly. We keep the matching prefix and receive one correct token at no additional cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This property places a bound on the downside.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the worst case, all four candidates might fail to match, but we would still have the one token the target model produced at the first position, which is exactly what plain decoding would have delivered from one forward pass. The wasted effort amounts to just the draft model’s compute and some extra effort in the verification pass. Both are drawn from otherwise available capacity. In a typical case where two of four candidates match, we get to keep two plus the free token, giving three tokens from one target model pass.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Draft length K is a tunable value, which is commonly set between 3 and 5. Larger values raise the ceiling on savings, since a fully accepted draft of eight saves more than a fully accepted draft of three. However, larger values also reduce the odds that later candidates survive, because the draft model conditions on its own unverified output as it moves forward. Past a certain point, the additional candidates get discarded often enough that the extra work outweighs the benefit.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" this point is whether the resulting text is still the text the target model would have produced.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Lossless Guarantee</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Speculative decoding produces text with the same statistical properties as the target model running alone. This is enforced by means of the acceptance rule.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Under greedy decoding, where we always take the highest-probability token, the rule is quite direct. A candidate is kept when it matches the target model’s top choice at that position, and dropped when it fails to match.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, sampling takes more care, since tokens get picked with some randomness. Both models produce a full set of probabilities across the vocabulary at each position. The rule compares the two sets:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>When the target model gave the candidate at least as much probability as the draft model did, the candidate is kept.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>When the target model gave it less, the candidate is kept part of the time. This is in proportion to how far apart the two numbers were.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>When a candidate is dropped, the replacement gets picked from an adjusted set of probabilities, with the draft model’s own scores subtracted out first.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This last step is critical. If we add up both paths, the candidates kept and the candidates replaced, the odds of any particular token appearing depend exactly on the target model’s own odds for it. This is regardless of what the draft model suggested.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are two qualifications to this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Matching odds still allow different wording, since sampling stays random either way. Running the same prompt twice can give varied text in both setups.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Computers store these numbers with limited precision, so rounding can flip the winner when two tokens sit almost exactly tied.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Acceptance Rate</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The size of the speed increase in this approach is governed by the acceptance rate, which is largely a property of the workload.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Acceptance rate is the fraction of candidate tokens the target model keeps, and acceptance length is the average number confirmed per verification pass, including the free token at the end.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Different workload types produce different results:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Structured and repetitive output produces high acceptance. For example, code generation, summarization, extraction, and retrieval-augmented answers reuse large amounts of text from the input, which makes the next token easy to predict from a small model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Open-ended output produces low acceptance. Creative writing and open conversation generate text with genuine variety, where a small model diverges from a large one far more often.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sampling temperature contributes as well. Higher temperature flattens the probability distribution, which increases mismatches between the two models and pushes acceptance down. If the acceptance falls below roughly 50%, the additional work outweighs the savings.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For reference, DeepSeek reported acceptance rates between 80 and 90 percent for the second predicted token in production serving of DeepSeek-V3, which translated to roughly 1.8x generation throughput.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The practical implication is that two teams can deploy the same configuration on the same hardware and get different results, because their users are asking different questions. Ultimately, acceptance depends on the quality of the candidates, which brings us to where candidates come from.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Candidate or Draft Sources</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The key question while choosing candidate or draft sources is where to obtain fast predictions cheaply. There are four answers in common use:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A separate small model:</span></strong><span> The original approach pairs the target with a smaller sibling, so a 1B model drafting for a 13B target, or a 3B to 8B model drafting for a 70B target. Same family and identical tokenizer are requirements in this approach. The cost is a second checkpoint to deploy and version, plus VRAM that comes out of the KV cache budget, which reduces how many concurrent requests the server can hold.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Extra prediction heads on the target model: </span></strong><span>Lightweight output heads predict tokens two or three positions ahead using the target model’s internal representations. DeepSeek-V3 trained these during pretraining to improve model quality, then reused them at inference as the draft source. The cost is training, which puts this option out of reach unless we control the model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A cheaper version of the same model:</span></strong><span> The draft runs the same weights under a reduced compute budget through quantization, layer skipping, or a compressed KV cache. For example, QuantSpec uses 4-bit weights and a 4-bit KV cache for drafting while verification runs at higher precision, reporting speedups above 1.78x with acceptance above 90 percent. The cost is implementation complexity, since draft and target share hardware and cache structures.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A search over existing text:</span></strong><span> This approach scans the prompt and previous output for a recent matching sequence, then proposes whatever followed it last time. Memory cost is zero, and a single model is involved. It contributes only when output repeats input, where it reaches 2x to 4x on tasks like document editing and summarization.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Selecting an option depends on the deployment. Also, tokenizer compatibility constrains pairing more tightly than model quality does. A stronger small model with a different vocabulary is unusable as a draft source without additional machinery. All four options depend on spare compute being available. This condition holds under some serving loads better than others.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Concurrency Limits</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The increase in speed also depends on the operating regime rather than on the technique alone. The gains shrink as server load rises.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Speculative decoding spends compute capacity that would otherwise go unassigned. When a server handles a single request, this capacity is genuinely available. As concurrent requests accumulate, the same weight read operation serves many requests at once, and the compute units approach saturation. Verification work has to compete with real requests.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One systematic evaluation reported up to 1.96x on a 70B model at batch size 1, declining to 1.21x at batch size 128. Under higher concurrency, the technique can fall below baseline throughput, at which point enabling it costs more than the benefits.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Serving systems try to handle this in different ways. For example, vLLM exposes a flag that disables speculation above a configurable batch size. It supports dynamic adjustment where draft length shrinks as concurrency rises and reaches zero under heavy load. The control signals routine operational tuning rather than an edge case.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another boundary is that the time to first token stays roughly the same, since speculative decoding applies to generation rather than prompt processing. Therefore, workloads with long prompts and short outputs have relatively little to gain.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>DeepSeek documented the tradeoff, describing multi-token prediction as slightly reducing throughput while significantly improving end-to-end generation latency.</span></p><div 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Speculative decoding rearranges when the processing happens rather than reducing how much the target model performs. Here are some key points we have understood:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Token generation is slow because every token requires reading the full set of model weights out of memory, while the arithmetic applied to those weights is comparatively small.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A transformer computes a prediction at every position in one pass, which makes evaluating several candidate tokens cost about the same as evaluating one.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A rejected draft truncates rather than wastes, since the verification pass supplies a correct token at the mismatch position regardless.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Output quality is preserved by the acceptance rule itself, so it holds without tuning.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The size of the gain depends on how predictable the output is and how much spare compute the server has available.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The variants differ in where predictions come from and what that source costs.</span></p></li></ul></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When an AI model handles a difficult question, it produces three separate pieces of text:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li 0;"><span>The first is the answer displayed on screen.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The third is the model’s full reasoning process, which is never displayed.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second piece of text is a summary of the third. It is generated separately and shown in place of the original reasoning process. The full reasoning runs longer. It also contains material that the summary leaves out. Most major providers withhold it. However, in place of the complete process, an encrypted version is shared with the client during the conversation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In August 2026, a team at MATS Research, the ELLIS Institute Tübingen, and the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems wanted to test whether the encrypted reasoning blocks that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google hand back to clients actually keep that reasoning private. They showed that the blocks can be replayed into a cheaper model in the same family, which will then print the hidden reasoning in plaintext. In other words, the AI model’s thoughts are stolen, exposing information that should ideally be hidden.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size:
