References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Reasoning Traces</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Modern frontier models first generate an extended internal sequence of text before producing a visible answer. For example, if we ask a model to solve a hard mathematics question, the model may generate two thousand words of exploration, dead ends, and corrections, which ultimately helps it write a clean two hundred-word answer. This longer sequence of exploration is the reasoning trace, which is also known as the chain of thought.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The trace holds intermediate hypotheses that the model may have tried and abandoned. It contains the raw output of any tools that were called, the user’s data as the model processed it, and whatever contextual secrets were present in the session. Unsurprisingly, this trace is much denser and more revealing than the final polished output.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, if we ask a coding agent to remove hardcoded credentials from a code repository, the agent has to read those credentials to do the work. In other words, the credentials pass through the reasoning trace before any answer is produced.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Concealment Rationale</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why do the model providers hide these reasoning traces?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are two separate motivations:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The first is commercial. A competitor can collect a large number of traces from a strong model to create training material for building a cheaper imitation of the strong model. This is because the final answer just provides the endpoint of a computation, whereas a trace provides the methodology behind the answer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The second is safety-related. A model sometimes has to generate reasoning about a harmful topic to refuse. The filtering that turns a completed trace into a safe visible answer runs after the trace already exists. Publishing the trace skips that filter and lets that information be seen by the user.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>State Management</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Withholding a trace from reaching the user does not mean that the trace is not needed. In a multi-turn conversation, the reasoning from an earlier turn has to be available on the next turn. For example, a request to a model API carries no memory of what came before. The continuity we see in a chat window is reconstructed by the client resending the full history with every message. However, the server is stateless, which means it stores nothing between requests.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This leaves us with two options:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The first option keeps the state on the server. The provider stores the trace in its own database, returns a meaningless identifier to the client, and looks it up when the next message arrives. This is straightforward but expensive because it means storing state for every conversation from every user of a global service.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The second option encrypts the trace and returns it to the client, which stores the block and sends it back with each subsequent request. In this case, the provider stores nothing.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google chose the second option. Confidentiality keeps competitors from reading the trace, integrity prevents an altered trace from being fed back, and statelessness removes the storage cost. As you can see, two of those are security goals, and the third is a cost goal.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Envelope Structure</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So what is actually inside the block that gets sent back to the client?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It consists of a long string of base64 text, which is a way of writing binary data using ordinary letters and digits so that it survives inside JSON. Once decoded, it is an AEAD envelope. AEAD stands for Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data, and it accomplishes two tasks at once: hiding the content and proving that the content was not altered. The associated data portion holds extra fields that stay readable while remaining tamper-protected.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The envelope carries a header. Depending on the provider, it can include the model name, block type, version, and key identifier. Alongside that is a nonce, which is a random value used once per encryption so that identical content produces different-looking output each time, an authentication tag, and the ciphertext. The field carrying all of this is called signature at Anthropic, encrypted_content at OpenAI, and thinkingSignature at Google.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Authentication here proves that the contents came from the provider and were not modified afterward. The model name and version are covered by that proof. However, the account that generated the block and the conversation it belonged to are absent from the authenticated fields entirely. To make this clear, since no provider has published a description of the scheme, the researchers inferred this mainly from observable behaviour. The evidence points toward a single global key used across an entire ecosystem.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Trace Compatibility</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If the authenticated fields provide no information about the origin, a valid block stays valid everywhere. The researchers have described three forms of this, each more permissive than the last:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cross-session compatibility means a block can be replayed out of order, and blocks from earlier sessions work in new ones. This supports editing conversation history and trimming long sessions to fit a context window.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cross-user compatibility means a block produced in one account is accepted when submitted from another.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cross-model compatibility means a block from one model is accepted by a different one, which supports switching models mid-conversation and automatic rerouting.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The researchers tested every source and target combination available in July 2026. Some of the findings were as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Claude accepted almost every combination, the exception being Fable 5, whose blocks were accepted only by Fable 5.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>GPT was organised by generation. The GPT-5.6 series accepted blocks from all earlier generations, while older models accepted only their own.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Gemini accepted every combination across every generation.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Extraction Method</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cross-model compatibility carries a lot of importance because protection inside a model family is uneven.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Flagship models such as Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.6 Sol receive anti-distillation training aimed at preventing disclosure of their own reasoning. It is present behind input and output filters that check for verbatim matches. However, smaller models in the same family, such as Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna, are optimised for cost and speed. As a result, they receive far less of that training. In other words, cross-model compatibility means the smaller model accepts blocks produced by the larger one.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The information extraction method is a direct result of this gap in training. Here’s what can happen:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A question is asked of the strong model, and the response returns a visible answer and an encrypted reasoning block.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The answer is discarded, and the block is kept.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Next, a fresh conversation is opened with a weaker model in the same family.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The reasoning block is placed into it as prior context, and the request asks for the attached reasoning to be transcribed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The weaker model outputs the stronger model’s reasoning in plaintext.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In other words, the strong model was queried once, with an ordinary question, and was never asked to disclose anything. Therefore, its refusal training was never engaged, and its output filter received only a benign answer.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: describe the weaker model as a fuzzy decoder, since it generates an approximation rather than performing exact decryption.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This results in a verification problem. Without access to the original trace, how do you establish that a reconstruction is faithful rather than a plausible invention? The researchers used billing records. API responses report the number of reasoning tokens consumed, and that figure is exact because the charge depends on it. Re-encoding the recovered text and counting its tokens produces a number that should match. Across 120 programming problems, the two counts tracked closely. It was roughly one to one for Claude.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The difficulty of this approach varied by provider. A single fixed prompt worked for Claude, while GPT required up to 50 candidate extractions per block and output chunked below roughly 50 tokens to avoid a rejection triggered by verbatim reproduction.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Attack Vectors</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The research paper talks about four consequences of this gap. These are split based on who produced the original block.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two of them use blocks the attacker generated:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Distillation:</span></strong><span> It involves training a copycat model on a target’s visible answers. Traces make it stronger, because a trace supplies the problem decomposition and the intermediate steps. For reference, earlier work using approximate traces raised the MATH500 accuracy of a fine-tuned model from 68.4 percent to 76.0 percent over answer-only training. Decoding 10,000 traces at Claude Haiku 4.5 pricing costs roughly $720, and where blocks come from public datasets, the frontier model is never queried.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Jailbreaking:</span></strong><span> Models are trained to withhold harmful content from visible output. However, they are largely not trained to avoid generating reasoning about harmful topics, since constraining trace content is believed to degrade the usefulness of traces for safety monitoring. In one demonstration, a prompt drew out extended reasoning about vehicle theft while the visible answer stayed within a responsible write-up aimed at manufacturers. The recovered trace contained specific vulnerable makes and model years.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other two vectors use blocks produced by other people.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Developers publish agent session logs routinely, for reproducibility or by committing them accidentally, and they sanitise the visible text before publishing. However, they cannot sanitise the encrypted blocks, because they cannot read them either.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The researchers collected 6,708 public agent trajectories from GitHub and Hugging Face and decoded 315,320 reasoning blocks, filtering the results through an automated pipeline to remove placeholders and benchmark fixtures. Here are some findings:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>From genuine user sessions, 62 API keys, 33 passwords, 24 access tokens, 7 private keys, and 30 personal email addresses</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Across all sources, 1,028 blocks holding at least one confirmed leak</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>328 of the 6,708 sessions leaking at least one item</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sanitisation operates on plaintext only, so even if every user in that sample had scrubbed their visible text perfectly, all 62 API keys would have remained in the reasoning blocks. This was a non-exhaustive scan of public traces, and logs held locally or produced by live services are likely to contain more.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c75057f-b5f3-4fb7-a75c-e0c1f5895537?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d93b34a9-6f49-4259-938e-853e41ef73b6_3014x1734.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":838,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":240051,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/210942397?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd93b34a9-6f49-4259-938e-853e41ef73b6_3014x1734.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The fourth vector is prompt injection. Long agentic runs are expensive to repeat. Therefore, it makes sense to resume a published run. Encrypted blocks make that possible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A block containing an instruction can be planted in a shared trace. When the session resumes, that block is processed as prior context. In one demonstration, a block carrying an instruction to upload PowerPoint files to an external address was ported into a conversation with GPT-5.6 Sol and paired with an unrelated slide-editing request. The resulting script added the requested slide and uploaded the presentation.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Field Observations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Recovering traces at this scale brought out findings unrelated to the vulnerability itself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Summaries and traces sometimes diverge. On an AIME 2025 mathematics problem, the summary returned by the API described methodical work through the geometry using the law of cosines. The recovered trace opened by stating the answer from memory and then working backward toward a justification, with several wrong guesses along the way. The researchers did not measure how often this occurs. However, they note that a smaller model summarising a larger one will compress the original.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Recovered GPT traces are frequently not fluent English. They are made up of compressed telegraphic notes with articles dropped and grammar abandoned. This carries a direct consequence for oversight, because trace monitoring depends on traces being legible.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Proposed Mitigations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The research paper ultimately makes one strong point, which is the cause of the overall problem. The envelope we talked about earlier authenticates the content of a reasoning block, but it does not authenticate the context in which that block was produced or replayed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cheapest fix for this problem should address cross-user replay. This involves embedding an account identifier inside the authenticated data at issuance, allowing the API to compare it against the authenticated caller and reject any mismatch. This closes the attack vector entirely without the need for server-side storage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cross-session binding is harder, because some genuine features depend on the same portability. Users can fork conversations, compact old turns out of long sessions, and downgrade models mid-conversation. Binding each block to the complete transcript would break all three. The proposal is a hash chain tying each block to its session and to the fingerprint of its predecessor, combined with a Merkle tree that retains only root fingerprints once older blocks are pruned. This approach preserves ordering cheaply while still allowing integrity checks over any surviving stretch.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Blocks already published present a separate problem, since they were signed under a key encoding neither user nor session. The only retroactive remedy is to rotate those keys and refuse to decode anything signed under a retired key identifier. This also invalidates legitimate continuations of old sessions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Other measures include moving to server-side storage entirely, configuring API gateways to reject envelopes from a different model version than the one queried, and training models to decline transcription requests regardless of framing.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’ve now understood the key points in the research paper. Here are some of the main takeaways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>This wasn’t a failure of cryptographic techniques. The guarantee made by the envelope remained throughout the flow. The missing piece was a binding between a block and the context that produced it, which is a decision about which fields go into the authenticated portion.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The summary displayed alongside an answer is a separate artifact from the trace it describes, and the two can diverge.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Sanitising a session log reaches the plaintext only. Encrypted blocks have to be removed rather than cleaned, since the person publishing them cannot inspect what they contain.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The security of a model family depends on its least protected member. Anti-distillation training on a flagship model provides limited benefits while a cheaper sibling model accepts the same blocks.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>At a select few tech companies, they write most of their code with their own, custom-built, internal AI coding agents. This is different from most of the industry which uses AI coding agents and harnesses like Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot, etc. At Ramp, their own version is called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a1c314f8-a18c-4bac-a5c5-a50f872da7f7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Inspect</span></a><span>, while at Block it’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bf77ea8c-5b68-40d7-99f3-d50c14fa7c8c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Goose</span></a><span> (open source), at Stripe it’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0afa727-d401-4f8e-af60-d2a594a77b8f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Minions</span></a><span>, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0c115fb-869b-4689-baec-3d10c4f31124?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>River</span></a><span> at Shopify.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But why not just use what frontier labs and coding harness AI startups already offer; why take the time and effort?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We reached out to Ramp, a fintech company big on building its internal AI infrastructure, and sat down with the founding team of Inspect and engineering leadership. We talked with CTO </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5bf890e3-6c13-4e66-93e8-5585da38dace?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Rahul Sengottuvelu</span></a><span>, head of engineering </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/528d6458-ecbb-4807-9a61-93f939472064?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Hamid Dadkhah</span></a><span>, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/28546ff0-0a20-44f7-8deb-ea9b1de26b36?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Zach Bruggeman</span></a><span>, principal engineer and founding engineer of Inspect.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>What is Inspect? </span></strong><span>Imagine an AI coding agent running on remote sandboxes with access to most internal data sources, and verifying all backend and frontend changes on the remote machine.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Why build your own background coding agent?</span></strong><span> Engineers and designers at Ramp were dissatisfied with third-party harnesses: they wanted to run more than a few agents in parallel – which local machines don’t support – to have better frontend tooling, and also faced demand for remote development environments.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>How Ramp uses Inspect:</span></strong><span> coding, bugfixing in Slack, debugging, and building internal agents like code review and incident management on top of the Inspect platform</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Tech stack and architecture: </span></strong><span>React/Vite, Cloudflare Durable Objects, SQLite, Cloudflare Agents SDK, Modal sandboxes.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>What makes Inspect so popular?</span></strong><span> The machine in the cloud is a developer machine, plus it has access to numerous internal integrations via API and MCP.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Inside the sandbox. </span></strong><span>OpenCode, services for development (e.g. Postgres, Redis, RabbitMQ, Temporal), Chromium, and VS Code Server. Plus, we check out smart tricks to make sandboxes spin up in five seconds or less(!!)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Collaboration & feedback. </span></strong><span>All Inspect sessions are public and open to collaboration, with no opt-outs allowed. More than 150 people at Ramp have contributed to the project.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If you’re like us, you might wonder what the point would be of building your own harness and investing the time and resources in it, given all the choices already out there. This article sets out to answer that question, to understand why other places chose a similar path, and how a non-AI frontier lab can build more efficient tooling than what the frontier AI labs offer. It looks like the “buy, don’t build” tooling convention might not apply to AI tools!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s get Ramp</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A couple of things make Inspect different from coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Remote sandboxes: </span></strong><span>Inspect spins up a sandboxed remote development environment which unlocks unlimited session concurrency, centralized setup configuration, and cross-functional session collaboration.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Internal integrations: </span></strong><span>Inspect is integrated across the org with the same tools and context that a Ramp engineer has; the only constraint on agents’ ability is model intelligence, not missing tools or access.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Inspect verifies all its changes. </span></strong><span>As a remote development environment with full tooling access, it can “close the loop” and confirm the changes it makes work:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Backend verification:</span></strong><span> Inspect runs tests, reviews telemetry and queries feature flags</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Frontend work verification</span></strong><span>: Inspect visually verifies its own work by providing screenshots and live previews to users.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At present, most third-party AI harnesses cannot do these kinds of verifications ‘out of the box’ because they lack internal integrations with things like telemetry and feature flag systems. Also, almost a year ago, Ramp built screenshot verification before it was supported by third-party vendors. Things like this placed Ramp months ahead of nearly all AI coding harnesses, and they could also build a far better feedback loop in their own harness.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Rapid adoption when background agent released</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The v1 of Inspect was a Chrome extension for designers to prompt AI to make minor website changes. A few months later, the v2 version with background agents followed.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 1);"><span>2. Why build your own background coding agent?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are a few reasons why Ramp decided to turn down tried-and-tested products and create their own:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Local machines are limited in how many agents they can run. </span></strong><span>Ramp found third-party products below expectations; they liked Claude Code on day 1, but were constrained by only being able to run one or two sessions on local machines.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Better frontend tooling. </span></strong><span>The web engineering team wanted to improve their frontend tooling so designers could make small UI tweaks. There was an opportunity to use AI to automate themselves out of that loop.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Need for remote dev environments. </span></strong><span>As Ramp scaled, so did the complexity, and with it there was more work at the intersection of systems, like debugging backward compatibility, and broken API contracts. The solution was to create remote dev environments.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inspect started as a designer’s frontend tool, and a good part of its team were frontend engineers with interests in UX and speedy performance. The v1 was a Chrome extension for visual edits, where a user could highlight an area and tell the AI what minor website changes to make, like copy edits and button placements. The task of building a tool for making UI edits with AI was given to two frontend engineers, Zach Bruggeman and Jason Quense, who aside from their frontend domain knowledge, brought a welcome adversarial perspective, as they were less than fully convinced by AI at that time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>People liked v1 but it wasn’t adopted because engineers already knew how to go to a file and edit a single line of code, so didn’t have a reason to use it, and it also required setting up a local development environment, making it too complicated for non-devs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For the current iteration of Inspect (released November 2025) the team pivoted. They built Inspect v2 as a remote development environment with a coding agent on top. Setting it up as a remote environment that they could configure centrally removed the need for local setup on each machine. They were also encouraged by seeing that OpenCode, the open-source coding agent which serves as Inspect’s harness, exposed an HTTP API which made it straightforward to set up, and was open-source, good enough, and importantly, offered model agnosticism.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Check out the episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/13ecd18f-2c37-4d86-a4e7-c000e68ee9f7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>with OpenCode creator, Dax Raad</span></a><span>.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After pivoting, adoption skyrocketed to where it is today:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure How Ramp uses Inspect</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Having built it, Ramp uses Inspect for a few things:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Coding</span></strong><span>: obvious use case; engineers prompt Inspect with small and medium-sized coding tasks that can often be one-shot passes. 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In detail:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>React / Vite: </span></strong><span>the frontend for the web interface; a React application that uses </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6eb4f5b2-7ba8-4739-b5e4-e58a6dfe6b57?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Vite</span></a><span> as its development server and build tool.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cloudflare Durable Objects</span></strong><span>: manages sessions for Inspect and is responsible for synchronizing state across all clients. This enables users to even kick off a session from their phone as and when they have an idea, and later, to pick up the PR or jump into the Inspect session on their computer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>SQLite</span></strong><span>: the database attached to the Durable Object. Stores all events that take place within an Inspect session, so that when another user joins, they can see the entire backlog of events. This enables ‘multiplayer’: two devs can work in the same session, or a PM can review the work inside a dev-started session.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cloudflare Agents SDK</span></strong><span>: a layer over the WebSockets Hibernation API that handles real-time streaming between the sandbox, API, and attached clients. Allows keeping sockets open without incurring compute costs when the connection is idle, which makes Inspect sessions economical.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Modal Sandbox</span></strong><span>: the sandboxing technology used to run each session in isolation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Fireworks and Modal</span></strong><span>: used as inference infrastructure and for fine-tuning to serve open-source models and their own fine-tuned models.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Interacting with GitHub</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>How Inspect interacts with GitHub is interesting:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Push a new branch. </span></strong><span>The Inspect sandbox pushes the branch it works on to GitHub. It also sends an event to the API with the branch name, and the session ID.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>API layer opens a pull request (PR) as the user. </span></strong><span>The API layer opens a pull request using the user’s token to tie the PR authorship to the user, which makes it impossible for the user to approve their own pull request, if it’s in a project that requires additional approvers.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>API listens to GitHub for PR status changes. </span></strong><span>The API listens to a GitHub webhook, which fires when the status of the PR is changed: e.g. when it’s updated, merged, or closed.</span></p></li></ol><p marketplace.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Inspect has an ‘automations marketplace’.</span></strong><span> 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Sentry error 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>TODO/FIXME burndown:</span></strong><span> search the code for TODO or FIXME comments, and resolve them</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>… and many more!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ramp’s automations marketplace reminds me a little bit of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/64e3d633-6868-4c62-9c18-0fea7b0d6e93?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Uber’s Agent Builder</span></a><span>, which is a collection of reusable agents. Except my sense is that while Uber’s Agent Builder was more geared for non-engineers, this automations marketplace is heavily used by engineers as well.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. </span><span>What makes Inspect so popular?</span><span> </span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every Inspect session runs a sandbox that’s near-identical to a fully set up local development environment. This means Inspect sandboxes can be used throughout the entire development environment: from ideas and prototyping, to review and shipping:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Ideas stage</span></strong><span>: Inspect can be part of the collaboration while a feature is being discussed in tools like Slack and Linear.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Prototyping</span></strong><span>: show off a web-based prototype for feedback by sharing the URL of the web server Inspect spun up.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Development</span></strong><span>: while building a feature, other engineers can connect directly to the sandbox to check out the work and give feedback – including to the agent.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Code review</span></strong><span>: The ReviewBuddy agent runs quality gates (linters and tests) invoking the Testo subagent, adds its own review, and decides who might be the best reviewer based on previous contributions and availability.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Running in prod & operations</span></strong><span>: when errors are raised with Sentry, anomalies are detected in monitoring with Datadog, or if incidents are raised in prod in incident.io, the OncallAssistant subagent is kicked off. This agent attempts to reproduce the issue in the sandbox. If it succeeds, it also proposes a fix. By the time the on-call engineer connects to the Slack thread, all the context is there and perhaps a fix is ready to review, as well.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The “secret sauce” of Inspect’s usefulness is the work put into the sandbox itself. </span></strong><span>When I hear about a company building its own AI agent harness, I usually focus on the </span><em><span>harness </span></em><span>itself. But in the case of Ramp, the harness is very basic; just OpenCode! The reason why adoption is high is because the agent runs a full-on development environment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is also why third-party coding harnesses like Codex or Claude Code are less used at Ramp: they don’t have access to all the capabilities an Inspect sandbox has.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Integrations with internal & external tools</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On top of local tools running on the sandbox, an Inspect session also gets access to internal and external tools that Ramp engineers use, as previously mentioned:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Integrated via API:</span></strong><span> Slack (chat), Linear (ticketing), LaunchDarkly (feature flags), Buildkite (CI/CD), GitHub (version control)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Via MCP</span></strong><span>: Datadog (observability), Sentry (application monitoring), and Langfuse (agent observability). MCP access is seen as exploratory, and is offered only for low-risk tools that don’t handle sensitive data</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Inspect has read-only, sanitized access to the prod database that no third-party tool could have. </span></strong><span>One benefit of Ramp having its own, internal coding agent is that it gives read-only access to a sanitized version of their production database. A group of security engineers and backend engineers built a sanitization layer through which Inspect can query the production database for things like masking or redacting personally identifiable information (PII), stripping data that should not leave the boundary, and other sensible optimizations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With all this access, Inspect is also capable of things like planning and running a database migration under supervision. CTO Rahul Sengottuvelu told us:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Inspect already has every major piece of context that is necessary for how to run a database migration. Does it have access to Datadog? Does it know how to use Datadog? Does it have access to Linear and Sentry? And GitHub and Notion? Does it know where it is in Notion? Does it know what the different repos are? It does, to all of these, and so it can plan complex things well, like a database migration.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. Inside the sandbox</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For building with Inspect, Ramp has set the following constraints:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Startup time</span></strong><span>: sandboxes need to start quickly, and Ramp has a 5-second budget to start a sandbox.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Session speed:</span></strong><span> this should be as fast as the model provider’s time-to-first token. Basically, the sandbox environment should not add to token streaming latency.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Fast restore</span></strong><span>: Idle sandboxes should be frozen and restored later. </span><em><span>One reason Ramp went with Modal’s sandbox implementation is because it uses filesystem snapshots to freeze and restore state.</span></em></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Achieving 5-second sandbox startup time</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ramp got to a five-second sandbox startup time by using a few tactical optimizations:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Regenerate repo snapshots every 30 minutes.</span></strong><span> Ramp sets up the environment once per repo, snapshots the finished state and stores it every half hour. The work includes:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cloning the repo</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Installing dependencies</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Running setup and build commands</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Running the test suite once, so cached files exist</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since the images are rebuilt every 30 minutes, there are only ever up to half an hour’s worth of changes to sync after a snapshot is created. Syncing is not a blocking operation. While syncing with the latest branch, Ramp allows the agent to </span><em><span>read </span></em><span>files using an OpenCode plugin to block file edits and writes. In a large enough repository, it is unlikely that an incoming prompt is going to modify a file changed in the last 30 minutes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ramp has 150+ repositories inside the company, which means 150+ snapshots to be rebuilt twice per hour. There’s an overhead aspect to this, but it’s the tradeoff to make for a snappy developer experience!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Warming up when starting to type. </span></strong><span>As soon as an engineer starts typing their prompt in the web interface, Inspect starts warming up the associated sandbox. It boots it up from the stored snapshot and catches up on changes since the snapshot was created. In practice, by the time you’ve finished typing, the environment is set up and ready to go!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. High-volume repos have a warm pool. </span></strong><span>For high-volume repos, Ramp keeps a “warm pool” of sandboxes. Snapshots reduce boot time, but you still need to wait for the sandbox to boot from the snapshot and sync recent changes, which takes a few seconds.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For popular repos, Ramp keeps a warm pool of sandboxes already booted and ready. When starting an Inspect session, users pick up an already-running sandbox. The warmed pool expires and is remade in sync with the 30-minute base image refresh.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s notable that the team which built Inspect was frontend engineer-heavy and this performance focus seems more than coincidental.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family:
