server</span></strong><span>: runs to allow engineers to make manual edits</span></p></li></ul><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Agent harness</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ramp decided to use </span><strong><span>OpenCode</span></strong><span> as the harness, which gives Ramp devs the option to choose their model provider. The LLM gateway routes to the selected model. Below are some reasons why Ramp likes OpenCode:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>OpenCode is an HTTP API at its core.</span></strong><span> It is a server first and foremost which enables Ramp to run many different clients (command line interfaces, CLIs, etc)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Avoids vendor lock-in. </span></strong><span>OpenCode is model-agnostic and so makes it easy to use the best model and model provider for a job, and to avoid vendor lock-in. Ramp currently defaults to GPT-5.6, and experiments with Fable as a model for planning complex tasks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Open source. </span></strong><span>LLMs can read OpenCode’s own code to understand its behavior, and this minimizes hallucinations about its capabilities.</span></p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. Collaboration & feedback</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>All sessions are collaborative with no opt-outs</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An Inspect session is collaborative by default and opt-outs aren’t available; the session is open for others to join and both the work and the prompting history are exposed. This “multiplayer-first” approach is deliberate, and has probably contributed to Inspect spreading as fast as it did. Interestingly, early on, the goal was just to be able to share sessions, and not to collaborate: this was a beneficial by-product.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are benefits to collaborative features being always-on:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>More context during code review. </span></strong><span>It’s helpful if a reviewer can see the thought process that went into the PR, and they may have to ask fewer questions about why you made a decision, as a result.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Easy to jump in when needed.</span></strong><span> Need to step away from work? Send your session to a coworker and they can take over and finish it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Helpful during performance reviews.</span></strong><span> You can just attach sessions to your performance review documents and the manager can look at them to see the work you’ve done. They should be able to write a fairer performance review based on several of your sessions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cross-disciplinary collaboration</span></strong><span>. Engineers, PMs, and designers can work together better, especially when collaboration starts on Slack, where the Inspect bot is. And because Inspect also does visual verification, showing screenshots or usable web demos means that designers/PMs/engineers can stay aligned during development.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An original author of Inspect, Zach, told us he feels that Inspect helped build a “system of trust” with AI tooling, which helped increase AI adoption at the company. In his words:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Inspect is not just a coding agent: it’s a system of trust.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s been this sentiment in the AI industry along the lines of ‘if you’re not using AI, if you’re not ahead, and you’re cooked, bro.’ What a horrible way to try and bring people on board to a very new paradigm of working!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With Inspect being out in the open</span><em><span>, </span></em><span>it has increased adoption of AI at Ramp because</span><em><span> </span></em><span>all you need to do is just go look at one of your teammates using it. The open part was not even a design goal at the start, it just happened to be something we really leaned into.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This network effect became super important. It brings this system of trust which means people learn to trust the AI to work properly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>You </span></strong><em><strong><span>trust</span></strong></em><strong><span> your teammates more because you see </span></strong><em><strong><span>their thought processes</span></strong></em><strong><span> and how they approach and break up a problem. </span></strong><span>You probably learn something about how to solve a problem from other people!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Companies of scale are all about building trust in each other, and I think Inspect in this paradigm has kind of shifted the bar.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Gathering feedback on Inspect</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Inspect team has two main Slack channels: one </span><strong><span>#project-ramp-inspect </span></strong><span>(for announcements) and </span><strong><span>#feedback-ramp-inspect </span></strong><span>(for positive and negative feedback).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They try to avoid the “we’ll get back to you” style of support; when someone reports a bug or makes a feature request, the Inspect team tags Inspect and starts working and iterating on it in public. And – of course – they share their session!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Inspect team also doesn’t dictate which features Inspect should/shouldn’t have. As Zach told us:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The things we hold precious are Inspect’s performance stability and slick UX. Other than those, we’re very open to adding a feature and then just making sure it fits in the ethos of the product.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Obviously, if a feature doesn’t get used we’ll remove it and let people know. In those cases, most people just go like ‘oh well, that makes sense’.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’re not trying to act like we think we know the direction of the product better than others. We tend to have the ‘let’s see what people ask for, then go from there’ type of approach.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Inspect team encourages others to contribute to the product. To date, about 150 engineers have contributed to Inspect. As a fun fact, in the past 30 days, ~90% of pull requests merged into the Inspect repo came from a Ramp Inspect session.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we’ve heard from folks at Ramp about why they elected to build their own, home-grown AI coding agent, and it comes down to a few things.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I have a feeling of deja vu with Cloud Development Environments (CDEs). </span></strong><span>A trend, pre-AI going mainstream for development, in 2023, was the popularity of Cloud Development Environments, which we covered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/82049e90-3ef0-424d-90d2-851ec0006081?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in a deepdive.</span></a><span> Companies like Uber, Slack, and Pipedrive figured out that their engineers would be a lot more productive if they could do development on a cloud machine, set up with source code checked out, tools installed, all ready to code and debug on. Those cloud machines were bigger than local ones, and devs could work on more than one problem and debugging sessions:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Reasons why CDEs were taking off in 2023. See </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/82049e90-3ef0-424d-90d2-851ec0006081?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>the full article</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was Developer Experience (DevEx) teams at mid-sized and large companies who were building CDEs, until around the end of 2023, when DevEx teams shifted focus to AI tooling, and CDE projects were frozen.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Ramp shows that AI agents get a lot more productive when they can run on a remote machine set up like a dev’s machine: basically, like a CDE! And so, CDEs are back – but this time as an infrastructure component for background agents.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Context + data + remote agents beats leading coding harnesses. </span></strong><span>For its coding harness, Ramp uses OpenCode, a well-built product that the likes of Claude Code and Codex aim to out-execute. Despite that, Ramp’s Inspect is far more popular internally than any coding harness built by leading AI labs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inspect out-executes the likes of Claude Code, Codex and Cursor because it has access to more internal systems and data at Ramp, including read-only access to their sanitized production database.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Honestly, the “forced collaboration” choice is very smart. </span></strong><span>Devs can easily collaborate remotely on the same Inspect session, while any dev at the company can view or join Inspect sessions. It’s not just devs: because Inspect also works in Slack, it means designers and PMs can “involve” an Inspect bot during discussions, giving it more instructions to work with.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But I do wonder if it could backfire if people start to assume this agent will just “get” what needs to be done from bits and bobs of information. It’s also possible that PMs, devs, and designers will have almost no reason to write down their plan or make a spec if Inspect is integrated everywhere. Is this good, or could it have unexpected side effects?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Ramp and Inspect show us the next wave of developer / agent productivity improvements: agents running on CDEs in the cloud. </span></strong><span>It’s not just Ramp, other in-house coding agents at the likes of Stripe, Uber, Block, and others are more productive thanks to integrations, and because the companies have background agents running on their own versions of CDEs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If there’s one thing that AI labs want to avoid, it’s for tech companies to move off their coding harnesses onto another setup that’s more productive for them! After all, once they move off their coding harness, a logical next step is to start using other AI models – including open ones – with custom harnesses. And should this trend spread of building bespoke, custom coding agents for better productivity, then it would be bad for business for frontier labs!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>OpenAI’s acquisition of Gitpod/Ona now makes so much more sense. </span></strong><span>In 2023, Gitpod </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b7f1660c-466f-4907-9f38-79e01d858ea0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>was the clear leader</span></a><span> among CDE vendors. In 2025, the company rebranded to Ona, and in June of this year, OpenAI acquired Ona, so that this technology could give Codex “a persistent place to work.” Basically, the Ona team is building cloud development environments that agents will be able to use.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Don’t forget the principle of staying ahead of the competition. </span></strong><span>A tempting argument might be to say that sure, Ramp has somewhat more productivity by building Inspect, but the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor and others surely will offer an off-the-shelf cloud coding agent and CDE product within months, so why build custom infra?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But this misses a few things:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Being very good at building AI is a valuable skill in itself.</span></strong><span> Even if Ramp only built an AI coding agent that matched the cutting edge, it could already be worth it in terms of a platform team getting hands-on experience of building AI infra! Building internal tools is a low risk approach to “upskilling” in AI engineering. Every company should want to upskill its engineers, so they are comfortable building with and on top of LLMs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Outperform competitors with better tools and by being more productive. </span></strong><span>Let’s take a competitor to Ramp that doesn’t have a tool like Inspect. Engineers there will spend more time fixing frontend issues (where Inspect helps out), spend more time debugging (which Inspect also helps with), and could ship more bugs in production (Inspect runs validation loops). So, that company could well ship slower or less frequently with the same number of engineers. For startups, such things matter!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>To attract and retain top engineering talent, being on the cutting edge matters. </span></strong><span>At the end of the day, Ramp is a fintech company and there are plenty of those. But how many of them are a few steps ahead of leading AI labs in areas like coding agents? By building cool and innovative stuff like this, Ramp could hire more easily, and engineers there might become harder for rival companies to poach if those engineers don’t want to move somewhere with inferior AI coding tooling, that doesn’t try to challenge the status quo by building something better than what already exists.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Can we take a moment to consider just how much development is changing, with agents working on developer machines in the cloud? </span></strong><span>If you said to me two years ago that we’d have AI agents fixing frontend bugs, running on a cloud machine which is like a developer machine – while taking screenshots to make sure a bug is fixed – I would not have believed it, and yet, here we are. The tooling is not widespread (as yet), but it is live at a company like Ramp, and will surely be at more companies in the near future.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>If your workplace does not yet use the concept of CDEs running in the cloud, then I hope this deepdive offers pointers on how it could be built, in order to help decide whether the tradeoff might be worth the investment. The prevailing wisdom of the “build vs buy” question is usually that it’s worth buying from a vendor instead of building infra yourself. But AI coding tools could be on course to change the calculus.</span></p></div></div><div class="post-contributor-footer" style="margin-top: 16px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div item.title: Adapting To AI: Leadership
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Adapting To AI: Leadership

Colin Breck

“Leaders are usually rewarded for being decisive, having a plan, and acting with certitude. One of the most difficult things a leader must do is sit with uncertainty. This capacity must be balanced with clear direction, a bias for action, a sense of urgency, and strong execution - otherwise it slides into indecision.“

#Leadership AI ChangeManagement
item.description: Adapting To AI: Leadership

item.title: Seeing Like A State
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Seeing Like A State

Mike Fisher

“This week, pick the single dashboard, metric, or report you rely on most, and go find the territory behind it. Sit with the people whose work becomes that number. Find the resident holder of metis and ask them what the report always gets wrong. Then come back and look at your tidy rows of data with new eyes.”

#Leadership Management Metrics
item.description: Seeing Like A State

item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Three Important Steps In My Maturation Process

Thomas Dullien

So perhaps it is natural that I am reflecting on “what were the important realizations that I made since my early 20s that had a profound impact on the way I think about the world?” This post tries to list them.

#CareerGrowth
item.description: Three Important Steps In My Maturation Process

item.title: You Should Never Be Angry At Work
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
You Should Never Be Angry At Work

Sean Goedecke

“Healthy workplaces route around anger in the same way that networks route around damage. Emotionally unreliable engineers will get left out of conversations that might cause them to blow up. Decision-making will get done around them in backchannels. I’ve seen this become a self-reinforcing cycle: angry engineers aren’t consulted on key decisions, which makes them angrier, which pushes them even further away from the spaces where decisions get made, and so on.”

#TeamHealth CareerGrowth
item.description: You Should Never Be Angry At Work

item.title: Your Executable Is A SQLite Database
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Your Executable Is A SQLite Database

Farid Zakaria

“I have been probably obsessed with two things in the last few years: Nix as a tool to explore innovative ideas that require the capability to rebuild the world and replacing ELF with SQLite as an executable format. You might have noticed that these two ideas are well suited to each other.”

#SQL DeepDive
item.description: Your Executable Is A SQLite Database

item.title: How To Report A Bug So It Actually Gets Fixed
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Report A Bug So It Actually Gets Fixed

Oscar Molnar

I wanted to make a blog post like this for a long time, because it’s something that I wish I could find more of myself. I think one of the things that helps us most in our careers as software engineers is knowing how to debug problems, how to reproduce them, and how to report them.

#Communication Debugging

A hijacked agent session is a live process you can kill.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/WorkOS_082426CTA","text":"Learn how it works →","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/9de8cc24-2e7d-4de2-8dbf-c0da80dc65db?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Learn how it works →</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The gap between code that executes fine and code that is actually safe to trust is growing wider pretty fast. For many years, writing code was the slow, expensive step, whereas reviewing it was a smaller task at the end. With the rise of AI-assisted coding, this balance is shifting.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>AI tools can now create a working function in seconds and a full feature in minutes. Teams are able to write more machine-generated code every month. In other words, producing code is now fast and relatively easy, whereas code verification is the harder part. A reviewer still has to read the change, understand it, and decide whether it belongs in production. In fact, more code written simply means more code that should be verified.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>We recently got a chance to speak with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2ad4e287-cbec-4b9e-8a8b-f9778e7a5f20?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span>Andrea Malagodi</span></a><span>, the CTO of Sonar (the company that has built some of the most used code verification software). He provided deep insights into code verification, especially in the context of AI and how Sonar is adapting to the recent changes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will look at how code verification works, why the rise of AI-generated code puts more pressure on it, along with the extremely useful insights from Andrea on what the future may look like.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>The Shift</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The shift with regard to code generation and verification is quite visible when we look at the data. One of the clearest signals comes from Google’s DORA research, a long-running study of how thousands of teams build and ship software. Their recent work found that as teams adopt more AI, delivery stability dipped. Trust in AI-generated code stayed low, with well over a third of developers reporting little confidence in what these tools produced [2]. In other words, more speed in writing code brought more pressure further down the line.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A controlled trial from the research group METR gives a similar indication. Its participants were experienced open-source developers working on their own mature projects, and each task was randomly assigned to allow or disallow AI tools. The developers expected AI to speed them up by roughly a quarter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>However, the result showed a totally different picture. AI-assisted tasks took about 19 percent longer [3]. Moreover, this happened after the developers internally believed that the AI helped them be more productive. Turns out, a lot of extra time went into prompting, waiting, reading the output, and correcting it. To be fair, the same team later reported a more confusing follow-up signal. This was partly because developers preferred to keep their AI tools [4].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Nevertheless, if we consider these results together, it is evident that while AI definitely increases the amount of code written, it also leads to more verification work down the line.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>So let us first understand what code verification actually means.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Earning Trust</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Code verification is the umbrella term for every check that ensures whether a piece of code is correct, safe, and maintainable enough to ship to production. In other words, it is the work of earning enough trust to put a change in front of real users. The key term to note here is “earning”. This is because trust arrives in degrees. It is built up one check at a time, rather than granted in a single stroke.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Think of a task of drafting a contract. Writing the words is one part of this task. However, the review, the legal checks, and the signatures are what transform those words into something people can actually rely on. Writing code works in a similar way. The moment a piece of code leaves an editor and is committed to a code repository, it carries an implicit claim about the functionality. Code verification is the process through which that claim gets tested until a team feels safe to use that code in a real production environment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Some domains push this stage to its limit through rigorous formal verification. In such domains, engineers have to mathematically prove that the code being deployed matches a precise specification. Such a process is standard for critical stuff like flight-control systems and kernels, where a single defect can risk lives. However, for most software, having a similar approach can cost far more than it returns. Therefore, teams opt for lighter checks that are arranged in layers.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>The Filter Stack</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Taking the layered analogy further, we can imagine code verification as a stack of filters. As you can see, each filter catches a certain type of problem.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/357f866e-6086-4550-a69a-8b6960b38a9e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/4a2d3614-d01b-425c-b2ee-3540bce75b52_2048x1365.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":970,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>At the top of the stack, we have the cheapest checks. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Type Checker: </span></strong><span>It confirms whether the values moving through your code are the exact type each operation expects. This way it can catch a whole class of mistakes before the code even runs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Linter:</span></strong><span> It scans for suspicious patterns and style problems.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These types of checks can run in an instant and cost almost nothing. Below this stack, we have tests.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A unit test runs a small piece of code with known inputs and confirms whether it returns the expected output. Tests can catch behavioral mistakes in the code that a type checker cannot detect. This is because a piece of code can have perfectly valid types while still computing the wrong answer. For example, consider a simple function that is supposed to add two numbers, but instead multiplies them. In such a case, the type checker and linter would not point out any issues. Only a unit test that compares the result of the operation against a known answer will reveal the mistake.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Below the layer of tests, we have the human review filter. This is basically the case where another developer goes through the change and judges whether it fits the system, solves the right problem, and is readable. This layer catches what machines can miss, such as a solution that works yet takes an approach the team standards don’t recommend.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Beneath all of these layers is the production monitoring setup. The job of this system is to observe the code under real traffic and flag problems that may have passed through every earlier layer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Real-world filter stacks can also hold more layers than this. This may include security scanners and dependency checks. However, the point is that each filter covers a specific weakness in the one above it. This is why serious teams run several such layers in a specific order before releasing any code into production.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Static And Dynamic Analysis</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The filters in that stack fall into two families:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Static Analysis: </span></strong><span>The filters in this family check the source without executing it, which makes this type of analysis fast and broad. With static analysis, we are able to scan an entire codebase in one pass. Type checkers and linters belong here. The tradeoff is that real behavior at runtime remains partly out of view. Therefore, static analysis can sometimes raise an alarm about a problem that might not exist during live conditions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Dynamic Analysis: </span></strong><span>The filters in this family run the code with real inputs and observe the result. Tests belong here. This family relies on checking actual behavior, but is limited by paths that are exercised. A test suite that only runs the happy path cannot detect a crash that might be waiting to happen on an empty input.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>Despite the extensive coverage, a clean scan and a green test suite together can still leave gaps. This is why code verification relies on many filters working together to be effective.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>False Alarms</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A tempting conclusion we might make is that more checking is always better. However, there is a tradeoff at the heart of code verification. Every filter can make two kinds of mistakes:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>False Positive: </span></strong><span>This means flagging something as a problem when the code is actually fine.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>False Negative: </span></strong><span>This means staying quiet while a real bug slips through.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If we tune a tool to catch every possible issue, it can flood the developers with false alarms. However, if we tune it to stay quiet unless it is certain, it can start to miss real defects. The two aspects pull against each other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>False alarms carry a pretty steep cost. When a tool raises frequent false alarms, developers start ignoring it. However, this habit can be catastrophic. Even an occasional real warning can get waved away with the rest. Research on static analysis tools describes this pattern, where high false-positive rates erode trust until teams switch the tool off or don’t pay attention to its warnings. However, doing so reopens the door to the very bugs the tool was meant to stop [7].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: justify"><span>This is why a good code verification setup cares as much about signal quality as about coverage. Andrea from Sonar described the balancing act as almost a CAP theorem for code verification. This was built from the classic idea that you can push some properties only at the expense of others. The three competing priorities in the case of code verification are speed, accuracy, and coverage, and no tool fully wins all three. Andrea’s team tries to keep the focus on humans with a simple rule that a finding a developer can act on is worth raising.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The positioning of the filter can also change the cost associated with a mistake. This brings us to the overall setup of the code verification pipeline.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>The Pipeline</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Filters run at different moments in the lifecycle of a change request. The timing determines their cost. If we spread the moments out in order, we get a pipeline. A change begins in the developer’s editor, moves to a set of automated checks that fire the moment code is committed, then to review, then to a merge, then out to deployment and live monitoring.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The same check becomes more expensive the later it runs. This is because more work piles on top of the mistake as development progresses. For example, catching a flaw in the editor may cost a brief moment of the author’s attention. However, catching that same flaw after it reaches production can result in an incident or a rollback. There might also be user impact. This is the real meaning of the phrase “shift left”: moving checks earlier in the pipeline so problems surface while they remain cheap to fix.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Often, vendors might try to market this approach with precise multipliers. You might come across claims that a bug costs ten times more at each stage. While the exact numbers deserve skepticism, the important takeaway is that the general direction of pushing checks earlier in the pipeline is beneficial from a cost point of view.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>AI Pressure</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This stack of filters was built for a setup where developers wrote most of the code. As we have seen, this assumption has weakened over the last few years with the rise of AI-coding tools. This change has an impact on every layer in two distinct ways.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The first pressure is volume.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>When an agent writes a thousand lines in the time a person once wrote a hundred, the review burden increases dramatically. There is also a subtle effect on batch size, meaning the amount of change bundled into a single review. AI-based coding tools tend to produce larger changes, which are harder to review. This is because attention spreads thin across a big diff and small mistakes can slip through more easily. Andrea mentioned this failure mode with a line many developers will be familiar with. The reviewer who faces a 5,000-line pull request types “looks good to me,” and figures that things will anyway surface during production.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The second pressure concerns the kind of mistakes that AI can make. A study across more than a hundred models tested the security of AI-generated code and found that it introduced a known security flaw in roughly 45 percent of cases [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Over the same period, while these models have become far better at producing code that runs cleanly, their security checks have remained mostly flat. In other words, AI has improved sharply at making the code work, but only a little at making that code truly safe. If anything, the gap between the two aspects has widened. A separate analysis of millions of code changes has also found rising duplication and falling reuse [6].</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Reviewing AI</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>When there is more code than developers can carefully read and analyze, the natural approach is to hand over some of the code verification to machines. This is why AI-driven code review has gained real momentum over the past few years.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>An AI code reviewer offers three main advantages:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Speed:</span></strong><span> It scans a change the moment it appears, before a human has time to look.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Coverage:</span></strong><span> It catches a meaningful share of bugs and security issues early.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Consistency:</span></strong><span> It applies the same standards across every change and every team member. Due to the probabilistic nature of AI code review, maintaining consistency can be challenging. It’s important to have multiple layers of review that include both AI-driven tools and other deterministic algorithmic tools.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This review process can also run inside the agent’s own loop. The agent writes a draft, the reviewer flags problems, and the agent corrects them before a human developer ever gets a chance to look at the code. This tightens the feedback loop and clears routine work off a human reviewer’s plate, ultimately helping teams handle larger volumes of generated code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" href="https://substack.com/redirect/f9fed959-f91e-47cb-beb5-c97da2a9ac07?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>However, this approach also has a risk. A reviewer model built from the same kind of model as the code creator tends to work with the same assumptions. It would therefore have the same blind spots. When both the writing of the code and reviewing it depend on similar training and similar patterns, the reviewer can confirm that the code looks right. The key question about whether the code does what was actually intended stays irrelevant. In other words, two similar models can resemble one opinion stated twice more than two completely independent checks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Consider an agent that turns a ticket into a function. An AI reviewer scans it and reports the code as clean. The code compiles, runs, and matches common patterns. Whether it does what the ticket truly meant cannot be answered by pattern-matching alone. This is where different views exist:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Some argue that the models have grown capable enough to reduce or even remove the human review step.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Others hold that people remain essential for judgment about architecture, context, and accountability.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Both camps make a fair case. The reasonable answer today is that it depends on what you are shipping and the cost of a potential mistake.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>The Modern Stack</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Let us now see how these ideas assemble into a real workflow.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Everything starts with the context. Most engineering happens in brownfield code, meaning large existing codebases with history and quirks, rather than greenfield projects that have started from scratch. An agent looking into that code without guidance works out the layout on its own, but it does so differently each time. Andrea called that inconsistency “a box of chocolates”, where the result you get back varies from one run to the next and from one developer to the next.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A mature setup handles this by feeding the agent a shared and consistent picture up front. This includes the real architecture, the coding guidelines for the language, and rules that try to capture the intended design. Three loops take care of the verification part. Here’s a brief breakdown of the loops:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Agentic Loop - Where agents iteratively build:</span></strong><span> It optimizes code generated within the agentic sandbox and improves agent effectiveness. It also reduces token costs, improves output quality, and reduces risk.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>CI verification loop - The validation pipeline for all code:</span></strong><span> Deals with code review, zero-trust, multi-layered verification, and quality gate at sandbox exit. It also merges fixes at high velocity and volume with confidence.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Code maintenance loop - Background remediation of tech debt:</span></strong><span> It continuously patrols to address legacy issues in the background agentically. Cleaner code makes it easier for coding agents to work efficiently.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Andrea also helped sketch what a mature setup in 2026 might look like. In the case of Sonar, the components of the modern stack are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Verification Engine:</span></strong><span> It consists of thousands of rules doing automated code analysis for reliability, maintainability, and security across more than 40 programming languages, frameworks, and IaC technologies. Sonar’s offerings, SonarQube (what it’s most known for) and Sonar Vortex (a new solution), provide this in the agentic loop.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>AI Code Review:</span></strong><span> A newer capability built from AI, that came through Sonar’s acquisition of Gitar. It uses carefully written instructions rather than fixed rules. Its real value is making each finding explainable to the reviewer, so that a 5,000-line change becomes something a developer can reason about. This sits in the CI verification loop.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Remediation Agent:</span></strong><span> Aimed at the existing backlog, working through old issues progressively to clean up history rather than only guarding new code. This covers the code maintenance loop.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Other companies are more or less converging on a similar idea.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>There is also a big advantage to keeping the code clean. The team at Sonar measured what happens when AI-generated code, which is often tangled and rather dense, is left to evolve across many developer sessions over half a year or more. They found that messy code ultimately starts to cost more tokens to work with. This is because the AI model needs to spend more effort understanding it every single time there is a change.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>One more aspect sits at the very front of this debate. It concerns secrets, meaning credentials like API keys and passwords. The danger with secrets is rarely intentional sabotage. Most of the time, someone pastes code or loads a configuration file into an AI session. The secret then rides along with the change, and it is usually caught too late, once it has already become part of a commit or a log file.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The fix for this is to run a scanner right at the terminal, before the developer pastes the code. In other words, the goal would be to stop it as early as the process allows. Sonar calls this approach “starting left”. This is one step earlier than the familiar shift left that we talked about. Andrea’s advice is that every developer should run a guard like this to ensure that the secrets remain safe.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Trust And Risk</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>All these points lead to one important practical question.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>How much code verification does a given change actually need?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The answer is that it depends on what a specific failure would cost. Determining the cost is the real skill that requires insight. For example, a typo on a marketing page and a bug in a payment system deserve very different scrutiny. A developer can probably fix the typo on a marketing page in a minute without much effort. However, the bug in the payment system can move money to the wrong place, break trust, and trigger an unwanted news item.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Mature teams treat verification depth as a dial dependent upon the risk factor. Low-risk changes pass through with light automated checking. However, high-risk changes often get routed to human eyes and undergo heavier scrutiny.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: justify"><span>Deciding the exact position of where the line should be drawn is a judgment call that should be made by the team. For example, a comma can be the difference between a working operating system and a crash, so the risk appetite has to be chosen in a deliberate manner. There is no fixed rule that can be applied to all situations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Agents take a change as far toward a clean and verified state as they can on their own, while staying within guardrails. They can merge low-risk work automatically while routing riskier stuff to a human developer. However, setting these tiers properly so that a change is routed to the right level of checking is an emerging practice that is only going to get more important with time.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The center of gravity in software development is shifting. Writing code has now become the faster activity. On the other hand, verifying that same code, confirming that it is correct, secure, and worthy of real users, is where the effort seems to be increasing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>As we have seen, code verification works as a stack of filters where each filter trades a bit of cost for a bit of confidence. Each filter covers a weakness in the one above it. Those filters divide into static and dynamic families. Every filter balances false alarms against missed bugs, and moving filters earlier keeps their mistakes cheap.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The flood of AI-generated code has an impact on all of it, raising both the volume and the risk. Also, the tempting shortcut of letting AI review for AI has a real catch, since a machine checking a machine can agree that code looks fine while the more important checks get ignored.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The human side to this shift is that as writing code gets cheap, the developer’s work becomes even more important. Developers need to spend more time orchestrating agents by providing instructions. They might have to focus more on the older and harder problem of knowing what to build at all. Cheaper code generation provides more room for spending time on that kind of judgment rather than removing the need for it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: item.title: Shipping video calling on Facebook
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Shipping video calling on Facebook

Philip Su

7 minutes by Philip Su Facebook's first video calling feature launched around 2011, built by a tiny team using Skype's unreliable technology, where 18% of calls simply failed to connect. Skype had no data tracking this, believing only user satisfaction reports mattered. The six weeks after launch meant around 16 hours of work daily to fix bugs. Despite junk food and poor sleep, the result brought genuinely new experiences to people, including the engineer's first ever video call with his own parents. Learn how leading teams are building and scaling AI agents in
item.description: Shipping video calling on Facebook

item.title: AI is removing the middle class of software engineering
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
AI is removing the middle class of software engineering

Florian Herrengt

7 minutes by Florian Herrengt AI tools let engineers ship code far faster than anyone can properly review it. This accelerates bad decisions and technical debt at a pace that quickly becomes unmanageable. The engineers who thrive will be those with enough judgment to guide and question AI output, not just prompt it. Those without that judgment now cause damage faster than ever before.
item.description: AI is removing the middle class of software engineering

item.title: The fastest double-to-string algorithm you’ve never heard of
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The fastest double-to-string algorithm you’ve never heard of

Victor Zverovich

6 minutes by Victor Zverovich A binary-to-decimal algorithm from the yyjson library runs faster than most alternatives by using just one multiplication instead of two or three. It finds the shortest decimal that converts back to the original float by testing four candidate values against a rounding interval. A visualization using an 8-bit float format shows how the algorithm works, including a boundary case where a small rounding correction in a lookup table changes which output gets chosen.
item.description: The fastest double-to-string algorithm you’ve never heard of

item.title: Quake shareware: CD just a little too full
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Quake shareware: CD just a little too full

Fabien Sanglard

6 minutes by Fabien Sanglard In 1996, id Software included encrypted versions of their game catalog on the Quake shareware CD, letting players unlock titles by calling a phone operator and paying by credit card. The plan fell apart within 39 days when hackers discovered the unlock code was generated entirely on the user's machine, making the phone call pointless. The CD's software simply checked user input against a code it had already calculated itself, with no secrets coming from the server. The scheme collapsed, leaving id stuck with 150,000 unsold discs.
item.description: Quake shareware: CD just a little too full

item.title: How Instacart built a modern search infrastructure on Postgres
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Instacart built a modern search infrastructure on Postgres

Ankit Mittal

13 minutes by Ankit Mittal Instacart moved search from Elasticsearch to Postgres, then added semantic search using pgvector instead of a separate FAISS service. This let them combine keyword and meaning based search in one system, cutting overfetching and easing maintenance. The switch also improved recall, leading to 6% fewer searches with zero results and a real revenue boost. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: How Instacart built a modern search infrastructure on Postgres

item.title: A field guide to .NET data formats
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A field guide to .NET data formats

Bipin Joshi

Different data formats each have their own query language suited to their structure. CSV relies on parsing libraries like CsvHelper before handing off to LINQ, while SQL remains the most mature standalone query language for relational data. XML uses XPath or LINQ to XML for tree traversal, JSON favors typed deserialization, and binary formats skip querying entirely. Most formats are just a path to in-memory objects, where LINQ takes over.
item.description: A field guide to .NET data formats

item.title: Building a distributed job scheduler
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Building a distributed job scheduler

Aaron Stannard

Akka.Cluster.Sharding and cluster routers both fall short for long-running jobs: sharding rebalances and kills in-progress work, while routers lack memory and recovery. A better approach uses a persistent singleton actor as a central scheduler that tracks job sizes, picks the least-loaded node, and never moves work already in flight. When nodes join or crash, only queued jobs are redistributed, leaving running jobs untouched.
item.description: Building a distributed job scheduler

item.title: Faster blob copying in azure blob storage
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Faster blob copying in azure blob storage

Mark Heath

Copying blobs between Azure storage accounts can be done in three ways, with speed varying wildly. Downloading and reuploading is the slowest, taking over an hour for a 10GB file, as it is limited by your local connection. A server-side copy is faster but still slow across accounts. The fastest approach splits the file into blocks and copies them in parallel entirely within Azure, completing the same 10GB copy in under 10 seconds.
item.description: Faster blob copying in azure blob storage

item.title: Introducing Postie
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Introducing Postie

Andrew McLachlan

Postie is a free, open source library for ASP.NET Core that removes boilerplate from the CQRS pattern. Instead of writing repetitive handler lambdas for every endpoint, you map commands and queries directly to routes in a single line. It works with its own built-in mediator or with MediatR, and handles common HTTP conventions like 201 responses and 404s automatically.
item.description: Introducing Postie

item.title: Parsing IP addresses in C# at crazy speeds
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Parsing IP addresses in C# at crazy speeds

Daniel Lemire

This article shows how to parse IP addresses in C# using AVX-512, a newer CPU instruction set. It uses masked loads to handle short strings safely, then locates dots and validates the address with vector math. The result is about three times faster than the standard library method, reaching roughly 71 million addresses per second on modern hardware. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Parsing IP addresses in C# at crazy speeds
