Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Graph Construction</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Building that graph from raw documents is a pipeline, and most of its cost concentrates in a single stage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For reference, Microsoft’s documented indexing workflow runs through six phases:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Documents are sliced into text units, the same chunking step standard RAG performs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A language model processes each text unit and extracts entities carrying a title, type, and description, along with relationships carrying a source, target, and description.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Entities sharing a title and type are merged across text units, and their descriptions collect into an array. A second language model pass compresses each array into one description. Relationships receive the same treatment.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Claim extraction runs optionally, producing time-bound factual statements about entities.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The assembled entity graph is clustered into a community hierarchy.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Community reports are generated, and text units, entity descriptions, and report contents are embedded into a vector store.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The merge step accounts for a lot of the expense. For example, a service mentioned across two hundred documents produces two hundred separate descriptions during extraction. Every one of those has to be reconciled into a single coherent description before the graph becomes usable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every extracted entity, relationship, and claim retains a pointer back to the text unit it came from. This pointer is what allows a generated answer to cite a specific paragraph in a specific document.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" model passes over an entire corpus add a substantial amount of inference. Microsoft’s documentation estimates graph extraction at roughly 75 percent of total indexing cost. Lastly, extraction quality also depends on prompts tuned to the domain.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a separate point, FastGraphRAG replaces the language model in extraction with traditional NLP, treating noun phrases as entities and co-occurrence within a chunk as a relationship. Indexing becomes far cheaper, and the resulting graph carries considerably more noise</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Community Detection</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A graph of entities and relationships answers connection questions well. However, answering whole-collection questions requires one more layer on top of it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GraphRAG runs hierarchical Leiden clustering across the entity graph. The algorithm recursively partitions the graph into clusters, called communities, and keeps subdividing until communities fall below a size threshold. The output is a hierarchy with several levels.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These levels behave like a resolution control over the same underlying graph. Level 0 contains a small number of broad communities, each covering a large region. Deeper levels contain many more communities, each covering a narrower region. A single payments community at level 0 might split into separate communities for retry behaviour, settlement, and fraud checks two levels further down.</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For every community at every level, a language model generates a community report. Each report contains an overview of that community along with its key entities, relationships, and claims. Reports are then summarized again into shorthand versions for compact use at query time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the step that makes whole-collection questions answerable. A summary of what a cluster of documents collectively says gets written during indexing, well before anyone asks about it. When a global question arrives, the material required to answer it already exists as text.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Which particular level supplies the reports is a decision with real consequences. Microsoft’s documentation states that response quality is heavily influenced by that choice. Lower levels produce more thorough answers because their reports carry more detail, but they also cost more time and more tokens because there are many more reports to process.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Query Modes</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With a graph and a hierarchy of reports sitting on disk, retrieval can follow two structurally different paths. GraphRAG supports both.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Local search begins by matching the query against entity description embeddings, which produces a set of entry-point entities. From each entry point, expansion proceeds along five directions in parallel:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Text units that mention the entity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Community reports that contain it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Neighbouring entities connected to it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The relationships forming those connections.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Covariates, meaning any extracted claims attached to it.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each of those candidate sets is ranked and filtered independently. The survivors are packed into a single context window of predefined size. The expansion is bounded, and the ranking is explicit, which makes local search closer to a structured gather-and-rank operation than to open-ended pathfinding across the graph.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Global search leaves the entity graph untouched. Community reports from a chosen hierarchy level are split into batches, and those batches are shuffled so that batch ordering stays randomized. A map stage runs each batch through a language model and produces an intermediate answer where every point carries a numerical importance rating. A reduce stage then collects the highest-rated points across all batches and generates the final answer from them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The mapping back to our payments questions can be made clearer now. The question: “Which service owns the retry logic” names an entity, so local search locates it and expands around it. Also, the question “Which failure causes recur most often” names no entity in particular, so global search aggregates across pre-written reports covering the whole corpus.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: search, blends the two. It starts by comparing the query against the most relevant community reports to produce a broad initial answer along with follow-up questions, runs local search against those follow-ups, and returns a hierarchy of questions and answers ranked by relevance.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GraphRAG also ships a basic search mode, which is plain top-k vector retrieval, for queries where that remains the appropriate tool. When an answer comes back broad and shallow, or narrow and precise, the query mode usually explains it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[Diagram 6. Local search and global search side by side] Left panel traces the query to matched entities, then the five parallel expansion streams, then per-stream ranking and filtering, then a single assembled context window. Right panel traces the query alongside shuffled community report batches, into parallel map calls producing rated intermediate answers, then filtering, then the reduce call producing the final answer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Cost Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What we have looked at so far are the various capabilities associated with GraphRAG. However, cost determines whether a specific capability is worth acquiring for a given system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Standard RAG has a modest cost at both ends, with one embedding pass at index time and one nearest-neighbour lookup per query. In contrast, GraphRAG redistributes the spending considerably. Index time absorbs two language model passes over the corpus plus report generation for every community at every level. Query time then splits, with local search running cheaply against a prepared context window, and global search running a language model across many report batches for a single question.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The index is also a derived artifact. New documents arriving means extraction, clustering, and summarization run again over the affected material, and the community hierarchy itself can shift as the graph grows. For a corpus that changes daily, this becomes an ongoing operational commitment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Microsoft’s own follow-up work addressed the cost directly. For example, LazyGraphRAG builds its index using NLP rather than a language model, skips summarization entirely, and defers all language model work to query time. In this case, indexing cost matches vector RAG and lands at 0.1 percent of full GraphRAG. Global-query quality stays comparable to global search while query cost drops by more than a factor of 700.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Microsoft still argues against making every deployment LazyGraphRAG. Their stated reasoning is that the pre-built entity, relationship, and community summaries carry value beyond question answering, because people read and share those reports directly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two findings from Microsoft’s own evaluations are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Vector RAG remains the stronger option for local queries, where the answer resembles the question and sits in a specific region of text.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>GraphRAG’s measured advantage lies in comprehensiveness, diversity, and supporting source material. On faithfulness, it scored at a similar level to baseline RAG.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second point matters whenever someone asks whether GraphRAG reduces hallucination. The evidence supports better coverage and better sourcing, but it stops short of claiming better factual accuracy per individual claim.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Agentic Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since different question types favour different retrieval strategies, committing to one strategy when a system is built gives up the others.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Agentic RAG helps formulate a response to that constraint.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A language model classifies the incoming query, selects a retrieval strategy, executes it, and synthesizes the result. Available strategies might include vector search for local questions, global search for corpus-wide questions, a SQL query for structured data, and web search for anything current.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/a80c317f-8011-49e0-bd04-2a5f5e9d653f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d7759dfb-dff4-4703-9aec-8a6428bab54a_3902x1818.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":678,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":272692,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/210945210?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd7759dfb-dff4-4703-9aec-8a6428bab54a_3902x1818.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bMmM!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd7759dfb-dff4-4703-9aec-8a6428bab54a_3902x1818.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LlamaIndex documents a two-layer version of this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A composite retriever selects which index to query, guided by a description supplied for each index.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Within the selected index, an auto-routed mode then selects which retrieval method applies to that specific query.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In other words, routing decisions happen at both layers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The approach carries its own costs. It adds a language model call ahead of retrieval, which increases both latency and per-query spend. Routing errors also produce a debugging problem, because a poor answer can come from a perfectly good retrieval running under the wrong strategy.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The overall progression from basic RAG through advanced RAG to GraphRAG and then agentic RAG describes a sequence of decisions about when a system commits to a retrieval strategy. It works well as a ladder where each step outperforms the one below it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we’ve gone deep into GraphRAG and understood it in detail. Here are the key learning points to remember:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Local queries have answers that resemble the question and sit in a small number of text regions, while global queries require reasoning across large portions of a collection.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Similarity search returns whichever chunks sit nearest the query vector, so global questions tend to retrieve vocabulary matches instead of the underlying pattern.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Larger context windows leave that gap open. Vector retrieval with 64,000 tokens still trailed on global questions in Microsoft’s testing.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A knowledge graph stores entities and typed relationships with descriptions, preserving connections that plain chunking discards.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>GraphRAG indexing runs two language model passes over the corpus, one to extract entities and relationships and one to merge their descriptions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Graph extraction accounts for roughly 75 percent of indexing cost, making it the first stage to examine when reducing spend.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Hierarchical Leiden clustering produces communities at several levels of resolution over the same entity graph.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A community report is generated for every community at every level, so summaries of what the corpus collectively says exist before any question arrives.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Local search expands from matched entities and ranks the results into one context window, while global search runs map-reduce across community reports.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The index is derived and perishable. LazyGraphRAG responds by moving language model work to query time, cutting indexing cost to 0.1 percent of full GraphRAG.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Vector RAG remains stronger for local queries, and agentic retrieval selects a strategy per query rather than committing to one when the system is built.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>In my ~20 years in this industry, I’ve not seen as many capable engineering leaders opting out or taking prolonged breaks as now, with some high-ranking engineering leaders – CTOs, VPs of Engineering, heads of engineering, etc. – quitting their high-status roles and departing, if not into the sunset, then at least with nothing lined up.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To find out what might be behind this spate of sign-outs, I talked with almost 20 engineering leaders currently on a career break – or seriously considering one – and they let me into their personal reasons for deciding to jam the brakes on their careers. </span><em><span>Thanks to everyone who shared their input!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Ten of the most common reasons for quitting, </span></strong><span>sometimes without the next gig lined up:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>1. The job got (much) worse</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>2. The startup is “losing” and becoming worthless</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>3. Not being AI-native enough for other skills to be relevant</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>4. Their predecessor saw the “writing on the wall”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>5. Long hours – rarely decisive</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>6. Smaller teams mean less need for leaders</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>7. Fractional CTO work preferred over fulltime positions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>8. AI startups pay ICs more than non-AI startups pay executives</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>9. Quitting to launch their own business</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>10. Burnout</span></p></li></ul></li></ul><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>“Founder mode” looks here to stay, so how to deal with it? </span></strong><span>And has it made the CTO and VPE roles become “low ROI”?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>‘Work at companies that truly want to drive change’. </span></strong><span>A personal account from someone who took the VP of Engineering role at Gitpod (later, Ona, now acquired by OpenAI) and enjoyed a rewarding experience. break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>“Just me?”</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span> I was recently messaged by a head of engineering in San Francisco, who said:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I’m talking to four startups in San Francisco about the head of engineering roles. Pretty normal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>But one interesting pattern is how founding CTOs/heads of engineering are stepping away to take a full career break. </span></strong><span>We’re talking about two of these four startups. And these are good startups!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Have you seen this trend? I have a small number of data points here, so you might have a broader view.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I asked around privately, and it turns out a majority of the CTO-level folks I spoke to are considering the very same thing, or are actually in the process of leaving the office for a long spell away; 6/10 engineering leaders said they’re on the way out.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. The job got (much) worse</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Unrealistic expectations, including about AI, by founders and CEOs are the leading cause of jobs turning bad for CTOs and VPEs right now in 2026:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>CTO expected to magically transform the company to be “AI-native”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>CTO must make significant engineering cost cuts of up to 20-50%, including morale-sapping job cuts</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“Do more with less” equals shipping more with fewer people (e.g., no backfills)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>CTO faces pressure on business results as AI coding bills rack up</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Founder slop: they want wonky AI prototypes shipped as full-blown products within weeks</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Hands-on founders with “AI psychosis” make the job predictably harder, </span></strong><span>according to one CTO who just signed out of his job:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Managing ‘AI psychosis’ with founders and executive peers has become very difficult. For example, what do you do when a founder ships a 60,000-line pull request into the product, gleaming with joy at how much more productive they’ve become with AI? They won’t see all the issues with that PR, and how do you bring up that they’ve created a massive amount of tech debt? Especially without looking like a ‘Debbie Downer’.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Founder slop issues begin when top leaders</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>get</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>excited about AI’s capability, then get hands-on and start issuing PRs, and shipping code to production. It can cause issues across the board:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Accountability. Who’s oncall when founder-shipped code breaks? In the “you build it, you own it” culture of startups, it’s confusing when a founder gets hands-on while not owning their work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Quality out the door: if a founder’s half-baked features are accepted, it sends the wider message that quality does not matter. Some people may adopt this attitude to their own work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A founder can overrule whatever was previously agreed with the CTO or VPE about what to build next. Vibes the founder has or feels are reason enough.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Another way that leadership roles have diminished is that craft and quality are less important, </span></strong><span>says a VP of engineering who’s in the process of signing out of their job:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Shipping software became all about speed. Finding differentiation with your product in the market is brutal, and speed / go-to-market becomes the biggest differentiator. Craft, quality, and care going into the product are taking a backseat.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Things also go bad when companies don’t ‘get’ AI+engineering, except as a way to cut jobs. </span></strong><span>CTOs I talked to mentioned the likes of Ramp, Stripe, and Notion as places that understand how to integrate AI into the engineering culture with a growth mindset without forsaking quality. Elsewhere, bad vibes dominate at places where going all-in on AI leads to the cynical conclusion that product management, design, and engineering leadership are irrelevant.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. The startup is “losing” and becoming worthless</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Director+ roles have a few differences from individual-contributor engineering ones:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Larger equity stake in the business.</span></strong><span> Base salary at these levels is often similar to a staff engineer’s, but usually with more generous equity grants – especially at the VP of Engineering and CTO levels. A good financial outcome depends on the company becoming more valuable, and – in the case of private companies – having a good exit by being acquired or selling shares.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Understanding of the business and competition is a baseline. </span></strong><span>At Director+ level, a big part of the job is making strategic decisions that grow the business and help the company get ahead. It’s a nice-to-have for an engineer to possess business acumen, but director-and-above folks use it much more than most individual contributors (ICs). Great engineering leaders are good at understanding business performance and outlook.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A company that adopts AI rapidly usually falls into one of three buckets:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>“AI-native”, building & selling AI products. </span></strong><span>The large AI labs and a select few “AI-native” startups are thriving, but many AI startups with VC funding struggle. Engineering leaders know this, and that their equity – usually issued as options – could end up worthless.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Software startups threatened by AI-native businesses. </span></strong><span>Good businesses in the pre-AI world can be threatened by AI today, like SaaS startups selling seat-based products in areas where agents are taking over the functionality. They have to pivot their businesses or seek an exit. Bending Spoons </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/78e706fc-af38-435a-8426-2d8ffe5d48e5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>buying Airtable</span></a><span> for less than the company raised is an example of a business threatened by AI and choosing to sell, instead of pivoting the whole business.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Unaffected by AI.</span></strong><span> Usually stable businesses which do more than software, such as with a real-world side to the operation like manufacturing or distribution.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The majority of software startups fall into one of the first two buckets of being AI-native or under threat. Senior leaders at such companies are in a good position to evaluate whether their company is a “winner” worth staying with.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Leaving due to equity becoming worthless</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A CTO who quit their startup told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>My company would have needed a massive exit for me to realize any upside.</span></strong><span> I had an equity grant that was 2% of the common shares. However, this equity was behind an already steep preference stack for investors, post Series A.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This CTO had a </span><em><span>very</span></em><span> generous equity grant at 2% of shares, so what made him leave it behind? They laid out how it will be difficult to get any benefit from them because the shares are most likely rendered worthless by rules about the order in which different investors get their share of the pie:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Assume that this company raised a $10M seed round at a $50M valuation, then a $100M Series A at a $500M valuation. So, a total of $110M was raised across two rounds.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Investors typically have a 1x preference. 1x preference would mean that upon any sale, they get the first $110M of the sale.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>But in this company, the Series A investors negotiated a 2x preference: so upon a sale, $210M goes to investors first ($10M to the Seed, and $200M to the Series A investors).</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The company now needs to sell for at least $210M for common shareholders (like the CTO) to make </span><em><span>any</span></em><span> money!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>If the CTO does not believe a $200M+ exit could happen, then their equity is worthless. A $200M+ exit is typically an acquisition, because a stock market flotation rarely happens at below a $10B+ valuation, these days.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If a VC-funded company does not have the revenue or customers to grow at a fast tick (circa 20-50% per year), then it’s often a struggle to raise the next round of funding, and the business’s actual value usually shrinks to 3-5x of annual revenue. So, if a startup is making $10M per year after raising $110M in funding, and growing 30% year-on-year, then the company is likely worth around $30-50M. Perhaps the right buyer would pay $100M, but if growth slows, the value is likely to drop.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An experienced CTO who takes a step back and assesses things can realize when there’s a high chance of their equity turning into smoke, removing a reason to not sign out of the job. It’s what happened to the CTO above, and when they couldn’t turn the business around, they quit.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Business stops growing</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When a VC-funded startup’s business stops growing, the prognosis can be dire in the sense that it’s unlikely to be worth as much as in the previous funding round. This is true even when the startup becomes profitable: this might mean it could theoretically go on forever; but with slow or no growth, it won’t win in another VC funding round.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s a VP of Engineering who saw their startup stop growing, partly due to wrong bets by the CEO:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“My founder/CEO was nontechnical, and was both moving too slow and too fast with AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Too slow, as in they did not take the time to understand what our customers wanted. We built a TON of AI stuff, it totally confused them, they churned, growth stalled, word-of-mouth growth was gone. Heck, I don’t think our customers ever wanted or needed anything with AI!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Too fast, as in they deprioritized core systems’ reliability in favor of shipping AI work to prod which did not have any commercial potential. So, our core offering started to have more outages and we lost customers because of this as well.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’d add that deprioritizing reliability in favor of building features may be sensible in the early days. The problem seemed to be that this company had not found product-market fit, and the new AI features didn’t resonate with customers. Basically, the CEO lacked customer understanding, business intuition, or both.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, good on the VPE for getting out when they saw the direction of travel. If the CEO won’t accept input from the VPE – who would’ve at least prioritized reliable operation – then there isn’t much left to stick around for!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Not being AI-native enough for other skills to be relevant</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The top-paying engineering leadership positions have one thing in common: experience of leading AI-native organisations is expected, and leaders are sought who have turned their current company AI-native, or work at such a place.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s new to see people signing out of large companies for feeling like they’re lagging behind in adopting new AI workflows. An ex-engineering director at a large bank told me they quit their job to accelerate their career:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I was not getting the opportunity to ‘close the loop’ on hypotheses enough. [...] To stay relevant in the industry, I feel like I need to pull out into the “fast lane.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like many others, I see the future of software development is with AI. If you don’t get hands-on with your team, working with AI tools day-in, day-out, you’re falling behind.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My plan is to get on the cutting edge of things through a mix of academia and consulting AI companies. I am not saying the plan is perfect, but I need more time to do things differently than I had in my job.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider this: if you stay in your job for two more years, do you expect to find career opportunities at cutting-edge companies in the future? If the answer is “no”, then there’s a risk in just staying put. Joining an uncertain startup or taking a career break to develop AI expertise is also risky, but the outcomes may be more controllable than letting your skillset become outdated, relatively quickly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>But it might actually be necessary to quit in order to get AI experience: you might be able to get this by transferring to an IC role.</span></strong><span> As Charity Majors, co-founder and CTO of Honeycomb, said </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e645e474-7262-43d9-9c85-c33c37e29329?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in last week’s episode</span></a><span> of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“You’ve got to get AI on your resume. You just have to. If you don’t, this is a huge career risk. If you’re working somewhere where you’re not getting these skills, I would do whatever I could to change that [including taking an IC role within the company].”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are companies where moving from Director+ to individual contributor is possible, even if these companies are the minority. If you happen to work at a place like this: consider if you can and will take advantage of this opportunity.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Most companies say they want to be AI-native, but never do</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Claire Vo – founder of ChatPRD and host of ‘How I AI’ podcast, and the former Chief Product & Technology Officer at LaunchDarkly – </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fd3a2e85-dde3-464c-ace1-c68e3f3b5edd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>says</span></a><span> most companies will never become “AI native” simply because most VP of Engineering or CTO folks don’t have what it takes to pull off such a transformation. In </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fd3a2e85-dde3-464c-ace1-c68e3f3b5edd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>her words</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The VPE role used to be primarily about deploying the dark arts to defend engineers from the roadmap, and now everyone thinks that’s BS and leaders are under tremendous pressure to inflect velocity or GTFO (get the f*** out).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Engineers are unhappy (don’t make me tokenmaxx, bro!), product and design sending slop PRs, and everyone good has left for a lab.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most of these companies’ EPD (Engineering, Product, Design) orgs will never go AI-native, not even close. Most VPEs aren’t good enough at change management to pull it off.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It looks like there’s a deadlock:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The current engineering org is frustrated by how AI is making engineering culture worse, morale is down, and people are frustrated and confused</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>To resolve this, drastic changes are needed to how everyone (engineers, product, designers) works</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>To pull it off, a VP of Engineering or CTO is needed who’s capable of this; someone excellent at change management, who’s ideally done it before.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>But most VPEs and CTOs are not experts at large-scale change management, nor have done it before.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>According to this, many VPEs and CTOs are doomed to fail at making the change they want, and it’s hard to know if that’s because organizations didn’t support them properly or resisted change.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Their predecessor saw the “writing on the wall”</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s (usually) a honeymoon period in a new job, when we believe in the business we’ve joined and in its direction. But when this phase passes, a fraction or all of the problems described above may emerge, and there’s a decent chance that some of them are why your predecessor signed out:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Has AI helped make the role worse?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Is the equity on course to be worthless?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Is getting AI-native experience actually possible, or is the organization resisting change?</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’ve talked with a CTO who replaced their predecessor and founding CTO. A few years into the job, the predecessor CTO realized their equity in the business was worth almost nothing due to stalled growth, all while they were also being out-competed by AI-native rivals. So, the new CTO also resigned after a short, six-month tenure.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. Long hours – rarely decisive</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two engineering leaders – a CTO and a VP of Engineering – mentioned “insane working hours” as a factor that contributed to them finally quitting. But there were other things as well:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The business struggling for growth</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Their equity grant’s value shrinking to nothing before their eyes</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>CEO/founder ignoring or overriding efforts to help the business succeed</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My sense is that at a thriving business during chaotic times like these, it’s unlikely that long hours alone would spur people to leave, if their contribution to current success counts and is valued. When things are going well, it’s possible to delegate more and take time to recharge batteries. But when things are going badly, it feels like every waking hour needs to be spent on working to turn things around.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. Smaller teams mean less need for leaders</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Several engineering leaders are stepping back into IC roles for more stability because engineering teams are smaller now.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Karthik Hariharan, engineering leader at DoorDash, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f7eda9fa-bc86-414c-b011-f61b2c49a65b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>notes</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Expectations have been shifting a lot in these roles, and a lot of folks qualified for them have consciously been stepping back into IC roles or joining bigger companies for stability and better compensation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Engineering teams are also smaller now. A VPE isn’t needed until the team is large enough to require it. A technical founder can run the team for a lot longer these days.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some reasons why engineering teams have shrunk:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Fullstack engineer” is mainstream, and was even before AI. </span></strong><span>Fullstack engineering was becoming relevant a few years ago in terms of a single engineer working on both the front and backends, instead of having a frontend engineer building the UI, and a backend engineer working on backend services. Fullstack frameworks like Next.js or Ruby on Rails made all this pretty easy before AI. Today with AI coding agents, you can rely on them to write decent code on platforms you’re unfamiliar with. There’s now little to no reason why a project would need multiple devs with different specializations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s normal for one, or a maximum of two fullstack engineers, to be working on any given project at Anthropic as well. Head of Claude Platform, Katelyn Lesse, shared </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb53c993-856a-4867-bfcb-6102a51092ce?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>how it works at Anthropic:</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“On an individual project, you often cannot have more than two people working on it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is because each engineer is already running several agents. And so as an engineer, you’re already fighting against your agents, which are stepping on each other’s toes on implementation. And in this setup, you just cannot have that many humans, who also come with all their agents!”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Frontend-only and native mobile teams are also getting smaller or disappearing. </span></strong><span>Even at companies where iOS and Android are a big part of the business, more places are building using cross-platform technologies where one engineer can do the work that used to need several. For example, social media app Bluesky had </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/048e7fec-1957-44f0-8599-ceccb92bc92f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>a single engineer build</span></a><span> its web, iOS, and Android apps for launch by using React Native and Expo. Bluesky later hired more people to work on the web and apps, but they all work across these three platforms. It’s not the same as hiring separate web engineers, iOS engineers, and Android engineers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We cover this in more detail in the deepdives </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/04178357-83d9-4a9a-a10a-c604738930e5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Cross-platform mobile development</span></a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/36e6ffd7-ebaa-4e3c-bac5-ad0b6c96870d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Is there a drop in native iOS and Android hiring at startups?</span></a><span> We also observed a steep drop in frontend engineers and native mobile engineers in our latest </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/99f6eefc-da54-49e0-9719-13036f00f02e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration:
