The trend has not stopped, and many – if not most – companies have increased the number of reports each engineering manager has, while reducing the number of layers in their organization.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. Fractional CTO work preferred over fulltime positions</span></h2><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Standout engineering leaders who have built strong reputations and are based in tech hubs like New York, San Francisco, and London, are increasingly hesitant to join startups for the reasons above. An alternative is “Fractional CTO work”, which usually means working one or two days per week on a contract basis at a startup, typically for cash-only and zero equity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For engineering leaders on a career break who don’t want to return to fulltime work just yet, a fractional role is a great way to stay in the game for lower time commitment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meanwhile, why would a startup hire a fractional CTO? It’s because they can start immediately, and if things don’t work out the parties can part ways quickly. It’s also useful learning material for hiring a permanent CTO later.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The fractional CTO whom I talked with in New York, said that they work with three companies, of which two wanted them to be the fulltime CTO. But this CTO is reluctant to make the move, mostly because they expect inflated expectations, they’re unclear about how viable either startup truly is, and the hours are set to be long.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>8. AI startups pay ICs more than non-AI startups pay executives</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s an open secret that compensation for very senior hires at AI labs is extremely generous, in the multi-million-dollar-per-year range, not accounting for equity appreciation. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have managed to get high-flying engineering leaders to join their ranks as a “member of technical staff”; that is, an individual contributor with no direct reports – at least, not initially.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One example: in April, Anthropic </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5f1478d4-081d-4b53-b064-48296c2e3eb7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>hired</span></a><span> Peter Bailis, Workday’s CTO (the HR software company being worth $50B) as an individual contributor. </span><em><span>In this example, Workday could be a more “traditional” company that’s not thriving in the business landscape that’s changing with AI.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>The latest news is that private equity giant Silver Lake is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1fb01789-c331-4bb0-9ecb-265f8f9d2dcf?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in talks to buy</span></a><span> the company, suggesting Workday predicts the business and stock price will struggle to grow in the coming years.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5a68304b-036c-4ea9-baa1-11b3469e0e19?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>as per levels.fyi,</span></a><span> Anthropic </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5a68304b-036c-4ea9-baa1-11b3469e0e19?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>offers</span></a><span> a median of $1.25M per year in total compensation for staff-level software engineers. This is total compensation (base salary plus equity), and while equity is currently not liquid, Anthropic has regularly held secondary stock sales. Plus, the company is expected to go public, perhaps </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5befb985-5433-40cc-b3da-f7169827f94c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>later this year.</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And $1.25M p/a is well above what most CTOs or VP of Engineering folks earn at smaller startups, or even some mid-sized companies. If a hands-on CTO can join an AI lab, become an IC, get the best possible AI-native experience, and make more money than before, then what’s not to like?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>9. Quitting to launch their own business</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With AI tools, it’s now easier than ever to build a prototype, a new product, or launch a startup. If you know what you want to build, then as a tech professional, you can have a working prototype within minutes and tweak it over a few days. The tricky thing about building a viable business is no longer coding: it’s identifying an unmet customer need, getting customers, and finding product-market-fit. Of course, this all takes time, while advertising and sales cost significant sums.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Experienced engineering leaders have two ways to start a business and for the process to be a lot more accessible than before:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Bootstrap an existing idea, and aim to build a lifestyle business. </span></strong><span>A lifestyle business is one that’s controlled by an owner – without investors to apply pressure for fast growth – who prioritizes work-life balance over maximizing profits and steep growth goals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Using AI tools, create a product you know there’s a need for, without needing to hire a team of engineers. Build it with AI agents, especially if you’re a hands-on leader who knows what it takes to build quality software. Use business acumen to get customers, generate revenue, potentially hire a couple of people to help with key tasks, and turn the whole thing into a small, profitable lifestyle business.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Raise funding to build an AI-related startup. </span></strong><span>Today, there’s more VC money in the market than before and most is going into AI startups. As an experienced engineering leader with strong pedigree, raising seed funding for an AI startup is probably more achievable. With funding, you can hire a strong team and give your idea a proper shot. Of course, building a startup is never easy, but building an AI-native one has the benefit that you become extremely hands-on with this new way of building software, and your future employability should be boosted, even if the startup doesn’t fly.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>10. Burnout</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI-related burnout seems to be an issue spreading across the industry – and not just for engineering leaders – as Charity discussed in depth on last week’s Pragmatic Engineer Podcast episode:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Receiving too much AI slop (e.g. via emails, code, social media posts)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Too much AI hype</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“Doom trolling”: a term </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d65374a4-bd4f-45bc-92d5-653467925497?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>coined</span></a><span> by Cal Newport to describe Anthropic and OpenAI’s public predictions of AI destroying jobs and creating economic hardship for society</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Scott Tolinski, cohost of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4160daad-4582-4491-aa8c-fc7844822c95?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Syntax.fm</span></a><span>, explored the topic of developer burnout in-depth in his video </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/feb1ae40-b44e-46d1-a0be-8c0a4704397f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The true cost of AI coding</span></a><span>. In the episode, they talked with Adam Elmore, an engineer of 17 years’ experience who works at OpenCode, who went through severe periods of burnout caused by AI coding tools. He ended up sick for more than two weeks, unable to even go for a walk. His burnout was preceded by the feeling of being ridiculously productive:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“[My burnout] was preceded by very intense AI usage. So, I think I burned myself out through just late nights. I could hardly sleep; I was so excited to just get the next prompt; I didn’t want the AI ever stalling. If it wasn’t burning tokens, I felt like I was leaving something on the table.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It felt very productive: getting stuff going, having multiple things going at once, refactors, and all this stuff. That sort of led to a pretty hard crash.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the video, Scott also talked with Dr. Courtney Tolinski, analyzing what leads to burnout in AI coding, and shared details from a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2b5f0b12-81e1-4971-a84c-aafb3865997b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>burnout-related survey</span></a><span>. He summarized:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“With AI, the data definitely shows that people feel like they need to produce more now than ever.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Among the people </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2b5f0b12-81e1-4971-a84c-aafb3865997b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>who answered this survey,</span></a><span> AI was changing more than how fast software gets made; it was changing the pressure, sleep, enjoyment, and how capable people felt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Individual limits only really come into play if the systems around you allow you to even stop working in the first place. So, before “maximum output 24/7, all the time” becomes the baseline for you, we need to figure out what healthy AI-assisted workflows actually look like in our lives.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>“Founder mode”: how to deal with it as an engineering leader?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/862ed13a-788f-4f3f-b8fa-08b7de8c4e78?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Uma Chingunde</span></a><span>, an experienced engineering leader believes one trend is the most significant for folks in leadership roles: ‘founder mode’. She </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/548c071f-356d-4efc-b11a-326850c6f733?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shared</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Talking to some peers who experienced either their CEOs getting AI-pilled and/or going founder mode, [founder mode] made the job increasingly miserable, low ROI.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This type of behavior was identified two years ago in the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b46b87e6-d071-4ee8-8d2e-3b664db64b6d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>“founder mode” essay</span></a><span> by Y Combinator founder, Paul Graham. From it:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“At a Y Combinator event last week Brian Chesky gave a talk that everyone who was there will remember.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The theme of Brian’s talk was that the conventional wisdom about how to run larger companies is mistaken.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In effect, there are two different ways to run a company: founder mode and manager mode. Till now, most people even in Silicon Valley have implicitly assumed that scaling a startup meant switching to manager mode. But we can infer the existence of another mode from the dismay of founders who’ve tried it, and the success of their attempts to escape from it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Whatever founder mode consists of, it’s pretty clear that it’s going to break the principle that the CEO should engage with the company only via his or her direct reports. “Skip-level” meetings will become the norm instead of a practice so unusual that there’s a name for it. And once you abandon that constraint, there are a huge number of permutations to choose from.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Founder mode” is when the founder of a company is extremely hands-on, to the point of micromanaging anything they can or believe they should. In the case of Airbnb, this approach seems to be working. Graham </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b46b87e6-d071-4ee8-8d2e-3b664db64b6d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>stated</span></a><span> that “founder mode” is superior to “manager mode” for startups:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Founder mode will be more complicated than manager mode. But it will also work better. We already know that from the examples of individual founders groping their way toward it.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The problem for VPs, CTOs, et al, is that in “founder mode”, there’s much less room for other senior engineering leaders. </span></strong><span>When a founder overrules or steps over their CTO, VP of Engineering, or head of engineering to directly instruct reports on what to do, this often conflicts with what was agreed with the manager. The jobs of engineering leaders become frustrating, as decisions are frequently countermanded, and time is spent on communicating the confusion to employees.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Undeniably, “founder mode” seems great from the founder’s perspective. Whatever they want done</span><em><span> </span></em><span>gets done </span><em><span>now.</span></em><span> Meanwhile, an experienced engineering leader may decide they’re seen as being in the founder’s way.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>‘Founder mode’ and a great engineering leader from Big Tech are not an ideal match, and it often causes tensions. </span></strong><span>But one tech giant, Apple, operated in what might be considered “founder mode,” for a long time. Again </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b46b87e6-d071-4ee8-8d2e-3b664db64b6d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>from Paul Graham</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“For example, Steve Jobs used to run an annual retreat for what he considered the 100 most important people at Apple, and these were not the 100 people highest on the org chart. Can you imagine the force of will it would take to do this at the average company? And yet imagine how useful such a thing could be. It could make a big company feel like a startup. Steve presumably wouldn’t have kept having these retreats if they didn’t work. But I’ve never heard of another company doing this. So is it a good idea or a bad one? We still don’t know. That’s how little we know about founder mode.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, how do you resolve tension with someone in “founder mode”? I see some pathways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Lean into supporting “founder mode” and proactively change your role. </span></strong><span>Be someone the founder can delegate stuff which they don’t care about, and don’t take it personally when the founder overrules you. Build trust with the founder more than in the past. This is tricky, and there are no guaranteed recipes for success as everyone is different. It might be the only way to stay relatively content in your role for a longer period of time.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Sign out and be an individual contributor (IC).</span></strong><span> Give up the engineering leader title and your direct reports to instead build high-impact things at the company. As a non-manager, you don’t have to worry how the founder manages engineering. Of course, you’ll still be a senior individual contributor and should have excellent business sense and social capital internally, so you can and should get the most complex projects done, and solve pressing problems. Ideally, be a “right hand” of the founder.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Consider quitting if not aligned with the founder, when becoming so seems unlikely. </span></strong><span>You might disagree with actions by the founder that harm the business, which they might be unable or unwilling to see. Or you might disagree with their decisions. Whatever the case, you are misaligned with them, and persisting like this will make it miserable to stay put. This is surely one reason why there’s so much churn within engineering leaderships right now!</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Founder mode makes the VPE and CTO roles “low ROI” at most startups</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A knock-on effect of “founder mode” is that over the past year, VP of Engineering and CTO roles became “low-return-on-investment (ROI).” In lots of smaller and mid-sized companies, founders flipped to ‘founder mode’ and took over directing most of engineering, while existing VPE or CTO folks left after seeing the writing on the wall (they’re no longer needed), or being nudged out or simply fired.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, people talk, and VPE and CTOs share their stories, including with me. It’s evident that over the course of the last decade or so, these roles have gotten pretty high risk, and many VPEs and CTOs who were pushed out of places took on heads of engineering, or Staff+ roles at other companies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now however, founders increasingly realize the benefit of a “right hand” in the form of a VPE or CTO to run the engineering organization, and search for solid VPE and CTO folks pushed out of their previous jobs at startups. These people could do the job, but they no longer want to!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>‘Work at companies that truly want to drive change’</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most engineering leaders I talked with found it tricky to identify a startup to join, but I did hear a success story. A year back, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7475a16f-c5ae-4792-890c-a9b7b27e43ba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Matt Boyle</span></a><span> left Cloudflare to join Gitpod as VP of Engineering. Gitpod was originally known for cloud development environments (CDEs), but with the spread of AI-coding tools, CDEs seem in retreat. Like other non-AI vendors, Gitpod looked at pivoting from “regular” infrastructure to AI infrastructure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few months after Matt joined as VP Eng, the company </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c9bdb35b-0877-4c1e-b71a-acb54b95be18?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>rebranded</span></a><span> to Ona and pivoted to be a platform for background agents. This change went well, and in June, OpenAI </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/71ea1704-5390-4b73-aaeb-acc1611dcf51?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> it would acquire Ona and integrate it as the backend for Codex.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Matt shared with us the questions he asked Gitpod while deciding whether to join:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“My best advice is to join a company that </span></strong><em><strong><span>actually</span></strong></em><strong><span> wants to drive change. </span></strong><span>Avoid joining one that is only planning to change because they </span><em><span>think</span></em><span> they need to, or because everyone around them is doing X or Y. The questions I asked Gitpod’s founders before deciding to join were:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What company are you trying to build over the next year? What about five years?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What is your right to win?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What advantages does Gitpod have that are durable?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What problem are you hiring me to own, and what outcome, specifically?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Which decisions across product, engineering, organization, and customers, can I make without your approval? Where’s the line?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>If I ask others in Leadership to describe my mandate, will they say the same thing as you?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>When we disagree, who makes the final decision, and what evidence would cause you to reconsider?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What would cause you to lose trust in me?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What does ownership mean at Gitpod?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Where are the biggest bottlenecks preventing you from going faster?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Building Ona will require immense talent density, and the profiles we need to hire will be very in-demand. What do you think about this?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Some customers will not want Ona, they will want Gitpod. What do you think about this? When is churn okay, and where do we re-orient?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>If this role fails despite good intentions on both sides, what will be the most likely reason?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>I think the best leaders I have ever worked with stayed “hands-on” in some capacity. In an AI-first world, I believe we all need to spend some time as an IC. Do you agree with this? If so, how have you (or how will we) build it into the company culture?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These questions helped me confirm that the existing leadership had firm beliefs, a plan for an AI-first world, and were running towards this.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Whenever one of the highest-ranked engineering leaders leaves a company, it’s worth asking why it happened. Having talked to many people who decided to leave impressive jobs, my sense is that two factors loom large in people’s reasoning for signing out of their jobs:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The impact AI is having on the business and their role. At companies where business is doing poorly, leaders seek the exit when they know there’s little they can do to stop the ship from sinking.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“Founder mode” sidelines them and makes the role less autonomous and relevant. Founders can be a lot more hands-on; as they (re)take responsibility, the scope of CTOs and VPEs shrinks, and opportunities become scarce.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, it’s worth asking about the impact on an org’s lower levels when there’s more than the usual amount of uncertainty at the top.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Getting hands-on AI experience at places that take a sensible approach to building software with LLM-based tools is table stakes for most engineering leaders to build long-term career stability. The same is true for engineers, I’d argue. If you work somewhere that’s modernizing its infrastructure, challenging how code reviews and deploys are done, how incidents are managed, etc., then that place is pretty close to the cutting edge of the industry.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s fine if that’s not where you work, but the longer you spend at places that are behind in new engineering practices, the harder it will be in the future to make the jump to startups and tech companies that integrate AI into most parts of their development workflows.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I hope this article has been interesting. If you have personal observations on this novel trend, or have experience of anything covered today, post a comment below.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper"
